The classification of websites into three source-based groups followed the categorization framework used in a previous study that assessed Turkish-language websites on anterior cruciate ligament injuries [ ]. In the DISCERN item-level analysis, the lowest mean scores across all website groups were observed in Q4 (source citation), Q5 (date information), Q7 (additional sources), Q11 (treatment risks), and Q15 (support for shared decision-making). These findings suggest that lack of references, absence of publication dates, limited reporting of treatment risks, and insufficient support for shared decision-making may represent common deficiencies in Turkish-language online information about BPPV. Similar gaps have been highlighted in the only previous BPPV-specific study, where Raja and Almansoor (2024) reported that the lowest-scoring DISCERN categories were clarity of aims, referral to areas of uncertainty, support for shared decision-making, and description of treatment risks [ ]. Beyond BPPV, comparable deficiencies have also been documented in evaluations of other Turkish-language websites across different medical fields. For example, studies have noted that websites often lack source citations (Q4) and do not provide dates for information (Q5), and have highlighted that these shortcomings may hinder patients’ access to reliable and current information [ , ]. Similarly, previous studies have also reported low scores for treatment risks (Q11) and support for shared decision-making (Q15), emphasizing that such omissions may lead to patients receiving one-sided or incomplete information [ , ]. As a result, our findings suggest that these deficiencies may increase the risk that patients will rely on outdated or inaccurate content and reduce opportunities for collaborative decision-making in the patient–physician relationship. At the section and total score levels of the DISCERN evaluation, significant source-based differences were observed. In Sect. 1 (reliability), Sect. 3 (overall quality), and the total DISCERN score, non-profit/general websites (Group 3) scored significantly lower than both hospitals/medical centers (Group 1) and individual health professionals (Group 2), whereas Groups 1 and 2 did not differ significantly. These results suggest that non-profit/general websites may lack consistent editorial control, periodic review, or structural quality safeguards. In Sect. 2 (treatment information), however, only individual professionals (Group 2) scored significantly higher than general websites (Group 3), while hospital/medical center websites (Group 1) did not differ from either group. This pattern may indicate that individual professionals tend to provide more detailed treatment-related information. When classified according to DISCERN categories, most websites in our study were of poor quality (40.0%) or fair quality (35.7%), with an additional 17.1% rated as very poor quality. Only a small fraction were categorized as good quality (2.9%) or excellent quality (4.3%). Overall, this distribution is consistent with the findings of Raja and Almansoor (2024), who reported that most English-language BPPV websites were of poor or very poor quality, with only one site rated as good and none rated as excellent [ ]. When evaluated by source, Group 1 (private hospitals/medical centers) and Group 2 (individual health professionals) were predominantly classified in the poor and fair quality categories, whereas Group 3 (non-profit/general health websites) was mainly concentrated in the very poor and poor quality categories. Although this finding is consistent with previous studies reporting source-based differences in quality [ , , , ], the overall results indicate that low quality was common across all groups. In this study, the readability of Turkish-language websites providing information on BPPV was evaluated using the Ateşman and Bezirci-Yılmaz readability formulas, both of which were developed specifically for Turkish [ ]. Although these formulas have limitations in fully assessing comprehension, they have been reported to be sufficient for a basic readability evaluation [ ]. According to the Ateşman formula, websites had a mean readability score of 52.21, corresponding to a “moderately difficult” reading level. A similar finding was reported by Özduran et al. (2022), who evaluated the readability of Turkish internet-based patient education materials on low back pain using the Ateşman formula and found that the texts were generally at a difficult readability level [ ]. Using the Bezirci–Yılmaz formula, websites corresponded to a readability level of approximately 12.22 years of education, equivalent to secondary education. Mean readability scores were statistically similar across website source groups, indicating that readability did not differ meaningfully by source. At the categorical level, the majority of websites (65.7%) were classified as “moderately difficult” by Ateşman, with none categorized as “easy” or “very easy.” Similarly, according to Bezirci-Yılmaz, most websites were classified as “secondary education” (51.4%) or “undergraduate” (40.0%). According to the 2025 Human Development Report, the average duration of education for individuals aged 25 and above in Turkey is approximately 9.0 years [ ]. Thus, the readability level of most websites in our study appears to exceed the national average education level. majority of websites (65.7%) were classified as “moderately difficult” by Ateşman, with none categorized as “easy” or “very easy.” Similarly, according to Bezirci-Yılmaz, most websites were classified as “secondary education” (51.4%) or “undergraduate” (40.0%). According to the 2025 Human Development Report, the average duration of education for individuals aged 25 and above in Turkey is approximately 9.0 years [ ]. Thus, the readability level of most websites in our study appears to exceed the national average education level. These findings are consistent with those reported by Raja and Almansoor (2024), who found that a significant proportion of websites on BPPV had readability levels above recommended reading ages [ ]. Similar distributions were observed across website source groups. These findings suggest that Turkish websites providing information about BPPV generally require at least a secondary education level and may therefore be difficult for the average reader to understand. This study found no statistically significant correlations between DISCERN total scores and readability scores (Ateşman: ρ = 0.004, p = 0.974; Bezirci-Yılmaz: ρ = 0.123, p = 0.311), indicating that quality and readability are independent attributes. This finding is consistent with Raja and Almansoor’s (2024) study, which also identified only weak correlations between readability and quality in online BPPV-related material [ ]. As noted by Raja and Almansoor, the absence of a strong correlation may be concerning. High-quality websites with poor readability may be less accessible to individuals with lower levels of education. Conversely, highly readable yet low-quality content may mislead patients and adversely affect health decisions. Therefore, despite the absence of correlation, it may be important for online health content creators to simultaneously consider both quality and readability. Addressing both aspects could help ensure that online resources are accurate, reliable, and easier to understand, thereby supporting informed decision-making and potentially improving patient outcomes. Emerging digital channels such as AI-generated content and video-sharing platforms have also become important sources of health information, further emphasizing the need to evaluate the quality and readability of online medical content [ , ]. From a practical perspective, the findings of this study may have several implications for different stakeholders involved in the production and dissemination of online health information. Clinicians may consider directing patients to reliable online resources and discussing the limitations of information available online. Health communication specialists and medical content developers may use these findings to improve the clarity, structure, and readability of patient education materials related to BPPV. In addition, digital health platforms and website providers may benefit from adopting clearer quality standards and readability guidelines when presenting patient-oriented information. Such efforts may help improve the accessibility and usefulness of online health information for the general public. Limitations The present study has several limitations. First, the websites were identified on a single date (March 1, 2025). Because online content and search engine algorithms are dynamic, the results represent a snapshot in time and may vary as ranking systems change, potentially influencing which websites users encounter. Second, only three keywords derived from Google Trends were used, and patients may search using alternative terms, which could affect the range of websites retrieved. Third, we included only freely accessible text-based content, excluding subscription-based sources and websites designed specifically for professionals, as well as visual or multimedia materials such as images, videos, and graphics. While this approach provided consistency, it limited the scope of the evaluation. Fourth, although DISCERN provides clear evaluation criteria, scoring involves subjective judgment, which may introduce bias. To minimize this risk, two authors independently performed the assessments, and good inter-rater reliability was achieved. Fifth, the readability evaluation relied on the Ateşman and Bezirci–Yılmaz formulas, which measure structural difficulty but do not fully capture comprehension or health literacy. In addition, readability formulas are based primarily on sentence length and word structure and may not fully reflect how easily readers understand the content. Similarly, although the DISCERN instrument provides standardized criteria for evaluating the quality of consumer health information, it focuses on the presentation and reliability of information rather than its factual accuracy, and scoring may involve a degree of subjective judgment. In addition, readability scores were calculated using a single software tool. Although two validated readability formulas (Ateşman and Bezirci–Yılmaz) were applied, different calculators or readability tools may yield slightly different results [ ]. Sixth, the sample consisted of 70 websites with unequal group sizes, which may not fully represent the breadth of Turkish-language online information on BPPV. Finally, the study was limited to Turkish-language websites on BPPV; therefore, the findings cannot be directly generalized to websites in other languages. However, the results may provide insights that could guide similar evaluations in different linguistic and cultural contexts. Future research should therefore consider longitudinal designs, broader search strategies, inclusion of multimedia and social media content, and additional tools validated for Turkish to provide a more comprehensive evaluation.

Finally, the study was limited to Turkish-language websites on BPPV; therefore, the findings cannot be directly generalized to websites in other languages. However, the results may provide insights that could guide similar evaluations in different linguistic and cultural contexts. Future research should therefore consider longitudinal designs, broader search strategies, inclusion of multimedia and social media content, and additional tools validated for Turkish to provide a more comprehensive evaluation. Strengths of the study This study represents the first evaluation of the quality and readability of Turkish-language online patient information on BPPV. The use of validated readability formulas specifically developed for the Turkish language strengthens the methodological reliability of the findings. In addition, the systematic website selection strategy based on search engine queries provides a realistic representation of the information that internet users are likely to encounter. Conclusion This study is the first evaluation of the quality and readability of Turkish-language websites that provide patient information on BPPV. Overall, the findings indicate that most websites were of poor or fair quality, with transparency, reporting of treatment risks, and support for shared decision-making identified as common deficiencies. Readability levels were generally “moderately difficult” and often exceeded the average educational level in Turkey, suggesting that many patients may find such content challenging to understand. Importantly, no correlation was found between quality and readability, highlighting that these attributes are independent and both require attention. Although professional and institutional websites tended to perform better than general/non-profit sources, poor- and fair-quality content predominated across all groups. These results suggest that source affiliation alone does not guarantee high-quality or easily understandable content. Given these findings, efforts to enhance both the quality and readability of Turkish-language patient information on BPPV may improve accessibility and support informed health decisions. Future studies with broader scope, inclusion of multimedia and social media content, and longitudinal approaches are needed to build on these results and further guide the development of reliable online health resources.

Introduction Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is an inflammatory condition of the sinonasal mucosa, which has been shown to have a high healthcare cost burden, estimated at $11 billion dollars/year in the United States [ , ]. The estimated prevalence of CRS is between 2.1 % and 13.8 % in the United States [ ]. The pathophysiology of CRS is multifactorial, with chronic inflammation secondary to air pollution a plausible cause for increased disease burden. However, the literature specifically looking at CRS pathophysiology and air pollution is limited albeit growing. A recent review paper identified only ten studies looking at CRS outcomes secondary to air pollution [ ]. The articles referenced in this review considered pollutant exposure by small particulate matter (PM2.5), coarse particulate matter (PM 10 ), nitrous oxide (NO x ), and black carbon (BC). Of these PM is the most well studied. For instance, one study by Park et al. [ ] determined that higher levels of PM 10 are associated with higher odds ratios of developing CRS. Current literature also shows that those living in areas of higher air pollution report worsening SNOT-22 scores and seek treatment for symptoms at a higher rate [ , ]. However, literature separated by CRS phenotype, CRS with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) versus without (CRSsNP) is limited. Within the review by Leland et al. [ ], only four studies examined the differing impact of pollution by CRSwNP versus CRSsNP, and three of these were in the same sample [ – ]. Three of these studies found varying degrees of disease burden between populations with CRSwNP demonstrating histopathologic changes not seen in patients with CRSsNP [ , , ]. Velazquez et al. [ ], however, found no significant difference in PM2.5 and BC exposure between CRSwNP versus CRSsNP populations. Yang et al. [ ], though not referenced in Leland et al. [ ], also found in a study of those with CRSwNP versus controls, that increased PM 2.5 exposure was significantly associated with disease manifestation. However, more data examining this specific phenotype of CRS is still required. One metric of air pollution less examined in the literature in relation to CRS is traffic proximity, which is defined in our study as the annual average daily traffic in a specific area [ ]. Unlike particulate matter which is formed from chemical reactions from vehicles and industrial plants, traffic proximity is a variable of pollution secondary to vehicles only [ ]. In order to comprehensively analyze the direct impact of traffic on CRS severity, traffic proximity should be examined as well. Further, the literature does not differentiate the impact of air pollution by CRSwNP and CRSsNP with the limited literature only examining a combined population of those with CRS. The purpose of this study is to utilize data from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to identify the association of traffic proximity and subjective symptom severity measured via the SNOT-22 in a clinical trial database of patients with CRS with nasal polyps (CRSwNP). 2. Methods 2.1. Setting and design The de-identified dataset from the NAVIGATE I and II randomized control trials from the OPTINOSE clinical trials for the Exhalation Delivery System with Fluticasone (EDS-FLU, XHANCE ® ) was used for the analysis [ – ]. An exemption was obtained from the local institutional review board. Included participants in these trials had to be 18 years or older with symptoms of nasal congestion/obstruction meeting subjective criteria of morning score ≥ 2 using a 4-point scale [0, none; 1, mild; 2, moderate; and 3, severe] for ≥5 of the 7 days during screening and bilateral nasal polyps. Patients with asthma or COPD had to have their symptoms well controlled with no exacerbations or use of inhaled corticosteroids exceeding 1000 μg/d for at least 3 months before screening with plans to continue use throughout the study. Participants with >5 sinonasal surgeries (lifetime) or sinonasal surgery in the prior 6 months, septal perforation, or >1 episode of clinical epistaxis within 1 month were excluded from participation in the parent clinical trials. Zip codes of the testing site locations were utilized to limit the current study to participants residing in the United States to allow use of EPA data for pollution analysis. All participants provided ethnicity, race, and sex information. Patients without SNOT-22 scores were excluded from the current analysis. 2.2. Variables and definitions Traffic proximity, the independent variable in our analysis, is defined as average annual daily count of vehicles at major roads within 500 m (or nearest one beyond 500 m) from the study sites divided by distance in meters [ ]. It is a measure of traffic density. Traffic proximity data was downloaded from the United States EPA website and matched to the zip codes of the testing centers that participated in the clinical trials [ ]. The

analysis. All participants provided ethnicity, race, and sex information. Patients without SNOT-22 scores were excluded from the current analysis. 2.2. Variables and definitions Traffic proximity, the independent variable in our analysis, is defined as average annual daily count of vehicles at major roads within 500 m (or nearest one beyond 500 m) from the study sites divided by distance in meters [ ]. It is a measure of traffic density. Traffic proximity data was downloaded from the United States EPA website and matched to the zip codes of the testing centers that participated in the clinical trials [ ]. The NAVIGATE I and NAVIGATE II trials were published in 2018 but the data was collected in 2016. EPA data for 2017 was utilized for comparison. Baseline SNOT-22 scores, the dependent variable examined in the study, was chosen as it is a validated standardized questionnaire with 22 questions developed for use in CRS with or without nasal polyposis. A previous study assessing the validity of SNOT-22 found high internal consistency for preoperative assessment of CRS and concluded that it was a reliable and easy method for assessing CRS symptoms in patients [ ]. For each question, patients select a response from 0 (no problem) to 5 (really bad problem) and these are then summed to form a total score of 0 to 110, with higher scores indicating increasing severity of symptoms [ , ]. Race, ethnicity, and comorbid conditions involving the airway, including asthma, history of rhinitis, and aspirin sensitivity, were extracted from the dataset. 2.3. Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics were estimated, including mean and standard deviation for the dependent variable SNOT-22 and independent variable traffic proximity, and percentages for categorical variables (sex, race, ethnicity, asthma, non-allergic and allergic rhinitis, aspirin/NSAID sensitivity). Multivariable linear regression was used to assess the relationship between traffic proximity and SNOT-22 after controlling for covariates. All analyses were conducted using R version 4.2.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria), with p < 0.05 indicating statistical significance [ ]. 3. Results 3.1. Sample characteristics Of the 181 participants, 44.8 % were female, 55.2 % were male, 84.5 % identified as Non-Hispanic White, 5.5 % identified as Hispanic White, 6.6 % identified as African American, 1.7 % identified as Asian, and 1.7 % identified as other race. The mean SNOT-22 score was 50.0 ± 18.1 across all participants. Descriptive statistics and bivariate associations of sample characteristics with SNOT-22 score and traffic proximity are represented in . Included baseline characteristics are possible confounders of SNOT-22 and were included in the dataset to illustrate prevalence within the sample population. 3.2. Analysis results In bivariate analysis, we found a significant positive correlation (β: 0.003; 95 % CI: 0.0002, 0.006; p = 0.03) between traffic proximity and SNOT-22. This relationship persisted and remained significant in multiple linear regression analyses after controlling for covariates (β: 0.003; 95 % CI: 0.0003, 0.006; p = 0.03) ( ). 4. Discussion This study examined the impact of traffic proximity on CRS severity in exclusively patients with CRSwNP. The advantage of traffic proximity is it is a direct measure of pollution attributable to automobiles. We found a significant relationship on multiple linear regression analysis between increasing traffic proximity correlating with increasing SNOT- 22 scores, indicating worsening disease severity in patients with CRSwNP. Traffic proximity along with PM 2.5 , PM 10 , and NOx are certified measures of air pollution by the EPA. The findings of this study align with prior studies that have looked at the above-mentioned markers. For instance, Padhye et al. [ ] found that higher neighborhood PM 2.5 levels in Chicago, IL were associated with higher incidence of CRS when controlling for asthma and atopy. Their findings were concordant with Zhang et al. [ ], who also controlled for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in addition to asthma. However, both of these studies were limited to specific geographic regions in the United States, and neither of these studies controlled for allergic rhinitis nor did they differentiate participants based on nasal polyposis. Mady et al. [ ] did attempt to differentiate the impact of pollution, specifically looking at BC, on patients with CRSwNP and CRSsNP however found no statistically significant impact of BC in those with CRSwNP. They did demonstrate a trend towards worsening symptom severity and BC exposure in patients with CRSwNP. Their study highlighted an important knowledge gap in understanding the effect of pollution on CRS phenotype. The strengths of our study are that we demonstrated a significant relationship while controlling for confounding variables that may impact perception of or severity of sinonasal symptoms including aspirin/NSAID sensitivity, which has not been controlled for in the current literature. Our study design is another strength as it includes a wide geographical area across the U.S. Participant data and EPA data from 37 zip codes

those with CRSwNP. They did demonstrate a trend towards worsening symptom severity and BC exposure in patients with CRSwNP. Their study highlighted an important knowledge gap in understanding the effect of pollution on CRS phenotype. The strengths of our study are that we demonstrated a significant relationship while controlling for confounding variables that may impact perception of or severity of sinonasal symptoms including aspirin/NSAID sensitivity, which has not been controlled for in the current literature. Our study design is another strength as it includes a wide geographical area across the U.S. Participant data and EPA data from 37 zip codes representing every region in the U.S was utilized in the analysis. We also controlled for CRS phenotype by only examining patients with CRSwNP for which the literature is limited in analysis. Moreover, our study is one of the first to look at the impact of the variable traffic proximity on CRS. Our study has limitations. Our sample size was small and thus may have lacked statistical power. In addition, we focused on SNOT-22 scores, which is a patient-reported health-related quality of life outcome measure and thus may be subject to bias. Our data pool was also from a pre-collected database and the zip codes utilized to match EPA data were of testing centers, not patient home addresses. Despite this, it is plausible to assume patient residences are within the same city or within close proximity to the testing center and less likely to have statistically significantly different air quality. Given the implications of the effect of air pollution on CRSwNP disease severity, our findings highlight the need for increased effort in regulating the quantity of air pollutants. Our findings also underscore the importance of a larger scale study in patients with CRS to better ascertain how and why disease burden may be impacted by traffic and by other air pollutants. Other future directions include examining the effect of pollution on CRS pathogenesis as this is not well understood. Increased eosinophilic aggregates and higher markers of inflammation were noted on histopathologic examination of nasal epithelium in patients with CRS exposed to air pollutants, however further study on how this impacts symptom severity is needed [ ]. 5. Conclusion Our study demonstrated a positive association between air pollution, measured by traffic proximity, and CRSwNP symptom severity, measured via SNOT-22 scores. Our observations are concordant with the data published on CRS outcomes secondary to air pollution. However, the literature examining this subject is limited and our study is one of the first to analyze traffic proximity reported by the EPA as a measure of air pollution in exclusively patients with CRSwNP. The impact of environmental factors such as pollution on CRS is clinically significant as it influences targeted treatment strategies for patients with CRS who present to urban centers versus suburban or rural practices. Further study into how air pollutants impact the nasal epithelium in patients with CRS is required to better understand the pathogenesis of this increased disease burden. Our study fills a knowledge gap in the literature by specifically looking at patients with CRSwNP, however, further work is required to better understand how symptom burden differs between CRSwNP versus CRSsNP.

The articles referenced in this review considered pollutant exposure by small particulate matter (PM2.5), coarse particulate matter (PM 10 ), nitrous oxide (NO x ), and black carbon (BC). Of these PM is the most well studied. For instance, one study by Park et al. [ ] determined that higher levels of PM 10 are associated with higher odds ratios of developing CRS. Current literature also shows that those living in areas of higher air pollution report worsening SNOT-22 scores and seek treatment for symptoms at a higher rate [ , ]. However, literature separated by CRS phenotype, CRS with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) versus without (CRSsNP) is limited. Within the review by Leland et al. [ ], only four studies examined the differing impact of pollution by CRSwNP versus CRSsNP, and three of these were in the same sample [ – ]. Three of these studies found varying degrees of disease burden between populations with CRSwNP demonstrating histopathologic changes not seen in patients with CRSsNP [ , , ]. Velazquez et al. [ ], however, found no significant difference in PM2.5 and BC exposure between CRSwNP versus CRSsNP populations. Yang et al. [ ], though not referenced in Leland et al. [ ], also found in a study of those with CRSwNP versus controls, that increased PM 2.5 exposure was significantly associated with disease manifestation. However, more data examining this specific phenotype of CRS is still required. One metric of air pollution less examined in the literature in relation to CRS is traffic proximity, which is defined in our study as the annual average daily traffic in a specific area [ ]. Unlike particulate matter which is formed from chemical reactions from vehicles and industrial plants, traffic proximity is a variable of pollution secondary to vehicles only [ ]. In order to comprehensively analyze the direct impact of traffic on CRS severity, traffic proximity should be examined as well. Further, the literature does not differentiate the impact of air pollution by CRSwNP and CRSsNP with the limited literature only examining a combined population of those with CRS. The purpose of this study is to utilize data from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to identify the association of traffic proximity and subjective symptom severity measured via the SNOT-22 in a clinical trial database of patients with CRS with nasal polyps (CRSwNP). 2. Methods 2.1. Setting and design The de-identified dataset from the NAVIGATE I and II randomized control trials from the OPTINOSE clinical trials for the Exhalation Delivery System with Fluticasone (EDS-FLU, XHANCE ® ) was used for the analysis [ – ]. An exemption was obtained from the local institutional review board. Included participants in these trials had to be 18 years or older with symptoms of nasal congestion/obstruction meeting subjective criteria of morning score ≥ 2 using a 4-point scale [0, none; 1, mild; 2, moderate; and 3, severe] for ≥5 of the 7 days during screening and bilateral nasal polyps. Patients with asthma or COPD had to have their symptoms well controlled with no exacerbations or use of inhaled corticosteroids exceeding 1000 μg/d for at least 3 months before screening with plans to continue use throughout the study. Participants with >5 sinonasal surgeries (lifetime) or sinonasal surgery in the prior 6 months, septal perforation, or >1 episode of clinical epistaxis within 1 month were excluded from participation in the parent clinical trials. Zip codes of the testing site locations were utilized to limit the current study to participants residing in the United States to allow use of EPA data for pollution analysis. All participants provided ethnicity, race, and sex information. Patients without SNOT-22 scores were excluded from the current analysis. 2.2. Variables and definitions Traffic proximity, the independent variable in our analysis, is defined as average annual daily count of vehicles at major roads within 500 m (or nearest one beyond 500 m) from the study sites divided by distance in meters [ ]. It is a measure of traffic density. Traffic proximity data was downloaded from the United States EPA website and matched to the zip codes of the testing centers that participated in the clinical trials [ ]. The

analysis. All participants provided ethnicity, race, and sex information. Patients without SNOT-22 scores were excluded from the current analysis. 2.2. Variables and definitions Traffic proximity, the independent variable in our analysis, is defined as average annual daily count of vehicles at major roads within 500 m (or nearest one beyond 500 m) from the study sites divided by distance in meters [ ]. It is a measure of traffic density. Traffic proximity data was downloaded from the United States EPA website and matched to the zip codes of the testing centers that participated in the clinical trials [ ]. The NAVIGATE I and NAVIGATE II trials were published in 2018 but the data was collected in 2016. EPA data for 2017 was utilized for comparison. Baseline SNOT-22 scores, the dependent variable examined in the study, was chosen as it is a validated standardized questionnaire with 22 questions developed for use in CRS with or without nasal polyposis. A previous study assessing the validity of SNOT-22 found high internal consistency for preoperative assessment of CRS and concluded that it was a reliable and easy method for assessing CRS symptoms in patients [ ]. For each question, patients select a response from 0 (no problem) to 5 (really bad problem) and these are then summed to form a total score of 0 to 110, with higher scores indicating increasing severity of symptoms [ , ]. Race, ethnicity, and comorbid conditions involving the airway, including asthma, history of rhinitis, and aspirin sensitivity, were extracted from the dataset. 2.3. Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics were estimated, including mean and standard deviation for the dependent variable SNOT-22 and independent variable traffic proximity, and percentages for categorical variables (sex, race, ethnicity, asthma, non-allergic and allergic rhinitis, aspirin/NSAID sensitivity). Multivariable linear regression was used to assess the relationship between traffic proximity and SNOT-22 after controlling for covariates. All analyses were conducted using R version 4.2.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria), with p < 0.05 indicating statistical significance [ ]. 3. Results 3.1. Sample characteristics Of the 181 participants, 44.8 % were female, 55.2 % were male, 84.5 % identified as Non-Hispanic White, 5.5 % identified as Hispanic White, 6.6 % identified as African American, 1.7 % identified as Asian, and 1.7 % identified as other race. The mean SNOT-22 score was 50.0 ± 18.1 across all participants. Descriptive statistics and bivariate associations of sample characteristics with SNOT-22 score and traffic proximity are represented in . Included baseline characteristics are possible confounders of SNOT-22 and were included in the dataset to illustrate prevalence within the sample population. 3.2. Analysis results In bivariate analysis, we found a significant positive correlation (β: 0.003; 95 % CI: 0.0002, 0.006; p = 0.03) between traffic proximity and SNOT-22. This relationship persisted and remained significant in multiple linear regression analyses after controlling for covariates (β: 0.003; 95 % CI: 0.0003, 0.006; p = 0.03) ( ). 4. Discussion This study examined the impact of traffic proximity on CRS severity in exclusively patients with CRSwNP. The advantage of traffic proximity is it is a direct measure of pollution attributable to automobiles. We found a significant relationship on multiple linear regression analysis between increasing traffic proximity correlating with increasing SNOT- 22 scores, indicating worsening disease severity in patients with CRSwNP. Traffic proximity along with PM 2.5 , PM 10 , and NOx are certified measures of air pollution by the EPA. The findings of this study align with prior studies that have looked at the above-mentioned markers. For instance, Padhye et al. [ ] found that higher neighborhood PM 2.5 levels in Chicago, IL were associated with higher incidence of CRS when controlling for asthma and atopy. Their findings were concordant with Zhang et al. [ ], who also controlled for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in addition to asthma. However, both of these studies were limited to specific geographic regions in the United States, and neither of these studies controlled for allergic rhinitis nor did they differentiate participants based on nasal polyposis. Mady et al. [ ] did attempt to differentiate the impact of pollution, specifically looking at BC, on patients with CRSwNP and CRSsNP however found no statistically significant impact of BC in those with CRSwNP. They did demonstrate a trend towards worsening symptom severity and BC exposure in patients with CRSwNP. Their study highlighted an important knowledge gap in understanding the effect of pollution on CRS phenotype. The strengths of our study are that we demonstrated a significant relationship while controlling for confounding variables that may impact perception of or severity of sinonasal symptoms including aspirin/NSAID sensitivity, which has not been controlled for in the current literature. Our study design is another strength as it includes a wide geographical area across the U.S. Participant data and EPA data from 37 zip codes

those with CRSwNP. They did demonstrate a trend towards worsening symptom severity and BC exposure in patients with CRSwNP. Their study highlighted an important knowledge gap in understanding the effect of pollution on CRS phenotype. The strengths of our study are that we demonstrated a significant relationship while controlling for confounding variables that may impact perception of or severity of sinonasal symptoms including aspirin/NSAID sensitivity, which has not been controlled for in the current literature. Our study design is another strength as it includes a wide geographical area across the U.S. Participant data and EPA data from 37 zip codes representing every region in the U.S was utilized in the analysis. We also controlled for CRS phenotype by only examining patients with CRSwNP for which the literature is limited in analysis. Moreover, our study is one of the first to look at the impact of the variable traffic proximity on CRS. Our study has limitations. Our sample size was small and thus may have lacked statistical power. In addition, we focused on SNOT-22 scores, which is a patient-reported health-related quality of life outcome measure and thus may be subject to bias. Our data pool was also from a pre-collected database and the zip codes utilized to match EPA data were of testing centers, not patient home addresses. Despite this, it is plausible to assume patient residences are within the same city or within close proximity to the testing center and less likely to have statistically significantly different air quality. Given the implications of the effect of air pollution on CRSwNP disease severity, our findings highlight the need for increased effort in regulating the quantity of air pollutants. Our findings also underscore the importance of a larger scale study in patients with CRS to better ascertain how and why disease burden may be impacted by traffic and by other air pollutants. Other future directions include examining the effect of pollution on CRS pathogenesis as this is not well understood. Increased eosinophilic aggregates and higher markers of inflammation were noted on histopathologic examination of nasal epithelium in patients with CRS exposed to air pollutants, however further study on how this impacts symptom severity is needed [ ]. 5. Conclusion Our study demonstrated a positive association between air pollution, measured by traffic proximity, and CRSwNP symptom severity, measured via SNOT-22 scores. Our observations are concordant with the data published on CRS outcomes secondary to air pollution. However, the literature examining this subject is limited and our study is one of the first to analyze traffic proximity reported by the EPA as a measure of air pollution in exclusively patients with CRSwNP. The impact of environmental factors such as pollution on CRS is clinically significant as it influences targeted treatment strategies for patients with CRS who present to urban centers versus suburban or rural practices. Further study into how air pollutants impact the nasal epithelium in patients with CRS is required to better understand the pathogenesis of this increased disease burden. Our study fills a knowledge gap in the literature by specifically looking at patients with CRSwNP, however, further work is required to better understand how symptom burden differs between CRSwNP versus CRSsNP.

chunks.content: Ningún fármaco está exento de presentar efectos adversos, de hecho cada año muchos son retirados del mercado por ese motivo. En este trabajo, se analizan 17 medicamentos que no obstante haber sido retirados en otros países, por efectos adversos, continúan disponibles en Argentina no estando justificada su permanencia en el 94% de los casos. El 29% fue retirado por posible efecto carcinogénico. Los prospectos del 65% de los fármacos analizados, no mencionan los efectos adversos motivo de su retiro en otros países. A partir de esta investigación se recomienda, a las autoridades reguladoras sanitarias nacionales, acciones a tomar con estos medicamentos. Por otra parte se advierte a los profesionales de la salud acerca de los riesgos de la permanencia de dichos fármacos en nuestro país. Conceptos clave Qué se sabe sobre el tema: Numerosos fármacos han sido retirados del mercado por sus riesgos de producir efectos adversos graves. Los fármacos son aprobados por las agencias reguladoras nacionales después de haber completado los estudios clínicos en fase III, que brindan principalmente datos de eficacia más que de seguridad. Ningún fármaco puede ser considerado inocuo, cualquiera puede llegar a producir una reacción adversa grave, por razones idiosincrásicas, o bien ser ineficaces por tolerancia o resistencia. Identificar en el mercado farmacéutico argentino (MFA) la presencia de medicamentos retirados en otros países por problemas de seguridad, es de interés a fin de analizar información sobre sus riesgos y proponer recomendaciones. Qué aporta este trabajo: En este trabajo se identifican en el MFA la presencia de 17 medicamentos retirados en otros países por problemas de seguridad, uno de ellos de venta libre. Se revisó la evidencia disponible sobre los riesgos de dichos medicamentos. El prospecto de 11 de los 17 fármacos no menciona los efectos adversos que motivaron su retiro. Se hicieron recomendaciones a la agencia reguladora en relación con estos medicamentos. Se consideró que la permanencia en el MFA de 16 de ellos debería ser reevaluada. Cinco de los 17 medicamentos analizados, fueron retirados de otros países por posible efecto carcinogénico, por lo que su permanencia en el MFA resulta especialmente preocupante. Se advierte a los médicos, acerca de los riesgos de la permanencia de dichos fármacos en nuestro país. INTRODUCCIÓN Numerosos fármacos han sido retirados del mercado por sus riesgos de producir efectos adversos (EA) graves o por falta de eficacia . Los fármacos son aprobados por las agencias reguladoras nacionales (ARN) después de haber completado los ensayos clínicos (EC) en fase III, que brindan principalmente datos de eficacia más que de seguridad . Los trabajos pivotales, son realizados generalmente en unos pocos cientos o miles de pacientes, cantidad insuficiente para detectar EA de menor frecuencia, pero muchas veces graves . La aprobación creciente de medicamentos mediante EC de "no inferioridad", pone en el límite la relación beneficio/riesgo (B/R) con la que dichos fármacos salen al mercado . La suspensión o retiro de la comercialización de medicamentos ya aprobados es realizada por las ARN, los ministerios o secretarías de salud y/o por la industria farmacéutica . Como los estudios clínicos post comercialización son en general insuficientes, poseen importancia los programas de farmacovigilancia (FV), tales como los de las agencias Food and Drug Administration (FDA) en Estados Unidos (EE. UU.) y European Medicines Agency (EMA) en Europa . Ningún fármaco puede ser considerado inocuo, cualquiera puede producir una reacción adversa grave, por razones idiosincrásicas, o bien ser ineficaces por tolerancia o resistencia . En ambos casos existen factores relacionados con el fármaco y sus excipientes, o con el paciente. La presencia de medicamentos que han sido retirados de países de alta vigilancia sanitaria (AVS) expresa una debilidad del funcionamiento del sistema de vigilancia y fiscalización de medicamentos del país . Históricamente, la frecuencia de retiros de medicamentos a nivel mundial osciló entre el 3-4% en un período de 20 años . No existe unanimidad entre las ARN respecto a los criterios para suspender un medicamento del mercado . Existen medicamentos autorizados y en venta en un país y suspendidos en otro, o alertas importantes sobre su seguridad, que no son consideradas en otros países . Onakpoya y colaboradores han revisado extensamente los patrones de retiro de medicamentos post-comercialización, hallando discrepancias e inconsistencias entre países en los fármacos retirados debidos a reacciones adversas. Las ARN de los países de AVS, como EE.UU., Reino Unido, Francia, Noruega, Japón y Australia , son las que proporcionan la mayor parte de la información sobre el retiro de medicamentos, debido a que poseen buenos programas de FV. Veinte años atrás ya se advertía de la presencia de medicamentos con relación B/R inadecuado en Argentina, que habían sido retirados de otros países por EA graves . Los objetivos de este trabajo fueron identificar en el mercado farmacéutico argentino (MFA) la presencia de medicamentos retirados en otros países por problemas de

en los fármacos retirados debidos a reacciones adversas. Las ARN de los países de AVS, como EE.UU., Reino Unido, Francia, Noruega, Japón y Australia , son las que proporcionan la mayor parte de la información sobre el retiro de medicamentos, debido a que poseen buenos programas de FV. Veinte años atrás ya se advertía de la presencia de medicamentos con relación B/R inadecuado en Argentina, que habían sido retirados de otros países por EA graves . Los objetivos de este trabajo fueron identificar en el mercado farmacéutico argentino (MFA) la presencia de medicamentos retirados en otros países por problemas de seguridad, analizar información sobre los aspectos de seguridad que fueron motivo del retiro de estos fármacos y proponer recomendaciones a la ARN. METODOLOGÍA El presente es un estudio observacional, descriptivo, de medicamentos retirados del mercado en otros países y presentes actualmente en el MFA. Se tomó como base una lista de 462 medicamentos retirados por razones de seguridad en uno o más países, entre los años 1953 y 2013, elaborada por Onakpoya y cols. ; se constató su presencia o ausencia en el MFA hasta mayo de 2021 a través de la revisión de los sitios web del Vademécum Nacional de Medicamentos (VNM) de la Agencia Nacional de Medicamentos Alimentos y Tecnología Médica (ANMAT) y del Manual Farmacéutico Alfabeta . Se exploró la comercialización actual de los medicamentos presentes en el MFA, en los sitios web de las agencias reguladoras de EE. UU, Reino Unido, Noruega y en la EMA . En el caso de la EMA, se tuvieron en cuenta aquellos medicamentos autorizados por el mecanismo centralizado o por el propio de cada país. Se definió como objeto de estudio a los medicamentos presentes en el MFA que no estuvieran autorizados en ninguno de estos países de AVS. Nueve revisores se distribuyeron el análisis de las acciones reguladoras a nivel internacional y de las pruebas y fundamentos de los retiros de los medicamentos a evaluar. Se registró la condición de venta de los fármacos presentes en el MFA como de venta libre, venta bajo receta o venta bajo receta archivada. Se analizaron los prospectos que contienen información sobre cada medicamento objeto de este estudio para evaluar la presencia en ellos de la mención del efecto adverso que motivó el retiro en otros mercados. Se consideró que, si al menos uno de los productos comerciales no lo mencionaba, esta información se clasificaría como ausente. Para la revisión de la evidencia disponible, se realizó una búsqueda en Medline desde noviembre de 2020 hasta mayo de 2021, utilizando las palabras claves: Cohort Studies, Case Control Studies, Observational Studies, Case Series, Case Reports, Randomized Controlled Trial, Systematic Review, y la denominación común internacional de cada fármaco. Se complementó con una búsqueda sistemática de información en Trip Database, Cochrane y Epistemonikos. Se procuró identificar los antecedentes bibliográficos de los problemas de seguridad que motivaron el retiro. Se elaboró una breve monografía, con la información recabada de cada fármaco sobre la descripción del medicamento, las acciones reguladoras a nivel internacional, las pruebas disponibles y fundamentos del retiro, conclusiones y recomendaciones. Para esta publicación, se han seleccionado los aspectos centrales de cada fármaco y la bibliografía clave, y se consensuaron recomendaciones que involucran: considerar el retiro del MFA: medicamentos con EA graves que hayan motivado el retiro de los mismos de otros países. considerar la permanencia en el MFA: medicamentos con EA leves. reevaluar la permanencia en el MFA: medicamentos con EA moderados que cuentan con alternativas en el MFA. modificaciones en el prospecto: agregado de información respecto a EA no mencionados, restricciones de uso y/o agregado de advertencias destacadas; en los casos en los que no se recomienda el retiro del medicamento del MFA. RESULTADOS En mayo de 2021 se identificaron en el Manual Farmacéutico Alfabeta 104 de los 462 medicamentos del listado de Onakpoya y cols. , aunque 5 ellos no estaban presentes en el VNM (3 no vigentes, 2 solo como excipientes), resultando en 99 (21,4%) el número de fármacos comercializados efectivamente en el MFA. Se constató que 78 (78,8%) estaban autorizados por al menos una de las agencias reguladoras de referencia consultadas. De los 21 fármacos restantes, 4 estaban aprobados por algún país de la Unión Europea. Los otros 17 fármacos restantes, son el objeto del presente estudio. ( ) ( ) Condición de venta y análisis del prospecto Sólo uno de los medicamentos se comercializa en Argentina como producto de venta libre (acetanilida); los otros 16 son de venta bajo receta y dos de ellos (clofibrato y mazindol), de venta bajo receta archivada. Se encontró que en el prospecto de 11 de los 17 fármacos estudiados (65%) no se hace mención a los EA que motivaron su retiro en otros mercados. Datos principales de las evaluaciones En primer lugar se describen

país de la Unión Europea. Los otros 17 fármacos restantes, son el objeto del presente estudio. ( ) ( ) Condición de venta y análisis del prospecto Sólo uno de los medicamentos se comercializa en Argentina como producto de venta libre (acetanilida); los otros 16 son de venta bajo receta y dos de ellos (clofibrato y mazindol), de venta bajo receta archivada. Se encontró que en el prospecto de 11 de los 17 fármacos estudiados (65%) no se hace mención a los EA que motivaron su retiro en otros mercados. Datos principales de las evaluaciones En primer lugar se describen los productos con potencial efecto carcinogénico como fenazopiridina , fenolftaleína , furazolidona , nitrofurazona y oxeladina que están presentes en el MFA: Fenazopiridina Es un analgésico urinario con escasa evidencia acerca de su eficacia y con un perfil de EA comunes como cefalea, erupciones cutáneas, prurito, vértigo, habiendo sido asociado además con metahemoglobinemia, pancitopenia, insuficiencia renal aguda, insuficiencia hepática, reacciones anafilactoides y anemia hemolítica crónica grave . Se considera posiblemente carcinogénico en humanos . No está incluido en la lista de medicamentos aprobados por FDA pero se comercializa en EE. UU . Fenolftaleína En 1997, el laxante fenolftaleína fue retirado de EEUU, Francia, Canadá, Alemania, Italia y Japón, por el potencial riesgo de carcinogénesis humana . En el año 2000, OMS clasificó a este medicamento, como posiblemente carcinogénico en humanos (grupo 2b) . Furazolidona Este medicamento y sus metabolitos han sido asociados a efectos carcinogénicos y genotóxicos en estudios preclínicos . En Argentina siguen vigentes 2 presentaciones comerciales en comprimidos y suspensión pediátrica. Nitrofurazona Es un antibacteriano de amplio espectro, con poca actividad contra Pseudomona s. Se utiliza para el tratamiento de heridas y quemaduras. En EEUU se ha discontinuado su uso en humanos, por evidencia de su acción mutagénica y carcinogénica en estudios preclínicos . Oxeladina Desde 1991 se informaron los primeros EA, fundamentalmente carcinogénesis y agranulocitosis con citrato de oxeladina , por lo que se retiró del mercado en 1994-1995 en varios países, entre ellos Alemania, Francia, Armenia, Canadá, y Reino Unido. No se identificaron EC de adecuada calidad que analizara el balance beneficio-riesgo de este fármaco. Considerando que fenazopiridina , fenolftaleína , furazolidona , nitrofurazona y oxeladina , han sido asociados a posibles efectos carcinogénicos en humanos y, al contar con opciones terapéuticas de mejor relación beneficio-riesgo, que no poseen este potencial efecto adverso, se recomienda considerar su retiro del MFA. El resto de los fármacos presentes en el MFA y analizados en este trabajo son: Acetanilida En este caso, existe evidencia sólida de sus EA hematológicos (metahemoglobinemia y anemia aplásica) , que han motivado su retiro en numerosos países. Al contar con medicamentos analgésicos y/o antipiréticos con un balance beneficio-riesgo más favorable, se recomienda considerar su retiro del MFA. Clofibrato Existen EC aleatorizados (ECA) que mostraron un aumento de la mortalidad no cardiovascular . Si bien los fibratos son los fármacos de elección para el tratamiento de sujetos hiperlipidémicos con hiperlipoproteinemia tipo III, así como de individuos con hipertrigliceridemia superior a 1.000 mg/dL, que tienen riesgo de pancreatitis, como gemfibrozil, bezafibrato o fenofibrato . En base a esta evidencia se recomienda considerar su retiro del MFA. Cumarina Se constató que fue retirada en varios países entre ellos Francia y Australia, por ser responsable de mortalidad por su hepatotoxicidad . Presenta además, otros EA a nivel del sistema nervioso central, piel, tejido subcutáneo, desórdenes respiratorios y hemorrágicos. Se recomienda considerar su retiro del MFA. Dihidroestreptomicina Si bien no existen actualmente en Argentina presentaciones para su uso sistémico como las que fueron retiradas en otros países, se encuentra en combinaciones a dosis fijas. No se hallaron estudios clínicos de calidad que demuestren su eficacia para el uso por vía local en afecciones intestinales y vaginales. Este medicamento tiene toxicidad renal, auditiva y vestibular mayor que otros aminoglucósidos . Ante la falta de beneficio demostrable y dada su potencial toxicidad, el balance beneficio-riesgo se considera desfavorable. En base a esta evidencia se recomienda considerar su retiro del MFA. Domperidona inyectable Utilizada para el tratamiento de náuseas y vómitos y administrada por vía endovenosa y en dosis superiores a 10 mg se asocia a eventos cardiovasculares graves (prolongación del intervalo QT, arritmia grave) y muerte súbita cardíaca . En EE. UU, no se encuentra aprobada por FDA. Por su baja relación beneficio-riesgo, y su asociación a EA potencialmente mortales, se recomienda considerar su retiro del MFA. Estolato de eritromicina Sus EA por hepatotoxicidad, han sido ampliamente demostrados desde el punto de vista clínico y experimental , llevando a su retiro del mercado farmacéutico de numerosos países. Otras sales de eritromicina también pueden producir el mismo efecto adverso, aunque con menor incidencia. El estolato alcanza concentraciones sanguíneas más altas , lo que podría explicar su mayor toxicidad. Si bien en el
