STATEMENT 10. SURGERY: Clinicians should advocate for surgery as a therapeutic option for patients with dysphonia with conditions amenable to surgical intervention, such as suspected malignancy, symptomatic benign vocal fold lesions that do not respond to conservative management, or glottic insufficiency . Recommendation based on observational studies demonstrating a benefit of surgery in these conditions and a preponderance of benefit over harm . Action Statement Profile: 10 • Quality improvement opportunity : To advocate that clinicians discuss and consider surgery as a therapeutic option for patients with dysphonia whose underlying etiology is amenable to surgical intervention. National Quality Strategy domains: Person and Family Centered Care; Prevention and Treatment of Leading Causes of Morbidity and Mortality. • Aggregate evidence quality : Grade B, in support of surgery to reduce dysphonia and improve voice quality among selected patients based on observational studies overwhelmingly demonstrating the benefit of surgery • Level of confidence in evidence : High • Benefit : Potential for improved voice outcomes among carefully selected patients • Risks, harms, costs : None • Benefits-harm assessment : Preponderance of benefit over harm • Value judgments : Surgical options for treating dysphonia are not always recognized • Intentional vagueness : None • Role of patient preferences : Small • Exclusions : None • Policy level : Recommendation • Differences of opinions : None Supporting Text The purpose of this statement is to encourage clinicians to discuss surgery as a therapeutic option for patients with dysphonia whose underlying etiology is amenable to surgical intervention. Such conditions can be broadly categorized into (1) malignancy, (2) symptomatic benign vocal fold lesions not responsive to conservative management, (3) recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, and (4) glottic insufficiency. Surgery is not the primary treatment for the majority of patients with dysphonia and should be targeted at specific pathologies. Suspected Malignancy Dysphonia may be the presenting symptom in malignancy of the upper aerodigestive tract. Surgical biopsy with histopathologic evaluation is necessary to confirm the diagnosis of malignancy in upper airway lesions. Highly suspicious lesions with increased vasculature, ulceration, or exophytic growth require prompt biopsy. For superficial white lesions (eg, leukoplakia) on otherwise mobile vocal folds, a trial of conservative therapy with avoidance of irritants 346 and treatment of laryngeal candidiasis should be instituted prior to biopsy. 268 , 347 , 348 Once a diagnosis of cancer has been established, additional surgical management is 1 possible treatment. Discussion of surgical management of laryngeal cancer is beyond the scope of this guideline. Benign Soft Tissue Vocal Fold Lesions A trial of conservative management is typically recommended prior to surgical intervention and may obviate the need for surgery. Many benign phonotraumatic vocal fold lesions are self-limited or reversible (eg, polyps, cysts, nodules). 349 - 356 Failure to address underlying etiologies may lead to postsurgical recurrence of some lesions. 323 , 357 - 359 Surgery is reserved for benign vocal fold lesions when a satisfactory voice result cannot be achieved with conservative management (eg, voice therapy) and the voice may be improved with surgical intervention. 349 Effectiveness of surgical treatment for benign vocal fold lesions is based on observational studies of polyps, cysts, and nodules refractory to conservative management. 360 - 362 Surgery can improve subjective voice-related QOL and objective vocal parameters among patients with dysphonia that results from benign vocal fold lesions. 361 - 365 Nodules are common in the pediatric population and, as with adults, are treated conservatively. Also as with adults, surgery should be reserved for severe cases refractory to conservative treatment. 366 Parents should be counseled that pediatric nodules typically resolve over time during normal developmental process 367 and that voice therapy should be considered the primary treatment. 368 The role of surgery for pediatric vocal nodules is limited. However, a paucity of data from small case series does demonstrate that pediatric nodules may be effectively removed via microsurgical approaches. 369 Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis Surgery is necessary in the management of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, a typically benign but aggressive neoplasm of the upper airway more commonly seen in children. Surgical removal with contemporary laryngeal instruments, including laser and microdebrider, can prevent airway obstruction and is effective in reducing the symptoms of dysphonia but is unlikely to be curative since the causative human papillomavirus is present in adjacent normal-appearing mucosa. 370 - 372 Because of the recurrent nature of this condition, it is imperative that every effort be made to

demonstrate that pediatric nodules may be effectively removed via microsurgical approaches. 369 Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis Surgery is necessary in the management of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, a typically benign but aggressive neoplasm of the upper airway more commonly seen in children. Surgical removal with contemporary laryngeal instruments, including laser and microdebrider, can prevent airway obstruction and is effective in reducing the symptoms of dysphonia but is unlikely to be curative since the causative human papillomavirus is present in adjacent normal-appearing mucosa. 370 - 372 Because of the recurrent nature of this condition, it is imperative that every effort be made to avoid injury to the underlying vibratory layers of the vocal folds to avoid long-term dysphonia related to scar formation. Glottic Insufficiency Glottic insufficiency generally means incomplete closure of the vocal folds. There are several etiologies, including impaired vocal fold mobility (eg, paralysis or paresis), bowing, and vocal fold soft tissue defects. This condition can result in a weak, breathy dysphonia with poor cough, dyspnea, and dysphagia. 24 , 60 , 139 , 140 , 146 Surgical correction of glottic insufficiency by medialization techniques can be done unilaterally or bilaterally and works by reducing the glottic opening during phonatory tasks to improve vocal efficiency. Vocal fold medialization can be achieved with temporizing injection of bulking agents into the affected vocal fold (injection medialization) or external medialization with open surgery (laryngeal framework surgery). Injection medialization can be safely performed in the office under local anesthesia or in the operating room under general anesthesia, 373 - 375 which generally provides comparable improvement in voice. 373 , 376 - 383 Collagen or lyophilized dermis injections can provide adequate vocal rehabilitation of pediatric patients. 384 The use of polytetrafluoroethylene as a permanent injectable implant is not recommended due to its association with foreign body granulomas that can result in voice deterioration and airway compromise. 385 - 387 Open medialization laryngoplasty (ie, type I laryngoplasty or thyroplasty, with or without arytenoid adduction) with a variety of implants demonstrated dysphonia reduction in appropriately selected patients. 388 - 391 Additionally, laryngeal reinnervation is a treatment option for patients with unilateral and bilateral vocal fold paralysis in addition to static procedures. 392 - 395 When analyzed by trained blinded listeners, the voices of 15 patients who underwent external laryngoplasty were indistinguishable from controls in loudness and pitch but had higher levels of strain and breathiness. 396 In all, 92% of patients reported satisfaction, but 87% still considered their voices abnormal. In a retrospective study of 117 patients with glottic insufficiency, patients who underwent type I laryngoplasty demonstrated better symptom resolution when compared with patients receiving voice therapy alone. 397 Survey data suggest a 5.4% revision rate for laryngoplasty. 398 STATEMENT 11. BOTULINUM TOXIN: Clinicians should offer, or refer to a clinician who can offer, botulinum toxin injections for the treatment of dysphonia caused by SD and other types of laryngeal dystonia . Recommendation based on RCTs with minor limitations and preponderance of benefit over harm . Action Statement Profile: 11 • Quality improvement opportunity : To expedite referral for suspected SD. National Quality Strategy domains: Person and Family Centered Care; Prevention and Treatment of Leading Causes of Morbidity and Mortality. • Aggregate evidence quality : Grade B, few controlled trials, diagnostic studies with minor limitations, and overwhelmingly consistent evidence from observational studies • Level of confidence in evidence : High • Benefit : Improved voice quality and voice-related QOL • Risks, harms, costs : Dysphagia, airway obstruction, breathy voice, direct costs of treatment, time off work, and indirect costs of repeated treatments • Benefits-harm assessment : Preponderance of benefit over harm • Value judgments : Botulinum toxin is beneficial despite the potential need for repeated treatments given the limited availability of other effective interventions for SD • Intentional vagueness : None • Role of patient preferences : Large • Exclusions : Allergy to botulinum toxin • Policy level : Recommendation • Differences of opinions : None Supporting Text The purpose of this statement is to expeditiously direct patients with suspected SD/laryngeal dystonia to clinicians who can diagnose the condition and offer treatment with laryngeal botulinum toxin injection. SD is a focal laryngeal dystonia most commonly characterized by a strained, strangled voice. 399 Patients demonstrate increased tone and voice breaks in the intralaryngeal muscle groups responsible for either opening (abductor SD) or closing (adductor SD) the vocal folds. This results in phonemic task-specific dysphonia; that is, affected patients experience voice breaks from voiceless consonants (abductor) or on vowels and voiced consonants (adductor). 400 The diagnosis can be subtle and masquerade as other forms of dysphonia (eg, MTD), which can cause significant delays in diagnosis, averaging 4.4 years. 401 Intramuscular injection of botulinum toxin into the affected muscles causes transient nondestructive flaccid paralysis of these muscles by inhibiting the release of

strangled voice. 399 Patients demonstrate increased tone and voice breaks in the intralaryngeal muscle groups responsible for either opening (abductor SD) or closing (adductor SD) the vocal folds. This results in phonemic task-specific dysphonia; that is, affected patients experience voice breaks from voiceless consonants (abductor) or on vowels and voiced consonants (adductor). 400 The diagnosis can be subtle and masquerade as other forms of dysphonia (eg, MTD), which can cause significant delays in diagnosis, averaging 4.4 years. 401 Intramuscular injection of botulinum toxin into the affected muscles causes transient nondestructive flaccid paralysis of these muscles by inhibiting the release of acetylcholine from nerve terminals, thus reducing the spasm. 402 SD is a disorder of the central nervous system that cannot be cured by botulinum toxin, 403 but excellent symptom control is possible with 3 to 6 months of interval treatment. 404 Injections can be performed on awake ambulatory patients with minimal discomfort. 405 While this treatment is not currently FDA approved for SD, a large body of evidence supports the efficacy of botulinum toxin (primarily botulinum toxin A) as an off-label use for treating adductor SD. The off-label use of botulinum toxin for SD/laryngeal dystonia is approved by the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Two double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trials of botulinum toxin for adductor SD with self-assessment and expert listeners found improved voice among patients treated with botulinum toxin injections. 406 , 407 Botulinum toxin treatment has also been shown to improve self-perceived dysphonia, mental health, and social functioning. 408 A meta-analysis concluded that botulinum toxin treatment of SD results in “moderate overall improvement”; however, it noted concerns of methodological limitations and lack of standardization in assessment of botulinum toxin efficacy and recommended caution when making inferences regarding treatment benefit. 326 Despite these limitations, botulinum toxin is considered the “treatment of choice” for adductor SD. 403 - 405 , 409 In the last 7 years since the 2009 publication of this guideline, the use of botulinum toxin for SD has continued and expanded to other indications. Large case series of SD patients followed over several decades documented its safety and effectiveness. 410 - 413 Botulinum toxin may be used for other disorders of excessive or inappropriate muscular contraction. 402 There are numerous reports addressing the use of botulinum toxin for spastic dysarthria, nerve section failure, anterior commissure release, adductor breathing dystonia, abductor SD, ventricular dysphonia (also called dysphonia plica ventricularis), essential voice tremor, chronic cough, bilateral vocal fold paralysis, 381 , 396 , 397 , 414 - 421 and granuloma. 323 , 422 Botulinum toxin injections have a good safety record. Blitzer et al 423 reported in 1998 their 13-year experience with 901 patients who underwent 6300 injections and updated this in 2010 to a 24-year experience of 1300 patients. 410 Adverse effects included mild breathiness (25%) and coughing on fluids (10%) for the patients with adductor SD and “mild stridor” for the patients with abductor SD. 423 Many other studies documented similar rates of adverse effects (breathiness and dysphagia, choking on fluids). 424 - 429 Postinjection dysphagia may be more common among patients with preexisting dysphagia. 430 Exertional wheezing, exercise intolerance, and stridor were more commonly reported for patients with abductor SD. 423 , 431 Adverse events may result from diffusion of drug from the target muscle to adjacent muscles (“black box warning” by the FDA). 402 Adjusting the dose, distribution, and timing of injections may decrease the frequency of adverse events. 429 , 432 Bleeding is rare, and vocal fold edema was documented for only 1 patient receiving saline as a placebo. 406 Reports of sensations of burning, tickling, irritation of the larynx or throat, excessive thick secretions, and dryness also occurred. 433 Systemic effects are rare, with only 2 reports of generalized botulism-like syndromes and 1 report of possible precipitation of biliary colic. 402 Acquired resistance to botulinum toxin can occur. 402 , 434 This can be successfully managed by changing to another botulinum toxin product or by extending the interval before resuming treatment. 435 Dedo began surgical treatment of adductor SD with unilateral resection of the recurrent laryngeal nerve. 436 This fell out of favor, as high relapse rates were subsequently reported 437 and botulinum toxin injection began use in the 1980s. Some patients do not like the temporary and variable effect of botulinum toxin or do not tolerate its side effects. For these patients, surgical treatments are available that provide the possibility of a long-lasting and stable result. These include bilateral selective laryngeal adductor denervation/reinnervation (SLADR) 438 - 440 and type II thyroplasty. 441 , 442 Medications to treat SD, as used for other forms of dystonia, were described in small series 443 , 444 and case reports, 445 but clinical trials have not been conducted. STATEMENT 12. EDUCATION/PREVENTION: Clinicians should inform patients with dysphonia about control/preventive measures . Recommendation based on observational studies, small-sample RCTs, expert opinion, and a preponderance of benefit over harm . Action Statement Profile: 12 • Quality improvement opportunity : To provide guidance to clinicians in educating patients on behavioral strategies and environmental measures that may prevent or decrease the risk of dysphonia. National Quality Strategy domains: Person and Family Centered Care; Prevention and Treatment of Leading Causes of Morbidity and Mortality. • Aggregate evidence quality : Grade C, evidence based on observational studies, small-sample RCTs, expert opinion, and a preponderance of benefit over harm • Level of confidence in evidence : High • Benefit : Possible decreased risk of recurrence of dysphonia; improved vocal hygiene may reduce dysphonia; possible prevention of dysphonia for persons at high risk • Risks, harms, costs : Time of education; cost of potentially ineffective interventions • Benefits-harm assessment : Preponderance of benefit over harm • Value judgments : None • Intentional vagueness : None • Role of patient preferences : Small role in terms of receiving information from clinician; moderate to large role in shared decision making that involves choosing specific preventive and control measures to use • Exclusions : None • Policy level : Recommendation • Differences of opinions : None Supporting Text The purpose of this statement is to provide guidance to clinicians in educating patients on behavioral strategies and environmental measures that may prevent or decrease the risk of developing dysphonia and promoting factors that encourage vocal health. Clinicians should document specific measures discussed in this educational conversation with the patient. Optimization of vocal health should be encouraged for all individuals but particularly those at greatest risk for developing dysphonia (eg, teachers, singers, elderly). Dysphonia risk factors relate to behavioral, environmental, and lifestyle choices. Voice hygiene measures include behaviors designed to decrease tissue injury and prevent dysphonia while promoting strategies that improve vocal health. 446 Preventive measures, such as adequate hydration, avoidance of irritants, voice training, and amplification, may reduce the risk of developing dysphonia. Behaviors to avoid include yelling or shouting, consumption of alcohol and caffeine products, smoking, use of certain drying medications, and dehydration ( Table 9 ). In a study of 422 teachers, absence of water intake was associated with a 60% higher risk of dysphonia, 447 while a study of amateur singers demonstrated less vocal fatigue with hydration and periods of voice rest. 448 Phonatory effort may also be decreased by adequate hydration, 449 and amplification may sustain voice quality during heavy use. 450 One RCT did find benefits of voice hygiene education among healthy student teachers; however, the small sample size prevented any inferential statistical analysis of the data. 446 The relationship of physical activity on the voice was examined in 1 large cross-sectional study of teachers. Researchers found that individuals who do regular physical exercise, ≥3 times a week, had a lower prevalence of dysphonia. 451 These findings clearly warrant further investigation regarding the possible role that routine physical activity plays in voice hygiene. Use of drying medications In addition, environmental conditions can affect the voice, such as background noise, poor air quality, and dryness. 452 - 454 Exposure to large amounts of environmental or occupational irritants, such as chemicals, smoke, particulates, and pollution, can increase the likelihood of developing dysphonia. One study of 10 symptomatic rescue workers at the World Trade Center disaster site associated the development of vocal cord dysfunction and hoarseness with exposure to large amounts of irritants found at the recovery site. 455 Dry or arid environments may also adversely affect the voice. Environmental humidification had some beneficial effects on superficial laryngeal dehydration, which may help prevent or reduce negative voice changes. 456 On the basis of the report of the surgeon general, 457 the CPG update panel concurred that avoidance of tobacco smoke (primary or secondhand) was beneficial to decrease the risk of dysphonia despite limited direct evidence in the literature. STATEMENT 13. OUTCOMES: Clinicians should document resolution, improvement, or worsened symptoms of dysphonia or change in QOL among patients with dysphonia after treatment or observation . Recommendation based on randomized trials and cohort studies with a preponderance of benefit over harm . Action Statement Profile: 13 • Quality improvement opportunity : To ensure that patients with dysphonia are followed until the dysphonia has improved or resolved or the underlying condition has been diagnosed and appropriately managed. National Quality Strategy domain: Effective Communication and Care Coordination. • Aggregate evidence quality : Grade C, recommendation based on randomized trials and cohort studies with a preponderance of benefit over harm • Level of confidence in evidence : High • Benefit : Document the final status of dysphonia, communicate with referring clinicians, document favorable outcomes or failures of treatment • Risks, harms, costs : Cost of follow-up visits • Benefits-harm assessment : Preponderance of benefit over harm • Value judgments : None • Intentional vagueness : The time frame for assessing outcome is not stated • Role of patient preferences : Small • Exclusions : None • Policy level : Recommendation • Differences of opinions : None Supporting Text The purpose of this statement is to ensure that patients with dysphonia are followed until the dysphonia has improved or resolved or the underlying condition has been diagnosed and appropriately managed. The responsible primary or specialty clinician to whom the patient has been referred should follow and document resolution of the dysphonia. In the setting of new-onset dysphonia, clinicians should document the status of the voice disorder and its resolution within a few weeks of symptom onset. If there is not resolution, clinicians should perform, or refer to a specialist for, laryngoscopy (KAS 4A/4B). Rationale for referral should be clearly documented. Follow-up on status and outcome of management may be in person or through telephone communication as appropriate. For patients with persistent dysphonia, an underlying diagnosis must be sought, as detailed throughout this guideline. Management strategies will depend on the underlying cause of the dysphonia and may widely differ. The managing clinician should follow up with patients after any intervention (eg, medications, surgery, voice therapy) and document the outcome of the treatment. Objective tools may be used for this purpose. Several validated patient-reported outcome measures are available to systematically assess voice, 458 but their use is not necessary to document resolution. If the patient has been referred to a provider with more advance training or capabilities, the clinician who ultimately treats the patient should document the outcome of therapy and communicate those results back to the referring clinician. A full-text version of the guideline will also be accessible free of charge at www.entnet.org . An anticipated barrier to diagnosis is distinguishing modifying factors for dysphonia in a busy clinical setting. This barrier may be mitigated through a laminated teaching card or visual aid summarizing important factors that modify management. Laryngoscopy is an option at any time for patients with dysphonia, but the guideline also recommends that no patient be allowed to wait >4 weeks prior to having his or her larynx examined. It is also clearly recommended that if there is a concern of an underlying serious condition, then laryngoscopy should be immediate. Tables in this guideline regarding causes for concern should help guide clinicians regarding when prompt laryngoscopy is warranted. The cost of the laryngoscopy and the possible wait times to see clinicians trained in the technique may hinder access to care. While the guideline acknowledges that there may be a significant role for antireflux therapy to treat laryngeal inflammation, empiric use of antireflux medications for dysphonia has minimal support and a growing list of potential risks. Avoidance of empiric use of antireflux therapy represents a significant change in practice for some clinicians. Educational pamphlets describing the risks and benefits of these medications may help facilitate this potential change in practice pattern. Lack of knowledge about voice therapy by practitioners is a likely barrier to advocacy for its use. This barrier can be overcome by educational materials about voice therapy and its indications. Hoarseness (dysphonia) clinical practice guideline algorithm. H&P, history and physical examination; KAS, key action statement. Research Needs While there is a body of literature from which these recommendations were drawn, significant gaps in our knowledge about dysphonia and its management remain. The guideline committee identified several areas where further research would improve the ability of clinicians to optimally treat patients with dysphonia. 1: Escalation of Care and Laryngoscopy and Dysphonia (KASs 3 and 4) Little is known about the natural history of voice disorders; thus, research is needed to better understand the normal course of these conditions to determine when and if early referral is helpful and/or if early intervention (eg, voice therapy, medical management, surgery) is effective at increasing the QOL or reducing health consequences related to other underlying conditions. A need exists to better define what “warning signs” and indications should prompt early referral for laryngoscopy. Moreover, education and dissemination of these “warning signs” and indications are important, and effective approaches should be investigated. 2: Antireflux Medication and Dysphonia (KAS 6) There is a need for a consistent “gold standard” definition of what constitutes LPR to reduce heterogeneity among comparative studies. This would allow for better estimates of disease burden and the degree of association with dysphonia and to determine what indications and what interventions are effective at treating this condition. Without an agreed-on definition, it is difficult to design rigorous comparative treatment and outcome studies. 3: Corticosteroids and Antibiotics in Treatment of Dysphonia (KASs 7 and 8) Research is needed to better understand the variation and overuse of antibiotics and steroids for acute laryngitis. Educational efforts should be directed at reducing their use and promoting conservative management in acute laryngitis. Despite frequency of corticosteroid therapy for acute or chronic laryngitis and for other voice disorders by various clinical specialties, little literature supports its use for these indications. Research is needed to better understand its effectiveness (benefits and harms) in this setting and for which indications they should be considered and/or avoided. 4: Surgery (KAS 10) Outcomes are difficult to compare for surgery, due to heterogeneity in the number and quality of outcome measures used. This is an issue for patient-centered outcomes and for “objective measures” (eg, cepstral analysis, aerodynamics). A better understanding of and standardization of what benign lesions are amenable to surgery is needed. Furthermore, more research is needed to understand the effectiveness (benefits and harms) of less invasive treatments

This is an issue for patient-centered outcomes and for “objective measures” (eg, cepstral analysis, aerodynamics). A better understanding of and standardization of what benign lesions are amenable to surgery is needed. Furthermore, more research is needed to understand the effectiveness (benefits and harms) of less invasive treatments (office based or medical therapy) for these conditions. 5: Botulinum Toxin (KAS 11) A need exists to better understand the pathophysiology of laryngeal dystonia to develop more effective treatments. It is also necessary to learn about which patients and factors predict better or worse outcomes with botulinum toxin and what other alterative interventions might be beneficial to this patient population. 6: Education/Prevention (KAS 12) Prevention and education are paramount to reducing the burden of disease and disease recidivism. This requires a clearer understanding of preventive factors, healthy behaviors, and effective methods to effect and disseminate this information. In addition, it is important to better understand what factors increase the likelihood of developing voice disorders such that these groups can be targeted for educational and preventive interventions. Further work is needed to better understand the underpinnings of MTD and functional dysphonia to help in prevention, education, and the management of these conditions. 7: Outcomes (KAS 13) Outcome assessment in voice disorders needs to be better standardized and refined. Patient-centered outcome measures and instrumental assessment need to be carefully and rigorously evaluated to determine their usefulness and reasonableness at the point of care. Better standardization of measurement would allow for better comparison across treatment and to better define disease severity and affect patient QOL and function. Disclaimer This CPG is not intended as an exhaustive source of guidance for managing dysphonia (hoarseness). Rather, it is designed to assist clinicians by providing an evidence-based framework for decision-making strategies. The guideline is not intended to replace clinical judgment or establish a protocol for all individuals with this condition and may not provide the only appropriate approach to diagnosing and managing this program of care. As medical knowledge expands and technology advances, clinical indicators and guidelines are promoted as conditional and provisional proposals of what is recommended under specific conditions, but they are not absolute. Guidelines are not mandates. These do not and should not purport to be a legal standard of care. The responsible physician, in light of all circumstances presented by the individual patient, must determine the appropriate treatment. Adherence to these guidelines will not ensure successful patient outcomes in every situation. The AAO-HNSF emphasizes that these clinical guidelines should not be deemed to include all proper treatment decisions or methods of care or to exclude other treatment decisions or methods of care reasonably directed to obtaining the same results. Appendix: Frequently Asked Questions about Voice Therapy Why Is Voice Therapy Recommended for Dysphonia? Voice therapy has been demonstrated to be effective for dysphonia across the life span from children to older adults. A1 , A2 Voice therapy is the first line of treatment for vocal fold lesions, such as vocal nodules, polyps, or cysts. A3 , A4 These lesions often occur in people with vocally intense occupations, including teachers, attorneys, and clergy. A5 Another possible cause of these lesions is vocal overdoing, commonly seen in sports enthusiasts; in socially active, aggressive, or loud children; or in high-energy adults who often speak loudly. A6 - A9 Voice therapy, specifically the Lee Silverman voice therapy method, has been demonstrated to be the most effective method of treating the lower-volume, lower-energy, and rapid-rate voice/speech of individuals with Parkinson’s disease. A10 , A11 Voice therapy has been used to treat dysphonia concurrently with other medical therapies, such as botulinum toxin injections for SD and/or tremor. A12 , A13 Voice therapy has been used alone in the treatment of unilateral vocal fold paralysis, A14 , A15 presbyphonia, A16 and vocal process granuloma, A17 and it has been used to improve the outcome of surgical procedures, as in vocal fold augmentation A18 or thyroplasty. A19 Voice therapy is an important component of any comprehensive surgical treatment for dysphonia. A20 What Happens in Voice Therapy? Voice therapy is a program designed to reduce dysphonia through guided change in vocal behaviors and lifestyle changes. Voice therapy consists of a variety of tasks designed to eliminate harmful vocal behavior, shape healthy vocal behavior, and assist in vocal fold wound healing after surgery or injury. Voice therapy for dysphonia generally consists of 1 or 2 therapy sessions each week for 4 to 8 weeks. A21 The duration of therapy is determined by the origin of the dysphonia and severity of the problem, co-occurring medical therapy, and, importantly, patient commitment to the practice and generalization of new vocal behaviors outside the therapy session. A22 Who Provides Voice Therapy? Certified and licensed SLPs are health care professionals with the expertise needed to provide effective behavioral treatment for dysphonia. A23 How Do I Find a Qualified SLP Who Has Experience in Voice? ASHA is an excellent resource for finding a certified SLP by going to the ASHA website ( www.asha.org ) or by accessing ASHA’s online search engine, called ProFind at http://www.asha.org/profind/ . You may also contact ASHA’s Action Center, Monday through Friday (8:30 am –5:00 pm ) at 800-498-2071; fax, 301-296-8580; TTY (text telephone communication device), 301-296-5650; email, [email protected] . Does Insurance Cover Voice Therapy? Generally, Medicare, under the guidelines for coverage of speech therapy, will cover voice therapy if provided by a certified and licensed SLP, if ordered by a physician, and if deemed medically necessary for the diagnosis. Medicaid varies from state to state but generally covers voice therapy, under the rules for speech therapy, up to the age of 18 years old. It is best to contact your local Medicaid office, as there are state differences and program differences. Private insurance companies vary, and the consumer is guided to contact her or his insurance company for specific guidelines for the purchased policies. Are Speech Therapy and Voice Therapy the Same? Speech therapy is a term that encompasses a variety of therapies, including voice therapy. Most insurance companies refer to voice therapy as speech therapy , but they are the same thing if provided by a certified and licensed SLP. Appendix References A1. Thomas LB, Stemple JC. documents.title: AAO-HNS clinical consensus on vocal fold paralysis

chunks.content: Background Unilateral vocal cord paralysis (UVCP) occurs when the motor nerve pathways controlling the laryngeal muscles are damaged, causing dysfunction in one vocal cord and impaired glottic closure [ – ]. This condition often manifests as hoarseness and swallowing difficulties, significantly impacting patients’ quality of life [ – ]. Currently, UVCP diagnosis and assessment primarily rely on laryngoscopy, a procedure that is both invasive and dependent on the advanced technical skills of specialized clinicians. Furthermore, the high cost of laryngoscopic equipment poses a barrier to its widespread adoption in primary healthcare settings and regions with limited resources, often resulting in delayed diagnosis and treatment for affected individuals [ ]. With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare [ ], automated methods using voice signal features have emerged as a promising approach for diagnosing and assessing UVCP. These tools offer significant advantages over traditional laryngoscopic examinations by enabling remote and frequent assessments, making them especially valuable in settings with limited resources or a shortage of specialized physicians [ ]. Although voice analysis cannot yet fully replace laryngoscopy, its non-invasive nature, simplicity, and low cost [ ] make it an effective supplementary tool in primary healthcare. It allows healthcare providers to perform initial assessments of UVCP severity and facilitates the monitoring of treatment progress, improving accessibility and continuity of care. Deep learning (DL), as a key branch of AI, enables the learning of complex information through multilayer neural networks. It has proven highly effective in tasks like speech recognition, image classification, and natural language processing [ – ]. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), a prominent DL architecture, excel in feature extraction, making them widely applicable for processing acoustic signals [ ]. Studies show that CNN-based models can identify diseases from speech signals, such as Parkinson’s disease [ ], depression, and other mental health conditions [ ]. Additionally, CNNs have shown strong performance in recognizing abnormal voice signals [ – ] and significant progress in classifying voice disorders. For example, Hu et al. [ ] developed a CNN model to classify voice signals from healthy individuals, patients with vocal cord atrophy, and UVCP, achieving 66.9% accuracy. Similarly, Jaemin et al. [ ] showed CNNs’ potential in differentiating laryngeal cancer, UVCP, and benign lesions, achieving 75% accuracy. These findings highlight CNNs’ expanding role in diagnosing and classifying voice disorders. Feature extraction is critical for enhancing model performance in voice signal processing tasks. Traditional acoustic features like fundamental frequency (F0), harmonic-to-noise ratio (HNR), and linear predictive cepstral coefficients (LPCC) are commonly used but often result in information loss or bias [ , ]. In contrast, the Mel-spectrogram captures comprehensive speech information in the time–frequency domain, preserving voice data integrity. Several studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of combining Mel-spectrograms with CNNs in disease diagnosis. For instance, Chen et al. [ ] reported a 92% recognition accuracy for abnormal voice detection. Similarly, Aseel et al. [ ] achieved a 97% accuracy rate in diagnosing COVID-19, Kim et al. [ ] reported an 85% accuracy rate in detecting laryngeal cancer, and Peng et al. [ ] achieved a remarkable 99.46% accuracy in classifying four voice types: healthy, hyperkinetic dysphonia, hypokinetic dysphonia, and flux laryngitis. These findings emphasize the potential of Mel-spectrograms as a reliable feature extraction method for voice-based disease diagnostics. Building on prior research, this study presents a method that integrates the constructed CNN model TripleConvNet with Mel-spectrograms and their first- and second-order differential features to assess the severity of UVCP. Incorporating first- and second-order differential features enhances the model’s ability to capture dynamic changes in speech signals, addressing the limitations of traditional convolutional networks in handling dynamic information. This design supports accurate classification of UVCP severity, offering strong technical support for disease evaluation. Beyond improving diagnostic efficiency for UVCP, this approach opens new avenues for automated voice pathology assessment and drives advancements in intelligent systems for this field. Result Experimental results for binary classification task In the binary classification task, individuals with well-compensated vocal cords and healthy participants were categorized as the “non-medical intervention group”, while those with insufficient compensation (decompensated and partially compensated states) were classified as the “medical intervention group”. As shown in Table , using only Mel-spectrogram features, the model achieved 94.1% accuracy, 0.945 sensitivity, 0.945 specificity, and an F1-score of 0.939. Adding first- and second-order differential features improved performance further, increasing accuracy to 95.4%, sensitivity to 0.957, specificity to 0.957, and the F1-score to 0.953. These findings demonstrate that first- and second-order differential features enhance the model’s ability to detect subtle differences between compensated and decompensated states, improving classification performance overall. These differences support the model's ability to distinguish effectively between the “medical intervention group” and the “non-medical intervention group”. Experimental results for three-class classification task To classify varying degrees of vocal cord paralysis, we conducted a three-class classification experiment to distinguish among compensatory, partially compensatory, and decompensatory states based on speech signals. As shown in Table , when the input features consisted solely of the Mel-spectrogram, the model achieved an accuracy of 80.3%, sensitivity of 0.801, specificity of 0.901, and an F1-score of 0.800. Incorporating first- and second-order differential features improved performance, with accuracy rising to 84.2%, sensitivity to 0.839, specificity to 0.921, and an F1-score to 0.840. Figures and present the ROC curve and confusion matrix, illustrating the model’s classification capabilities and error distribution, highlighting the enhanced discriminative power of first- and second-order differential features. Table reports that the Minkowski distance between the compensated and partially compensated states is 78.19, the Euclidean distance is 27.62, the cosine distance is 0.0039, and the correlation distance is 0.0041, indicating a close relationship between the two states. In contrast, the Minkowski distance between the decompensated and partially compensated states is 69.45, the Euclidean distance is 27.76, the cosine distance is 0.0023, and the correlation distance is 0.0025. These results indicate that the partially compensated and decompensated states have a higher degree of feature space overlap, making their differentiation more challenging in the three-class classification task. However, incorporating first- and second-order differential features allowed the model to detect subtle variations, improving the overall accuracy of the three-class classification. Experimental results for four-class classification task A four-class classification experiment was conducted to evaluate the model's performance across healthy voice, compensated, partially compensated, and decompensated states. As summarized in Table , using only the Mel-spectrogram resulted in an accuracy of 70.7%, a sensitivity of 0.719, a specificity of 0.900, and an F1-score of 0.714. After the inclusion of first- and second-order differential features, the accuracy increased to 74.3%, with a sensitivity of 0.747, a specificity of 0.914, and an F1-score of 0.743. The ROC curve and confusion matrix, shown in Figs. and , respectively, provide an intuitive visualization of the model's classification performance and error distribution across different feature combinations. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating first- and second-order differential features in enhancing classification accuracy and robustness. In the four-class classification task, the model exhibited suboptimal classification accuracy, which can largely be attributed to feature space overlap between the compensated state and healthy signals. As shown in Table , similarity measurement results highlight the distances between different states. Specifically, the Minkowski distance between the compensated state and healthy signals is 66.84, the Euclidean distance is 25.25, while the cosine distance and correlation distance are 0.0013 and 0.0012, respectively. These metrics underscore significant alignment in feature orientation, resulting in substantial overlap in the feature space. Similarly, the Minkowski distance between the decompensated and partially compensated states is 69.45, the Euclidean distance is 27.76, the cosine distance is 0.0023, and the correlation distance is 0.0025. These values indicate a high degree of directional similarity between the two states, further complicating the model’s ability to distinguish them. This pronounced similarity manifests as feature space overlap, posing significant challenges in differentiating these pathological states. While the inclusion of first- and second-order differential features yielded a marginal improvement in classification performance, it failed to entirely mitigate the impact of feature space overlap. Discussion The TripleConvNet model exhibited significant variability in performance across different feature configurations in this study. Experimental results indicate that the model achieved relatively high classification accuracy using only the Mel-spectrogram as the input feature, with notable improvements following the integration of first- and second-order differential features. In the binary classification task, incorporating first- and second-order differential features increased the model’s accuracy to 95.4% (a 1.3% improvement). Sensitivity and specificity both increased to 0.957 (a 1.2% improvement), while the F1-score rose to 0.953 (a 1.4% improvement), significantly bolstering the model's ability to distinguish between the “medical intervention group” and the “non-medical intervention group”. In the binary classification task, incorporating first- and second-order differential features increased the model’s accuracy to 95.4% (a 1.3% improvement). Sensitivity and specificity both increased to 0.957 (a 1.2% improvement), while the F1-score rose to 0.953 (a 1.4% improvement), significantly bolstering the model's ability to distinguish between the “medical intervention group” and the “non-medical intervention group”. In the three-class classification task, which aimed to distinguish between decompensated, partially compensated and fully compensated states, the inclusion of first- and second-order differential features resulted in a notable improvement in performance. The model's accuracy improved from 80.3% to 84.2% (a 3.9% improvement), while sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score increased by 3.8%, 2.0%, and 4.0%, respectively. Similarity measurements revealed substantial overlap in the feature space between the decompensated and partially compensated states. However, the incorporation of first- and second-order differential features markedly enhanced the model’s capacity to address this overlap, enabling more accurate classification within these challenging categories. In the four-class classification task, the model was tasked with classifying healthy, compensated, partially compensated, and decompensated states. Using only the Mel-spectrogram as input, the model achieved an accuracy of 70.7%. With the integration of first- and second-order differential features, the accuracy improved to 74.3% (a 3.6% increase), accompanied by sensitivity and specificity gains of 2.8% and 1.4%, respectively. Although substantial feature space overlap was observed between decompensated and partially compensated states, as well as high directional similarity between compensated states and healthy signals (cosine distance of 0.0013), which posed challenges for classification, the inclusion of first- and second-order differential features significantly enhanced the model’s ability to distinguish these states. This improvement was particularly notable in differentiating compensated states from healthy signals, as the model demonstrated greater sensitivity to nuanced variations in vocal tract dynamics. Overall, the results confirm that incorporating first- and second-order differential features improves the classification accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of the TripleConvNet model, demonstrating their effectiveness in analyzing complex speech signals. This is because these features not only capture instantaneous spectral fluctuations, but also reflect their rate of change over time, thereby enhancing the model’s sensitivity to dynamic vocal abnormalities. The first-order features short-term variations in frequency and amplitude, which are often exaggerated in pathological voices. Prior research has shown that conditions such as vocal fold paralysis and muscle tension dysphonia lead to increased instability in both pitch and energy, which is reflected in irregular spectral dynamics [ ]. First-order features are thus effective in detecting such instability. Second-order features, in turn, model the acceleration of spectral changes, capturing the volatility in how vocal parameters evolve. In pathological phonation, impaired glottal closure and disrupted neuromuscular control often result in abrupt transitions and discontinuities in the acoustic signal. These are effectively captured by second-order features, which highlight micro-instabilities such as vocal tremor or voice breaks [ ]. The integration of both first- and second-order spectral features not only boosts the overall classification performance, but also provides acoustically grounded insights into pathological mechanisms of voice production, offering clinically interpretable value for diagnostic applications. Currently, data used in deep learning research on voice disorders are mainly derived from two major speech databases. The first is the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary (MEEI) Voice Disorder Database, one of the most extensively utilized resources (available through KayPENTAX Inc.). This database includes 53 healthy voice samples and 662 pathological voice samples [ ]. However, the samples were recorded at varying sampling rates (10 kHz, 25 kHz, and 50 kHz) and in two distinct environments for healthy and pathological voices [ ], which may affect the consistency of the data and limit its comparability across studies. The second major resource is the Saarbruecken Voice Database, which includes voice samples from over 2000 participants. All recordings were made at a consistent 50 kHz sampling rate and 16-bit resolution [ ], ensuring high audio quality. While this database covers 71 different types of voice disorders, it lacks detailed categorization for individual pathologies. This limitation, restricts its applicability in studies focusing on specific voice disorders, despite the consistency in recording settings. In comparison, our constructed database offers notable advantages across various dimensions. All voice data were recorded under standardized conditions with a consistent sampling rate, and they underwent rigorous quality control. Additionally, our database includes detailed severity classifications specifically for UVCP. These high standards in data management and classification significantly enhance its clinical research value and ensure the reproducibility of scientific findings. As a result, this database is uniquely suited for precise studies on voice pathology, addressing the limitations of existing resources. As a result, this database is uniquely suited for precise studies on voice pathology, addressing the limitations of existing resources. In addition, this study selected six Mandarin vowels/a, o, e, i, u, v/as input features, encompassing the core characteristics of the Mandarin phonetic system. Compared to the single vowel (e.g.,/a/) or three-vowel combinations (/a, i, u/) commonly adopted in prior studies [ , , , ], the inclusion of multiple vowels offers a more comprehensive representation of the dynamic characteristics of the vocal tract. This approach also improves the model’s robustness across varying dialects, emotional states, and speech rates [ , ]. Furthermore, the use of multi-vowel input provides richer spectral and temporal acoustic information, with particular effectiveness in distinguishing compensated states from healthy speech. This design ensures the model's reliability across diverse speech conditions, offering a flexible and generalizable solution for clinical applications. Although this study has made substantial progress, several limitations persist in its practical application. First, all speech data were collected under ideal, controlled conditions—specifically, in a quiet recording studio using high-quality recording equipment. These controlled environments differ significantly from real-world clinical settings, where factors such as background noise and variability in recording equipment can compromise speech data quality. To address this, future research should prioritize the development of noise suppression and signal enhancement techniques to reduce the impact of diverse recording conditions and enhance the model's robustness and clinical applicability. Second, inter-individual differences in phonation patterns and vocal intensity may substantially influence the model’s classification performance. Prior studies have demonstrated that using intensity-invariant feature extraction methods can maintain high classification accuracy despite such variability [ ]. Future work could integrate these techniques to further improve model stability. Moreover, due to the absence of internationally recognized guidelines for grading the severity of unilateral vocal cord paralysis, the vocal fold compensation state classification proposed in this study is exploratory and grounded in the research team’s long-standing clinical experience. To validate its broader applicability, future studies will incorporate multicenter data to assess the classification system across various types of voice disorders, ultimately contributing to the development of a more standardized and systematic evaluation framework. Finally, all speech data were sourced from a single medical institution, limiting both the diversity and representativeness of the dataset and, consequently, the evaluation of the model’s external validity. To enhance the model’s generalizability and applicability in different populations and clinical contexts, future research should pursue multicenter collaborations, expand the dataset, and incorporate more diverse and representative speech samples to further validate and refine the model’s performance. It is important to note that the intended users of the model are clinicians rather than patients. The model is designed to function as part of a clinical decision-support system, not as a replacement for human judgment. All treatment decisions must be made in conjunction with the patient’s subjective symptoms, functional status in daily life, and clinical evaluation. Future research will focus on further optimizing the diagnostic performance of the model by integrating electronic medical records (e.g., medical history and treatment details) with voice features to enhance diagnostic accuracy. Previous studies have highlighted that incorporating individualized information can significantly improve the precision of pathological diagnoses. For instance, Fraile et al. [ ] demonstrated that including gender information significantly enhanced the diagnostic performance for laryngeal diseases. Similarly, Tsui et al. [ ] identified significant differences in demographics and symptom presentations among glottic tumors, vocal cord trauma, and vocal cord paralysis, highlighting the potential of these features to improve the automatic classification of voice disorders using machine learning algorithms. Fang et al. [ ] further confirmed that combining patient medical records with voice features significantly enhanced the classification performance of voice-based diagnostic models. Building on these insights, this study aims to integrate multimodal data, including electronic medical records, to capture individual differences and enable more precise and personalized diagnostic outcomes. This approach is expected to not only enrich the diagnostic information for pathological conditions, but also support personalized treatment decisions. It will be particularly valuable in monitoring treatment outcomes and adjusting follow-up strategies for patients with unilateral vocal cord paralysis, providing a robust foundation for clinical decision-making. By leveraging this integration, future research has the potential to significantly improve diagnostic accuracy and elevate the clinical utility of voice-based models. By leveraging this integration, future research has the potential to significantly improve diagnostic accuracy and elevate the clinical utility of voice-based models. Conclusions This study proposed a deep learning model based on Mel-spectrograms and CNN for the precise stratification of UVCP severity. Leveraging the innovative TripleConvNet model, combined with the first- and second-order differential features derived from Mel-spectrograms, the model delivered substantial accuracy improvements in pathological state classification tasks. The research results indicate that, compared to models using only the Mel-spectrogram as input, models incorporating first- and second-order differential features achieve significantly higher accuracy in multi-class classification, with particularly strong performance in three-class classification. This finding suggests that the model can serve as a decision-support tool for medical professionals, assisting clinicians in more accurately stratifying patients and evaluating treatment efficacy, thereby optimizing individualized treatment plans. Moreover, this approach provides a non-invasive, convenient, and efficient method for disease assessment, laying a solid foundation for personalized treatment planning and efficacy evaluation in clinical practice, and demonstrating broad prospects for clinical applications. Methods Study subjects With informed consent, this study analyzed 2,538 voice samples from 423 individuals, sourced from the Eye and ENT Hospital of Fudan University’s voice database, including patients and healthy controls, at the Eye and ENT Hospital of Fudan University from April 2016 to April 2024. Each participant provided six vowel samples (/a, o, e, i, u, v/), ensuring consistency in data collection. Among these, 786 samples were obtained from 131 healthy participants, and 1752 samples were from 292 patients newly diagnosed with UVCP. The 292 UVCP patients were divided into three groups according to vocal fold compensation status: decompensated ( n = 84), partially compensated ( n = 98), and fully compensated ( n = 110). To establish a scientifically robust classification system for vocal fold compensation states, this study employed a set of multidimensional voice assessment parameters. Initially, two laryngologists with over five years of clinical experience evaluated voice samples from the healthy control group to confirm the absence of any voice disorders. All participants underwent laryngoscopic examination to exclude structural lesions of the vocal folds. For patients with UVCP, compensation status was classified based on five objective and subjective measures: the minimum glottal gap angle, maximum phonation time (MPT), the breathiness (B) score on the GRBAS scale, the voice handicap index (VHI), and clinical manifestations of aspiration and coughing. All cases with divergent initial assessments were adjudicated through consensus discussions by a panel of three otolaryngology experts, each with more than 25 years of clinical experience. Based on these assessment outcomes, UVCP patients were divided into three categories: decompensated, partially compensated, and fully compensated. Detailed classification criteria are presented in Table . In this study, MPT was adopted as a key indicator for identifying significantly impaired glottal function, based on evidence from previous studies [ , ]. Additionally, prior research has demonstrated a significant correlation between changes in the minimum glottal gap angle and both phonatory performance and perceived breathiness in patients with unilateral vocal cord paralysis [ , ]. The breathiness (“B”) component of the GRBAS scale has likewise been shown to effectively reflect glottal closure adequacy, supporting its utility in evaluating vocal fold compensation status [ , ]. Clinical signs such as aspiration and ineffective cough further indicate glottal decompensation [ ]. For subjective evaluation of voice disorders, the VHI captures patients’ perceived voice-related impairment [ ]. However, as VHI scores are subject to variation based on occupation, communication needs, and psychological factors, they may not always align with objective phonatory measures. Consequently, in this study, the VHI was used solely as a supplementary reference in classification and was primarily considered in cases where objective assessment results were inconclusive. This study employed a multi-expert evaluation approach, in which three otolaryngologists with over 25 years of clinical experience collaboratively assessed the patients'vocal fold compensation status. The assessment was based on a comprehensive evaluation of key objective parameters, including the minimum glottal gap angle, maximum phonation time (MPT), and the'B'(breathiness) component of the GRBAS scale, to ensure the rigor and reliability of clinical judgment. To further enhance the objectivity and reliability of the study, we invited an independent review panel of three senior otolaryngologists to rigorously evaluate key assessment metrics through collective discussion and consensus-based decision-making. By integrating expert consensus and evaluation, this study aims to minimize subjective bias due to individual variability, improve the consistency of assessment standards, and enhance the scientific rigor and clinical applicability of the data. By integrating expert consensus and evaluation, this study aims to minimize subjective bias due to individual variability, improve the consistency of assessment standards, and enhance the scientific rigor and clinical applicability of the data. To ensure sample homogeneity, participants were aged 19 to 65 years. Pregnant individuals and those with a history of vocal cord surgery or radiation therapy were excluded. Gender distribution details are provided in Table . Data collection and division Voice recordings were conducted under a background noise level of 40–45 dB using a head-mounted condenser microphone (C544L, AKG Pro Audio, Los Angeles, CA, USA) positioned 3–4 cm from the speaker’s mouth at a constant vocal intensity. Six Mandarin vowels (/a, o, e, i, u, v/) were recorded, each lasting 1–3 s. Voice signals were recorded in mono using an audio interface (UR44, Steinberg Media Technologies, Hamburg, Germany) connected to a laptop (ThinkPad E480, Lenovo, Hong Kong, China). The sampling rate was 44,100 Hz, with a resolution of 16 bits. Audio files were anonymized and securely stored in uncompressed.wav format on a password-protected workstation to maintain data integrity and confidentiality. This study’s dataset included 131 healthy voice samples and 292 samples from patients newly diagnosed with UVCP. The dataset was split into training (80%, 340 cases) and validation (20%, 83 cases) sets. This split ensured robust model training and reliable performance evaluation. Feature extraction This study uses Mel-spectrograms as input features, mapping speech signals to a nonlinear scale that aligns with human auditory perception [ ], enhancing feature representation. The Mel-spectrogram captures the human ear’s nonlinear sensitivity to frequencies, emphasizing high-frequency details and producing spectral representations resembling auditory traits [ ]. This representation converts voice signal frequency distributions into images, providing an efficient foundation for deep learning analysis. Additionally, first-order and second-order differential features were extracted to capture dynamic properties of speech signals in the temporal domain. First-order features capture instantaneous changes, while second-order features represent changes in acceleration. Integrating these features enhances the model’s ability to detect subtle variations and minute perturbations in voice signals, improving feature representation robustness and precision. Consequently, the model achieves greater stability and discriminatory power when analyzing voice data. The feature extraction process begins with pre-emphasis, which enhances high-frequency components of the speech signal, compensating for attenuation and preserving critical information. Next, the speech signal is segmented into short-time frames to enable short-time Fourier transform (STFT). A Hamming window function is applied to each frame to minimize boundary effects and spectral leakage. The windowed signal undergoes fast Fourier transform (FFT), converting it from the time domain to the frequency domain to identify frequency contributions [ ]. A Mel filter bank is then applied to the spectrum, reallocating frequencies on the Mel scale to align with human auditory perception. The energy for each Mel frequency is calculated to generate the Mel-spectrogram, which visually represents the temporal evolution of frequencies in the speech signal, with color intensity reflecting energy levels. First-order differential features, capturing temporal dynamics, are extracted from differences between adjacent frames. Second-order features, representing higher-order temporal dynamics, are derived from changes in first-order features. This multidimensional approach enhances the model’s ability to capture subtle details and dynamic speech characteristics, improving its accuracy and robustness in practical applications. The Mel-spectrogram and its first- and second-order difference feature maps are shown in Fig. . Data preprocessing The input images were uniformly resized to a fixed dimension of (1000, 400) and normalized based on the precomputed mean and standard deviation of healthy samples to ensure data standardization. This normalization step is critical for facilitating rapid model convergence and ensuring stable training. To address the issue of class imbalance in the dataset, the compute_class_weight function from the sklearn library was employed to calculate class weights, mitigating the impact of imbalance on model training. This approach effectively prevents the model from being biased toward classes with larger sample sizes. During the data loading phase, a WeightedRandomSampler was utilized to perform weighted sampling of the dataset based on the computed class weights. This ensured a relatively balanced representation of samples from each class during training, thereby improving the model's performance in recognizing minority classes. Deep learning algorithms The TripleConvNet model uses a classic CNN architecture with three convolutional units and fully connected layers to efficiently extract temporal and spectral features from speech signals. The model balances performance and complexity, reducing parameter counts and improving its feasibility for clinical applications. The model’s structure is shown in Fig. . This ensured a relatively balanced representation of samples from each class during training, thereby improving the model's performance in recognizing minority classes. Deep learning algorithms The TripleConvNet model uses a classic CNN architecture with three convolutional units and fully connected layers to efficiently extract temporal and spectral features from speech signals. The model balances performance and complexity, reducing parameter counts and improving its feasibility for clinical applications. The model’s structure is shown in Fig. . The input layer receives data and extracts multilevel features hierarchically through convolution and pooling operations. Each convolutional unit includes four components: a Conv2 d layer for spatial feature extraction, a BatchNorm2 d layer for stabilizing feature distributions and speeding up convergence, a ReLU layer for enhancing nonlinear representation, and a MaxPool2 d layer for down-sampling features to retain key information and reduce computational demands. This design effectively captures multidimensional features. After feature extraction, a Flatten layer reshapes feature maps into a one-dimensional vector for processing by fully connected layers. The fully connected section has two stages: the first uses ReLU activation for nonlinearity and applies Dropout to enhance generalization and reduce overfitting, while the second acts as the output layer, generating task-specific predictions. TripleConvNet combines efficient feature extraction with a lightweight structure, offering superior performance and computational efficiency over traditional deep convolutional networks, making it well-suited for clinical applications. Training configuration Loss function Cross-entropy loss with class weights was used to address class imbalance. Higher weights were assigned to underrepresented classes to mitigate its effect on predictive accuracy. Optimizer The Adam optimizer was used with an initial learning rate of 1 e - 5 , decayed by a factor of 0.1. This low learning rate ensures stable parameter updates, preventing excessive weight adjustments and improving model convergence. Training procedure The model was trained for 100 epochs with a batch size of 16, ensuring stability and thorough training. Model performance evaluation metrics The performance of deep learning models in distinguishing phonation states is evaluated using metrics such as accuracy, specificity, sensitivity, and F1-score, offering a comprehensive assessment. Accuracy is a key metric for evaluating a model's overall predictive performance. It represents the proportion of correct predictions and is calculated as: Accuracy % = TN + TP TP + FN + FP + TN . Sensitivity (recall) evaluates the model's ability to correctly identify instances of each class, defined as the ratio of true positives in a given class. Its formula is: Sensitivity % = TP FN + TP . Specificity measures the model’s ability to correctly identify non-target instances, reflecting its capability to distinguish between different classes. Its formula is: Specificity \% = TN TN + FP . The F1 score combines sensitivity and precision as the harmonic mean, offering a balanced measure of the model’s performance across classes. Its formula is: F 1 Score = 2 ∗ Precision ∗ recall Precision + recall . In this context, recall is defined as TP / ( TP + FN ) ,and precision is defined as TP / ( TP + FP ) 。 The parameters involved in these metrics are defined as follows: TP (true positive): The count of samples the model correctly identifies as belonging to a target vocal state. TN (true negative): The count of samples the model correctly identifies as not belonging to the target vocal state. FP (false positive): The count of samples the model incorrectly identifies as belonging to the target vocal state. ▯ FN (false negative): The count of samples the model incorrectly identifies as belonging to other states. Speech signal analysis To evaluate the similarity of speech signals across different phonation states, this study used several methods, including Minkowski distance ( p = 1), Euclidean distance ( p = 2), cosine distance, and correlation distance. Minkowski and Euclidean distances measure absolute deviations in signal amplitudes. Cosine and correlation distances capture directional variations. The formulas are: Let vector x = x 1 , x 2 ⋯ x n , y = y 1 , y 2 ⋯ y n , the similarity measurements between x and y are defined as follows: Minkowski distance d x , y = ∑ j = 1 n x j - y j p 1 p Euclidean distance d x , y = ∑ j = 1 n x j - y j p 1 2 . In this context, x · y represents the dot product of the two vectors, ‖ x ‖ 2 and ‖ y ‖ 2 represent the Euclidean norms of vectors x and y, respectively. The cosine distance measures the directional difference between two vectors rather than their magnitude difference. Correlation coefficient distance d x , y : The correlation coefficient distance is based on the correlation between two vectors and is defined as: d x , y = 1 - r x , y . In this context, r x , y represents the Pearson correlation coefficient, and its calculation formula is as follows: r x , y = cov x , y cov ( x , x ) · cov ( y , y ) . chunks.content: Introduction The first S3 evidence- and consensus-based guideline of the German Respiratory Society (DGP) on the diagnosis and treatment of patients with acute and chronic cough was published in 2004. S2k (consensus-based) updates were made in 2010 and 2019 [ ]. The German Society for General Practice and Family Medicine (DEGAM) published its S3 guideline on cough for general practitioners in 2014 and 2021 [ ]. This is the English translation of the new 2025 published Cough Guidelines of the German Respiratory Society [1A]. The guideline group was established according to the specifications of the Association of the Scientific Medical Societies (AWMF) by the DGP. Participants included representatives of the participating specialties accredited by their respective specialist societies and a patient representative. The guidelines were coordinated by a representative of AWMF. The lead author is Peter Kardos (Frankfurt am Main). The addressees of this new S2k guideline on cough (German ICD-10 classification codes: R05 and U69.6) are pulmonologists who diagnose and treat adult patients – usually referred by general practitioners. The Society for Pediatric Pneumology (GPP) [ ] is also preparing a pediatric S2k guideline for cough. These guidelines provide a freely accessible, up-to-date scientific basis for the diagnosis and treatment of all patients with cough. The current guidelines also address gastroenterologists and ear, nose, and throat specialists on reflux-related cough or cough triggered by the upper airway (so-called “upper airway cough syndrome”). We describe idiopathic chronic cough (UCC) and refractory chronic cough (RCC), which has been established as a separate disease entity with adding the German ICD code U69.6 to the international symptom code for cough R05. What Is New? 1. The most important change is the new form of the guideline: we have limited the guidelines to 12 essential clinical “key questions”, i.e., the most important aspects of the diagnosis and treatment of various phenotypes of cough. The questions and recommendations in short form have been tabulated. For each question/recommendation, a background text with literature was created and the evidence for each recommendation was formulated as strong or weak. If for a “key question” no clear evidence was available, we used a “maybe” formulation, e.g., a specific treatment or diagnostic procedure may be prescribed as a joint individual decision – in consensus with the informed patient. In the following “overview of recommendations,” we use the following graphic characters: For “strong” recommendations: ↑↑ For “weak” recommendations: ↑ “Maybe” if no sufficient evidence exists: ⇔ The development and consensus-building process took place under the methodological supervision of the representative of AWMF; all statements and recommendations were voted on in face-to-face or virtual consensus conferences. The statement in key question 5 (SARS-CoV-2 infection and cough) was adopted by the majority; for almost all other recommendations and statements, there was strong consensus (100% agreement) in the guidelines. 2. The scope of the guidelines was significantly reduced by the “key questions” methodology. This makes it more suitable for practical applications. 3. All statements and recommendations were classified as newsworthy, modified or unchanged if compared to the 2020 guidelines. 4. The guidelines are available and searchable in the Smartphone Application Leila PRO, available in App Stores and usable free of charge. Every patient retains the right to an individual diagnosis and treatment. In a specific, justifiable case, it may make sense to deviate from the guideline recommendations. Overview of Recommendations and Statements on Key Questions 1–12 Chapter 1 – Background Information on Key Question 1: Classification and Clinical Causes of Cough Cough is a very common symptom of many different diseases. For the purpose of diagnostic confirmation and therapeutic intervention, it has proven most useful to classify cough according to its duration [ – ]. Characteristics of Classification by Duration The most common cause of coughing is an acute, spontaneously resolving viral illness of the upper and/or lower respiratory tract (“common cold”). If a physician is consulted, generally the medical history and a physical examination should be carried out to make this diagnosis (see the Choosing Wisely [“Klug entscheiden”] initiative of the German Society of Internal Medicine [ ]). In the case of chronic cough, a diagnostic workup is essential because of the resulting therapeutic consequences. It should begin as soon as the patient presents. In about 30–40% of patients [ , ] who consult a specialist due to chronic cough, no clear cause can be identified. Such cases are referred to as UCC or RCC if there is a possible cause, such as reflux, but the cough does not respond to guideline-based reflux therapy. A population-based study in Canada found that 3.3% of all patients suffer from RCC [ ]. Taking into account the need for a complex diagnostic workup for chronic cough, cough of shorter than 8 but longer than 3 weeks duration is classified as subacute. It is often the result
