Such cases are referred to as UCC or RCC if there is a possible cause, such as reflux, but the cough does not respond to guideline-based reflux therapy. A population-based study in Canada found that 3.3% of all patients suffer from RCC [ ]. Taking into account the need for a complex diagnostic workup for chronic cough, cough of shorter than 8 but longer than 3 weeks duration is classified as subacute. It is often the result of a prolonged infection or a seasonal allergy and does not usually require technical examinations. However, the classification of cough by duration is arbitrary and there is a smooth transition between the categories. Characteristics of Classification by Sputum: Productive and Dry (Irritating) Cough Another feature of the classification of chronic cough is the categorization into productive and dry (irritant) cough. Productive cough means secretion of 5–30 mL phlegm (corresponding to 1 teaspoon to two tablespoons) [ , ] or more in 24 h. However, the urge to cough – a consequence of the irritation and hypersensitivity of the cough receptors – is often perceived by the patient as “phlegm”, although there is no mechanical cough trigger, i.e., sputum or mucus coating on the mucous surface in the pharynx, larynx, or bronchi. The diagnostic and therapeutic workup for chronic productive cough (e.g., chronic bronchitis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease [COPD], bronchiectasis) [ , ] differs from the procedure for chronic dry cough, and the prognosis is worse compared to dry cough [ ]. Assignment of typical characteristics of the sputum to possible clinical entities is as follows: - Mucous (slimy): smoker’s chronic bronchitis - Serous (foamy): pulmonary edema - Purulent (yellow/green): COPD exacerbation, asthma, eosinophilic bronchitis, bronchiectasis - Blood; hemoptysis, exacerbated bronchiectasis, COPD, tumor, coagulation disorder – caveat red flag - Bronchial casts: allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, severe asthma, COPD Chapter 2 – Background Information on Key Question 2: Acute and Subacute Cough The Acute Cough The viral common cold is the most common cause of acute cough. It can affect both the upper and lower respiratory tract, and it is almost impossible to distinguish between a cold and acute bronchitis [ ]. Typical additional symptoms are “general malaise”, chills, increased temperature, sore throat, runny nose, obstructed nasal breathing, and sneezing. Frequently, coughing is the most disturbing and longest lasting (2–3 weeks) but also self-limiting symptom [ ]. If there is a typical history of common cold and no clinical evidence of red flags – (question 3) that would suggest prompt action – it is advisable to wait up to 8 weeks before initiating basic diagnostic procedures. Most usual causes of the common cold are rhinovirus (30–50% of cases), as well as corona virus, parainfluenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus, influenza virus, adenovirus, enterovirus and metapneumovirus. Bacterial pathogens: isolated acute bacterial bronchitis is mostly due to Mycoplasma pneumoniae , Chlamydia pneumoniae , and Bordetella pertussis ; acute bacterial sinusitis to Streptococcus haemolyticus , Haemophilus influenzae , Streptococcus pneumoniae , and Staphylococcus aureus . Bacterial infections are much less frequent than viral infections. If the patient desires relieving treatment, expectorants (ambroxol, N-acetylcysteine), antitussives (dextromethorphan), and phytopharmaceuticals can be prescribed. The efficacy of dextromethorphan [ ] and several herbal drugs was shown in RCTs. They shorten the duration and relieve symptoms of the common cold [ – ]. Allergic Diseases of the Upper Airways Allergic rhinitis (“hay fever”), often associated with sinusitis, conjunctivitis, pharyngitis, and laryngitis, can also elicit acute cough [ ]. The differential diagnosis to viral infections consists in the current allergen exposure and in the results of the allergy test. The symptoms differ from viral infections: Itchy eyes, nose, and throat as well as multiple sneezing attacks are often the main symptoms. Treatment options include nasal corticosteroids, systemic and topical antihistamines [ , ]. Asthma Among acute cough patients in a clinic in Japan, asthma was diagnosed in 29.5% of cases and cough-variant asthma in 19.6% [ ]. Asthma due to acute infections or intermittent allergen exposure is a common cause of acute dry cough. Usually, asthmatic cough responds well to asthma treatment [ ]. Aspiration The cough reflex protects against the consequences of aspiration. Aspiration of foreign bodies elicits acute coughing, particularly in children aged 1–3 years. Care-dependent elderly patients with an impaired cough reflex – for example, after a stroke – the acute cough may be too weak to eliminate the foreign material with consequent aspiration pneumonia. Appropriate diagnostic tools for foreign body aspiration are a chest X-ray and/or a CT scan alongside with a diagnostic and therapeutic bronchoscopy. Acute Intoxication by the Inhaled Route (E.g., due to Accidents at Work, Fires, “Sniffing” Solvents) The diagnosis is based on medical history,

[ ]. Aspiration The cough reflex protects against the consequences of aspiration. Aspiration of foreign bodies elicits acute coughing, particularly in children aged 1–3 years. Care-dependent elderly patients with an impaired cough reflex – for example, after a stroke – the acute cough may be too weak to eliminate the foreign material with consequent aspiration pneumonia. Appropriate diagnostic tools for foreign body aspiration are a chest X-ray and/or a CT scan alongside with a diagnostic and therapeutic bronchoscopy. Acute Intoxication by the Inhaled Route (E.g., due to Accidents at Work, Fires, “Sniffing” Solvents) The diagnosis is based on medical history, physical examination, lung function analysis including determination of CO diffusion capacity and blood gas analysis. Inpatient observation is often necessary, and intensive medical treatment is frequently required. Poison control centers ( www.medknowledge.de/patienten/notfaelle/vergiftungszentralen.htm ) can provide information on inhaled noxious substances and treatment options. Suitable first-line treatment consists of high-dose inhaled corticosteroids (ICS). Pneumonia Acute cough is a classic symptom of pneumonia. Regarding diagnosis and treatment, please refer to the current guideline from the Paul Ehrlich Society and DGP [ ]. Exacerbation of COPD Acute or acute worsening of chronic cough is the defining feature of an exacerbation of chronic bronchitis or of COPD, often accompanied by sputum production. For diagnosis and treatment of exacerbations, please refer to the new GOLD recommendation (2026 GOLD Report – Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease – GOLD ( goldcopd.org ) and the National Disease Management Guideline (NVL) COPD (2021 edition) (AWMF guideline register). Acute Pleurisy Acute pleuritis can elicit acute cough with chest pain and the diagnosis is easily overlooked. Pulmonary Embolism Acute cough with and without hemoptysis occurs in 22.9% and 7.6% of cases with confirmed pulmonary embolism, respectively. Small recurrent pulmonary emboli are easily missed on examination. The diagnostic procedure and treatment can be found in the AWMF S2k guideline ( https://www.awmf.org/uploads/tx_szleitlinien/065-002l_S2k_VTE_2016-01.pdf ). Pneumothorax An acute pneumothorax is often accompanied by dry cough with chest pain and dyspnea [ ]. Acute Cardiac Diseases Acute left heart failure with pulmonary congestion can lead to bronchial hyper-responsiveness [ ], bronchial obstruction (formerly known as cardiac asthma), and cough. Furthermore, bradycardia in high-grade atrioventricular (AV) block is associated with a reduction in cardiac output, consecutive pulmonary congestion and coughing. Coughing can itself trigger a grade II or III AV block – presumably via severe vagotonia [ ]. Total AV block is discussed as a possible pathomechanism of cough syncope [ ]. Subacute Cough Cough lasting 3–8 weeks is considered subacute cough. Subacute cough is usually of post-viral origin. The most common pathogens for prolonged infection are adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, Bordetella pertussis , influenza virus [ ] and SARS-CoV-2 [ ] (see background text question 5). Other usual pathogens are Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydia pneumoniae . Pertussis Whooping cough is increasingly found as the cause of a postinfectious, protracted cough. An acute infection with B. pertussis can cause an acute febrile illness with a characteristic “pertussiform” long-lasting staccato cough, mainly in (unvaccinated) children, but adults may also be affected (e.g., during the 2024 pertussis endemics in the Czech Republic [ ] and Denmark [ ]). Particularly in the presence of bronchial asthma or COPD, pertussis-related complications emerge with an incidence of 10% of cases [ ]. The treatment of choice is macrolide antibiotics, which are only effective during the catarrhal phase. Antitussives can provide relief. Post-Viral Rhinosinusitis Regardless of the causative pathogen, post-viral rhinosinusitis can last up to 12 weeks. It has a biphasic and self-limiting course [ ] (see background text question 7). Postinfectious Cough If the cough persists for longer than 3 weeks after an acute respiratory infection, a postinfectious cough may be present, which usually lasts no longer than 8 weeks and is self-limiting [ ]. The diagnosis of postinfectious cough (without exacerbated bronchial hyper-responsiveness) is based on a careful history of the past infection and by ruling out other causes. It may be symptomatically treated like the common cold. In contrast to a pertussis infection, the cough in these patients may respond to ICS [ ]. Asthma Exacerbated by Acute Infections A temporary increase in bronchial reactivity triggering the cough reflex – without or with mild bronchial obstruction – can develop in the context of an acute infection, regardless of the type of the pathogen. It is often associated with eosinophilia, but without other signs of asthma [ ]. Usually, this cough subsides spontaneously after 8 weeks. ICS shorten the duration of the cough [ ]. Generally, an ICS or ICS/LABA therapy for 10–14 days is sufficient. Antibiotics for Acute Cough Antibiotics are generally not indicated for acute cough due to the common cold [ ], which is usually a viral infection. Antibiotics have little effect on viral infections. In otherwise healthy subjects they are not indicated for acute cough.

Chapter 4 – Background Information on Key Question 4: Chronic Cough Chronic cough is a frequent symptom of all pulmonary and a few non-pulmonary diseases. We focus in this background information not on the classic respiratory diseases, which are listed in Box 1; for detailed information, see respective textbooks and guidelines. In addition, key questions 5, 7, 8, 9, and 10 deal with further chronic diseases usually associated with the symptom cough. Key question 6 is dedicated to chronic refractory and idiopathic cough, a disease in its own right that is diagnosed when – despite thorough diagnostic workup – no underlying cause for the cough is found. The symptom chronic cough affects quality of life beyond the level of the underlying disease [ – ] and may also cause important psychiatric comorbidities, particularly depression and anxiety [ ]. The sensitivity of the cough reflex is increased to varying degrees in most pulmonary diseases, which determines the severity, frequency, and intensity of the cough. In asthma [ , ] and bronchiectasis, cough is a cardinal symptom with important impact on the severity of the underlying disease. Interestingly, however, the assessment of asthma control according to the specialist S2k guideline [ ] of the German Respiratory Society, the NVL National Asthma Guidelines, and the GINA document does not include cough as a coefficient of severity or asthma control. Thus, a patient can have fully controlled asthma, still coughing day and night. Furthermore, the Bronchiectasis Severity Index also does not include cough as a relevant factor of the severity of bronchiectasis ( https://register.awmf.org/de/leitlinien/detail/020-030 ). Box 1. Cardiac Causes of Chronic Cough Cardiac causes of chronic cough include chronic heart failure, cardiac arrhythmias, or side effects of cardiac medications – most commonly ACE inhibitors. Ventricular arrhythmias and chronic heart failure in particular can elicit cough by pulmonary congestion, irritating vagus afferents or the phrenic nerve. The appearance of edema (with rapid weight gain) and/or signs of pulmonary congestion can indicate chronic heart failure. In addition to the basic diagnostic measures, the workup of chronic cough should therefore include personalized cardiac diagnostics, i.e., electrocardiogram, echocardiography, and the determination of BNP or NT-proBNP. The treatment depends on the underlying cardiac disease, e.g., the use of diuretics for chronic pulmonary congestion. Bronchiectasis It may remain undetected on the chest radiograph. The diagnosis is made on clinical grounds (productive cough) and dilated bronchi on the multi-slice CT scan with 1 mm reconstructions. Newly diagnosed patients with bronchiectasis should be routinely investigated for at least the most common causes such as common variable immunodeficiency, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, non-tuberculous mycobacteria, tuberculosis, inflammatory bowel disease, and the presence of pulmonary fibrosis. Cystic Fibrosis As a result of improved diagnostic and therapeutic options, more than half of CF patients in industrialized countries are over 18 years old [ ]. Therefore, chronic cough with expectoration of viscous secretions in adults should also be considered in the differential diagnosis of this congenital systemic metabolic disorder [ ], which is usually diagnosed in childhood, but in about 10% of cases only in adulthood [ ]. Treatment should consider guideline-based treatment with CFTR modulators, all existing organ manifestations (paranasal sinuses, lungs, pancreas, intestines, kidneys, diabetes, bone metabolism), treatment of any bronchopulmonary infections, adequate nutrition, and prevention [ ]. Rare Isolated Diseases of the Tracheobronchial System If there is clinical suspicion or CT evidence of thickening, dilatation, irregularity or collapse of the bronchial wall, diagnostic bronchoscopy, and histology are indicated. Obstructive Sleep Apnea Coughing can be considered as a possible consequence of obstructive sleep apnea. The two common diseases (obstructive sleep apnea and chronic cough) can statistically coincide, but the association of both diagnoses is more frequent than can be expected from coincidence alone. The cause might be the triggering of laryngopharyngeal reflux by apneas with intrathoracic pressure fluctuations as well as inflammatory vibration trauma of the mucous membranes due to snoring. Continuous positive airway pressure therapy may alleviate the cough, but the evidence is currently insufficient [ , ]. Somatic Cough Syndrome and Cough Tic The term psychogenic cough should be replaced by “somatic cough syndrome”, i.e., the somatization of psychogenic stress as cough. Characteristics: anxiety; the cough significantly impairs the patient’s life, attaching exaggerated importance and giving disproportionate weight to the cough [ ]. This entity occurs mostly in children; in adults, it was considered a rarity. A retrospective study found, however, a ratio of almost 5% in patients with chronic cough associated with psychiatric conditions such as depression [ ]. A tic is a repetitive involuntary motor or vocalization phenomenon in children (e.g., blinking, throat clearing, coughing, crying). A tic cough can occur in children in isolation, also in the context of Tourette syndrome as a somatic cough syndrome [ ]. Chapter 6 – Background Information on Key Question 6: Refractory and Idiopathic Chronic Cough Chronic cough is usually a symptom. It can occur in the context of smoker’s bronchitis, COPD, manifest asthma, interstitial lung diseases, and lung tumors. In the case of productive cough, chronic lung infections (e.g., tuberculosis) and bronchiectasis should be considered. The amount of sputum is diagnostically relevant. (a) More than 30 mL (approx. 2 tablespoons) in 24 h: highly suspected chronic infection or bronchiectasis disease. (b) 5–30 mL in 24 h: chronic infection or bronchiectasis should be considered. (c) Up to 5 mL (one teaspoon) in 24 h: low suspicion, other causes than chronic infection or bronchiectasis are likely. In the presence of (a) or (b), further workup for chronic lung infections with or without bronchiectasis is indicated. Chronic cough is often the main symptom of pulmonary diseases. They can be diagnosed using examination methods established in guidelines. Every patient with a chronic cough should undergo basic diagnostics [ ] immediately on the first presentation (box 3, see also key question 11). Alarm signs (“red flags”, see key question 3) should be preferentially observed. Box 3. If despite careful workup the cause of the chronic cough, e.g., smoking, COPD, and interstitial lung disease, was not identified, the cough is a disease in its own right: idiopathic (unexplained) chronic cough (UCC) [ ]. Gastroesophageal reflux (GERD), diseases of the upper airways, and eosinophilic diseases of the lower airways (asthma without manifest bronchial obstruction, eosinophilic bronchitis without asthma) can also be associated with chronic cough. However, the majority of patients suffering from these common diseases do not complain of cough. If, despite guideline-based treatment of the above-mentioned diseases, the cough does not respond to the targeted therapy, then it is called Refractory Chronic Cough (RCC), merely a comorbidity of asthma, GERD or upper airway diseases. ACE inhibitors and some other medications can also cause RCC (see key question 10). UCC and RCC are similar in their clinical presentation and pathomechanism (see below). It is a dry or minimally productive cough. The European Cough Guidelines do not make a distinction [ ] and they only refer to RCC. With a prevalence of chronic cough in Germany of 6.5% [ ], the proportion of UCC and RCC is not known. The prevalence of RCC/UCC is 1–2% in Sweden [ ] and 1% in the USA [ ]. The prevalence of RCC/UCC is 1–2% in Sweden [ ] and 1% in the USA [ ]. Patients with RCC and UCC suffer from an increase in the sensitivity of the cough reflex [ , ], including the central regulatory mechanisms with response to low-threshold thermal, mechanical, and chemical stimuli. This can be quantified in the capsaicin provocation test; however, the test should be used in scientific studies only. Healthy women have a higher sensitivity of the cough reflex compared to men [ ]. Therefore, the majority of patients with RCC and UCC are women in their 6th or 7th decade of life. The ratio of women to men is 2:1. Female patients often recall the onset of cough many years ago – after a common cold. Compared to patients with an established cause of chronic cough that responds to appropriate therapy, the duration of symptoms in RCC/UCC is significantly longer, the FeNO is lower, and capsaicin sensitivity is higher [ ]. Histologically, one study found a thickening of the basement membrane but no increased mucus production or inflammation [ ]. RCC and UCC are caused by afferent hypersensitivity of the cough reflex with central modulation, and it can be considered as neuropathy of the cough reflex, “hypertussia”, like hyperalgesia of the pain reflex [ ]. Patients react to stimuli that do not trigger cough in healthy individuals, called “allotussia”, in analogy to the allodynia, consisting of the hypersensitivity of the pain reflex [ ]. The trigger of neuropathy is usually inflammation, infection, or allergy. The afferents from the upper airways, especially from the larynx, are often affected [ , ]. Box 4. A personalized diagnostic approach based on the patient’s medical history, the typical cough triggers and clinical findings are required. For example: without concrete evidence of GERD, such as heartburn, belching, or a connection between coughing and food intake, the patient does not require a gastroenterological exam. In this case, a trial of PPI therapy also should not be carried out. In contrast, if an eosinophilic airway disease is suspected as the cause for RCC, a trial course of ICS or ICS/LABA therapy for 2–4 weeks is recommended; if the cough abates, the diagnosis is considered confirmed (see also key question 9). In daily practice, patients suffering from RCC/UCC with negative workup are often “overdiagnosed” with unnecessarily repeated negative tests. Therapy (see key question 12): antitussives (and secretomotoric drugs) are approved for short-term use for acute cough only (up to 4 weeks). Gefapixant (Lyfnua ® ), a P2X3 receptor antagonist, developed for the treatment of UCC/RCC in a dosage of 2 × 45 mg daily, is approved in Germany, but it is not marketed by the manufacturer. Chapter 7 – Background Information on Key Question 7: Cough in Chronic Upper Respiratory Tract Diseases Chronic Inflammatory Diseases of the Upper Respiratory Tract as Triggers of Chronic Cough Chronic diseases of the upper respiratory tract, i.e., chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) and allergic and non-allergic rhinitis can trigger chronic cough. Chronic cough based on these diseases is referred to as “upper airway cough syndrome (UACS)” [ ]. The complex mechanisms of chronic cough in UACS are not fully understood yet. Possible underlying mechanisms include postnasal drip (PND), a chronic inflammation of the airways with nervous sensory hypersensitivity [ , ]. In the case of UACS, an ENT assessment should be performed. Chronic rhinosinusitis is characterized by the occurrence of at least two of the symptoms listed below for more than 12 weeks: Typical symptoms: - Nasal obstruction - Anterior and/or posterior secretion - Facial pain - Olfactory disorder Optional: - Fever - Headache To determine the diagnosis, the symptoms of CRS must be confirmed by pathological findings either in rhinoscopy, nasal endoscopy or by imaging CT, digital volume tomography, or MRI of the paranasal sinuses. The presence of nasal polyps in rhinoscopy or nasal endoscopy divides the disease into a phenotype without polyps and a phenotype with polyps (CRSwNP) [ ]. In a substantial percentage of cases, CRSwNP is associated with comorbid bronchial asthma. Treatment initially consists of the topical application of corticosteroids and the use of NaCl nasal irrigation for 8–12 weeks. If there is no improvement in symptoms, functional sinus surgery should be performed in accordance with the guidelines. For severe courses of CRSwNP, several biologics are available for long-term therapy [ ]. Allergic rhinitis can also be

Allergic rhinitis can also be associated with anterior and posterior rhinorrhea (“postnasal drip”) and nasal obstruction, and often also presents with sneezing and itching of the nose. The symptoms of non-allergic rhinitis may be difficult to distinguish. In addition to detailed medical history, allergology workup is available by means of a prick test and/or diagnosis of allergen-specific immunoglobulin E (IgE) in the serum. Additional intranasal provocation may be useful in excluding a clinically silent sensitization. Various drugs are available for the symptomatic therapy of allergic rhinitis. The most important drugs include the following. - Intranasal corticosteroids - Intranasal, ocular, and oral antihistamines - Fixed combinations of intranasal corticosteroids and intranasal antihistamines - Leukotriene receptor antagonists - Mast cell stabilizers (cromones) - Anticholinergics - Anti-IgE antibodies Allergen immunotherapy is the only causal treatment. The treatment of non-allergic rhinitis is based on the underlying causes. A distinction is made between senile rhinitis, gustatory rhinitis, occupational rhinitis, hormonal rhinitis, drug-induced rhinitis, and finally, idiopathic rhinitis, a diagnosis of exclusion. The latter form accounts for around 50% of the diseases. While the occupational and drug-induced forms focus on avoiding triggering substances or medications, topical corticosteroids are primarily used for the hormonal form. In many cases, senile rhinitis can be treated with topical anticholinergics. In gustatory and idiopathic rhinitis, locally applied capsaicin has shown long-lasting benefits. Surgical procedures with application of cold to the posterior nasal nerves, including neurectomy, have been documented [ ]. The subsequent cough will improve with the disease, except in RCC ( ). Posterior rhinorrhea – formerly called Post-nasal drip (PND) – is a symptom of the described inflammatory diseases and is most frequently observed in CRS. Although it is considered by many cough patients to be the cause of their cough, few patients with PND in CRS report a chronic cough [ , ]. Inducible Laryngeal Obstruction, Vocal Cord Dysfunction Inducible laryngeal obstruction (ILO), formerly vocal cord dysfunction (VCD), describes the symptoms of inspiratory breathlessness with characteristic inspiratory stridor, caused by a transient, reversible obstruction of the larynx. Although the term vocal cord dysfunction has become the dominant term for such symptoms in literature over time, it only describes ILO at the glottic level [ ]. Because supraglottic dysfunction has also been documented in some cases, ILO has been defined as an umbrella term [ ]. The etiology of ILO is multifactorial, complex, and not yet fully understood. Predisposing factors are as follows [ ]: - Laryngeal hyper-responsiveness - Physical exertion - Increased psycho-vegetative vulnerability - Mechanical factors - Cough (can be both a trigger and a symptom of ILO) Clinically, affected patients show a sudden onset of breathlessness at rest or triggered by physical exertion. This breathlessness is described as inspiratory and is accompanied by a corresponding inspiratory stridor. The symptoms are usually of short duration (seconds to minutes) but can also last for hours to days in individual cases. Both diagnostic and therapeutic distinction from bronchial asthma is decisive. It should be diagnosed clinically by audible sounds, i.e., typical inspiratory stridor. Combined asthma-ILO disorders frequently occur [ ]; an incipient asthmatic bronchial obstruction can trigger an ILO and progress to ILO attacks, which can cause secondary, sometimes severe, psychological impairments, i.e., anxiety or panic disorders and even reactive depression. On the other hand, many ILO patients are psychologically unstable. In addition to a targeted medical history, it is diagnostically important to have both examination by respiratory and ENT physicians to rule out severe, apparently refractory bronchial asthma, that does not respond even to the most intensive asthma therapy on treatment step 5 in adults and step 6 in children. The ENT specialist and the speech therapist must rule out mechanical causes, e.g., pharyngo-laryngeal tumors. Randomized studies on the management of ILO are still lacking. Establishing the diagnosis and providing sensitive, detailed information about the causes and emphasizing that even severe symptoms are not a vital threat (reassurance) often results in a therapeutic effect [ ]. In addition to visualizing the laryngeal dysfunction to gain understanding of the condition for patient and therapist, respiratory physiotherapy/speech therapy exercises are important [ ]. Chapter 8 – Background Information on Key Question 8: Reflux The relationship between GERD and chronic cough (GERC: gastroesophageal reflux cough) is complex. If it is the sole cause of a chronic cough, the elimination of GER (gastroesophageal reflux) should reliably – with a certain time latency – lead to the elimination of the cough. This has not yet been proven in controlled studies. The reasons for this may be that: The diagnosis of GERD and GERC was wrongly assumed when heartburn was considered only in the medical history; GER was or is not the sole cause; or – even more likely – that Successful treatment of reflux symptoms or lesions is not synonymous with elimination of GER. The PPIs used for GERD change the acidity of the reflux, but not the reflux per se. Due to this difficult situation and in the absence of a diagnostic procedure that can reliably demonstrate the causal relationship between GER and cough, the Bradford-Hill criteria must be used to prove a possible causal relationship [ ]. GERD and chronic cough occur together more frequently than statistically expected, but a temporal association or even a biological gradient (severity correlation between GERD and cough) have not been proven [ – ]. It should also be noted that reflux can cause cough and vice versa [ ]. Pathophysiologically, the “reflux theory”, i.e., reflux of gastric contents into the pharynx or airways, and the “reflex theory”, i.e., stimulation of the central cough reflex from the distal esophagus, are discussed [ ]. There is no conclusive evidence for the reflux theory in adults to date; rather, the data support the reflex theory, whereby the volume of reflux appears to be more important than acidity [ – ]. This assumption is supported, on the one hand, by the success of cough outcome after antireflux surgery in uncontrolled studies [ , ] and, on the other hand, by observations that esophageal motility disorders can be associated with cough [ ]. Placebo-controlled intervention studies with PPIs have shown a significant effect (approx. 15–20% over placebo) on cough if GERD has been confirmed by appropriate diagnostics and typical reflux symptoms (heartburn, acid or nonacid regurgitation) [ – ]. The study results suggest that PPI therapy should be high-dose (e.g., 2 × 40 mg esomeprazole preprandial) and should be carried out consistently for up to 12 weeks in individual cases [ , ]. According to a recent meta-analysis of 15 uncontrolled studies, antireflux surgery (fundoplication) can achieve elimination of GERC in 58% of patients and an improvement of >50% in 86% [ ]. There was no significant heterogeneity between the studies. However, the long-term effect of surgery is not sufficiently documented. There are no conclusive studies on the effect on cough after (successful) treatment of an esophageal motility disorder. From a gastroenterological perspective, the management algorithm shown in is based on the available data. Once other causes of chronic cough have been ruled out, an adequately used, prolonged high-dose PPI therapy should be initiated if typical reflux symptoms are also present [ , ]. If treatment is unsuccessful, a complex gastroenterological diagnostic workup is recommended in accordance with Lyon Consensus 2.0 and the S2k guideline of the German Society for Gastroenterology, Digestive and Metabolic Diseases [ , ]. In the absence of typical reflux symptoms, only in exceptional cases (e.g., psychological fixation on reflux genesis), a complex diagnostic workup may be recommended with the aim of ruling out an esophageal cause definitively. If there is a discordant response of reflux symptoms and cough under PPI, antireflux surgery in a qualified center can be considered in individual cases. shows the management algorithm for suspected reflux cough. Chapter 9 – Background Information on Key Question 9: Cough-Variant Asthma The prevalence of bronchial hyper-responsiveness in the general population is around 30% [ , ]. Some patients are symptomatic and have chronic cough [ , ]. The transition from such “chronic cough as asthma equivalent” (cough-variant asthma) to classic asthma with shortness of breath and obstruction is smooth, with around 30–40% developing classic asthma in the later course [ ]. The pathology includes eosinophilic mucosal infiltration and airway remodeling [ , ]. FeNO measurements in exhaled air yielded inconsistent results [ ]. Non-asthmatic eosinophilic bronchitis (NAEB) is another clinical entity from the eosinophilic spectrum [ ]. Affected patients have a chronic cough, sputum and bronchial mucosal eosinophilia, but neither shortness of breath nor bronchial hyper-responsiveness. The FeNO in exhaled air is usually elevated [ , ]. Both entities are common causes of cough in nonsmokers with normal chest X-ray and without ACE inhibitor therapy. In patient collectives with chronic cough proportions of 31%–50% have been described [ , ]. Both disease entities respond well to inhaled steroid therapy (also in combination with a long-acting bronchodilator for cough-variant asthma). If one of the two entities is suspected, a trial of ICS therapy should be initiated [ , ], although the formal evidence from an older Cochrane meta-analysis, due to the heterogeneity of the studies, was only weak [ ]. Chapter 10 – Background Information on Key Question 10: Drug-Induced Cough Pathomechanism Three main potential pathomechanisms play a role in the protussive effect of medication: Increase in sensitivity of cough receptors, e.g., ACE inhibitors Dose-dependent, direct pulmonary toxicity, e.g., amiodarone Local physical irritation of sensitive cough receptors (hypertussia, allotussia), e.g., asthma dry powder inhalers. ACE inhibitors are a common cause of chronic, usually dry cough. They lead to a bradykinin-mediated hypersensitivity of the cough receptors [ ]. This is a class effect. About 10% of all women and 5% of all men develop chronic cough with ACE inhibitors. The latency from the beginning of intake to the onset of cough can last a few days, but also several months [ ]. In each case of chronic cough while taking ACE inhibitors, the ACE inhibitor should be discontinued, as they increase the sensitivity of the cough receptors even in healthy individuals (hypertussia, allotussia) [ ]. If necessary, alternative substance classes should be prescribed. If the chronic cough persists for longer than 3 weeks after switching medication, further diagnostics should be carried out in accordance with key question 1. Other drugs have a potential protussive effect due to their pulmonary toxicity (alveolitis, ILD), with an overall lower incidence than with ACE inhibitors (selection in , [ ]). Amiodarone causes cough in 1%–5% of cases, the onset of which is typically observed after about 8 weeks of treatment and at higher daily doses (from 400 mg/day). Usually, cough occurs less frequently after starting treatment with beta-receptor blockers. Therefore, all medications used by the patient should be checked for the side effect of cough. Summary In case of chronic cough while taking ACE inhibitors, the ACE inhibitor should be discontinued. All medications used by the patient should be checked for the side effect cough. Chapter 11 – Background Information on Key Question 11: Basic and Personalized Diagnosis of Cough Basic Diagnostics for Chronic Cough A systematic approach consisting of a targeted, detailed medical history including an allergy and medication history (especially ACE inhibitors) and a thorough physical examination enables a rapid diagnosis in many cases [ ]. Recognizing “red flags” and their differential diagnostic classification and, if necessary, immediate treatment have top priority (see question 3). A posteroanterior and lateral chest X-ray and a pulmonary function test should be performed as a basic diagnostic test. In most cases, the diagnosis or at least the direction of further personalized diagnostic measures can be determined in order to diagnose the disease underlying the symptom cough in accordance with the guidelines. Evidence of allergy - Trigger of cough (inhaled chemical and physical stimuli, dependence on body position), “urge to cough” (cough irritation in the throat) [ ]. - Sputum (teaspoonful or more in 24 h; mucous or purulent) [ ]. - Upper respiratory tract symptoms (nasal stuffiness, rhinorrhea, sneezing fits, “frog in the throat”, hoarseness) - Gastrointestinal complaints: heartburn, belching, regurgitation - Dry cough accompanied by shortness of breath and audible wheezing over the lungs, - Nocturnal coughing - Previous therapy Physical examination checking the following points: - Heart failure - Pharyngitis, mucus tracks in the throat - Wheezing - Fibrosis: Velcro rales If the results of the basic diagnostic procedure do not answer the question: “Do the findings explain the cough?” personalized diagnostic workup should be performed. Personalized Diagnosis of Chronic Cough If the patient’s medical history, physical examination and basic diagnostic tests are not conclusive, further diagnostic measures are indicated. A complete implementation of all possible technical tests listed above is not practicable. Therefore, a further, possibly interdisciplinary investigation [ ] in the sense of personalized medicine should be carried out. If the upper airways are suspected (“upper airways cough syndrome”) causing the chronic cough, extended diagnostic workup is indicated in this area. Chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyps or PND should be ruled out by means of anterior and posterior rhinoscopy. A simple oral cavity inspection with the finding of mucus tracks on the posterior pharyngeal wall can also provide indications of upper airway involvement. Further diagnostics consist of performing a CT or MRI scan of the paranasal sinuses (S2k guideline on rhinosinusitis, AWMF guideline register). Laryngopharyngoscopy completes the ENT examination, checking for swelling and inflammation, particularly of the posterior parts of the larynx. If functional irritation of the larynx is suspected, a phoniatric examination may be useful. If allergic rhinitis or allergic asthma is suspected, an evaluation with prick testing, determination of the differential blood count and, if necessary, determination of total IgE and specific IgE should be performed. Specific provocation tests are seldom necessary. The respiratory workup includes pulmonary function testing with FeNO measurement (also relevant for NAEB [ ]), a unspecific bronchial provocation test, e.g., with metacholine, and the collection of blood, sputum and bronchial samples for further diagnosis [ , ]. Alternatively, a 4-week ex juvantibus therapy with a medium- or high-dose ICS/LABA combination is possible, if there is reasonable suspicion of cough-variant asthma (e.g., predominantly nocturnal or exertion-induced cough, elevated Th2 biomarkers (blood eosinophilia, FeNO)) [ , , ]. Chronic cough in the presence of classic GERD symptoms (heartburn, regurgitation) should be treated ex juvantibus with twice the standard dose of PPI for up to 90 days (see question 8). If there is no response, in justified individual cases complete gastroenterological workup, i.e., endoscopy, impedance pH probe, esophageal manometry should be performed. This also applies to clinically justifiable individual cases without classic GERD symptoms. Causality between cough and reflux can only be assumed if the SAP (symptom association probability) is 95% or higher (see question 8). In the case of chronic cough with sputum, the first step after basic diagnostics should be a microbiological sputum examination (including mycobacteria), followed by a CT scan of the thorax without contrast medium with 1 mm reconstructions. Bronchiectasis can be detected (see guidelines of the German Respiratory Society for bronchiectasis ( https://register.awmf.org/de/leitlinien/detail/020-030 ) as well as other diseases that are not evident on the chest X-ray, i.e., occult tumor, ILD, emphysema, etc. If the personalized diagnostic algorithm has remained inconclusive, a CT chest examination and, if there is clinical suspicion (e.g., of tracheobronchomalacia [ ], mucus plugging [ ], chronic infection, occult tumor) a bronchoscopy is also recommended. A cardiological investigation should be carried out if, despite a negative basic diagnosis of chronic cough, a cardiac cause (e.g., occult pulmonary congestion during exercise, arrhythmia, valvular heart diseases) appears possible in the context of the personalized assessment of the patient (see NVL Chronic Heart Failure, https://register.awmf.org/de/leitlinien/detail/nvl-006 ). Personalized diagnostic measures ENT – Oral cavity inspection – Anterior and posterior rhinoscopy – Laryngopharyngoscopy – Sonography and/or CT, MRI of the paranasal sinuses Gastroenterology – Esophago-gastro-duodenoscopy (EGD) – Esophageal manometry – 24-h impedance pH probe Allergology – History – Prick test – Differential blood count – Total IgE – If necessary, specific IgE and IgG analysis Respiratory medicine – Spirometry – Body plethysmography FeNO – Nonspecific inhalation provocation test – Sputum microbiology – Bronchoscopy – CT thorax scan native Cardiology – Electrocardiogram – Transthoracic and transesophageal cardiac echocardiography – Cardio-MRI Neurology – Neurological assessment Diagnostic algorithms are shown in – for acute, subacute, and chronic cough, respectively. Chapter 12 – Background Information on Key Question 12: Cough Therapy Respiratory Physiotherapy Productive Cough Respiratory physiotherapy in patients with secretion retention, impaired mucociliary clearance, and impaired cough clearance aims to improve secretion elimination and reduce symptoms. Techniques that support secretolysis, mobilization, transport, and secretion elimination by opening airways can reduce cough, the amount of sputum and significantly improve quality of life and cough-related symptoms [ , , ]. Active cycle of breathing techniques, secretion-promoting techniques including autogenous drainage, coughing techniques, positioning, vibration, and percussion can be supplemented with devices, inhalation, positive expiratory pressure devices with/without oscillations, high-frequency chest wall compression devices and air-stacking. In the case of a peak cough flow <160 L/min (measurable when coughing into a simple peak flow meter) and severely weakened patients, the cough should be assisted manually or with equipment [ ]. An up-to-date overview of the non-pharmacological treatment options for coughing described below can be found in the work by Peng et al. [ ]. Dry “Chesty” Cough The respiratory physiotherapy treatment of patients with dry irritating cough, such as RCC/UCC, aims to control cough to prevent or reduce the high symptom burden. This includes education on chronic cough including recognizing trigger factors, restoring physiological breathing patterns including nasal breathing and diaphragmatic breathing as well as techniques for cough irritation avoidance, cough prevention and cough attenuation [ , – ]. A review with 5 studies and 157 included patients found an improvement in cough-related quality of life, a significant reduction in cough frequency and a decrease in cough reflex sensitivity [ ]. Many years of clinical expert experience point to the great importance of patient education. A perceived cough stimulus (urge to cough) does not necessarily have to be answered with a subsequent cough. Speech Therapy Laryngeal Hypersensitivity and Coughing The speech therapy of coughing [ – ] and ILO (former terminology VCD) is based on the speech therapist's and medical diagnostic results. Usually, it consists of the following components: Speech therapist’s diagnostics includes symptom assessment of the cough and detection of functional imbalances of the larynx, vocal function, and swallowing. To clarify the role of the larynx, the questionnaire by Vertigan et al. [ ] is recommended. The consequent speech therapy includes the following components: - Psychoeducation: conveying the patient that the cough is not “imaginary”, promoting motivation and adherence, development of realistic treatment goals. - Counseling and initiation of measures, e.g., for voice hygiene; development of adapted suppression techniques and adapted coughing behavior with less subglottic pressure. - Advice on voice-damaging noxious substances and typical laryngeal stimuli, e.g., alcohol, reflux, dehydration [ ]. - Evaluation of the above-mentioned Vertigan questionnaire. - Offering and training of breathing techniques. - Adapted elements from the voice therapy. Speech therapy for chronic cough can be prescribed in accordance with the guidelines for diagnosis and treatment of voice function disorders https://register.awmf.org/de/leitlinien/detail/049-008 , SC2 “Swallowing disorders’ and SP6 “speech motor disorders”, if necessary, with patient-specific leading symptoms. Drug Therapy Most importantly, the disease underlying the symptom cough should be treated in accordance with the respective guidelines, i.e., causal treatments should be prescribed. For acute and subacute cough, evidence-based herbal and synthetic secretomotor drugs and antitussives are approved as symptomatic therapy for a treatment period of approximately 4 weeks. There is scientific evidence for their efficacy [ ]; see also key question 2. They may relieve and shorten the cough duration in the common cold. Their prescription is “off label” for chronic cough. If the cough does not occur as a symptom but as a disease on its own (RCC and UCC), secretomotor and antitussive drugs (see key question 2) can be prescribed intermittently for a limited period of time. These medications are not approved for long-term treatment of chronic cough. Gefapixant [ ], a P2X3 receptor antagonist, has been approved in Germany in a dosage of 45 mg bid for the treatment of RCC/UCC since September 2023. It is marketed in Austria, Switzerland, Norway, etc., but not in Germany. RCC and UCC are considered hypersensitivity (“neuropathy”) of the cough reflex. Pregabalin (300 mg daily) or gabapentin (up to 1,800 mg daily, usual dose up to 900 mg) [ ] act as effective neuromodulators in about 20% of patients; the prescription for cough is “off label”. Low-dose morphine retard [ ] (2 × 10 mg) (special prescription for opioids necessary) is effective in some patients (in about 20% with

been approved in Germany in a dosage of 45 mg bid for the treatment of RCC/UCC since September 2023. It is marketed in Austria, Switzerland, Norway, etc., but not in Germany. RCC and UCC are considered hypersensitivity (“neuropathy”) of the cough reflex. Pregabalin (300 mg daily) or gabapentin (up to 1,800 mg daily, usual dose up to 900 mg) [ ] act as effective neuromodulators in about 20% of patients; the prescription for cough is “off label”. Low-dose morphine retard [ ] (2 × 10 mg) (special prescription for opioids necessary) is effective in some patients (in about 20% with RCC/UCC); increasing the dose in this indication does not increase the treatment effect. Long-term morphine therapy is “off label” for RCC/UCC but approved for palliative indications. Dihydrocodeine (prescription only) is approved for the short-term indication only. Dihydrocodeine is not recommended as it is metabolized in the body to an unpredictable extent to morphine and acts as such. The correct dosage is therefore difficult to determine. Future Therapies Chronic cough is not a uniform clinical entity [ ], and the efficacy of future drugs depends on the phenotype. For example, partial opioid µ and κ receptor agonists/antagonists work well in pulmonary fibrosis, for which there is recently published evidence available [ , ]. Cough triggered from the upper airways appears to respond to local osmotic rehydration therapy; a phase 3 trial is in preparation [ ]. Camlipixant, another P2X3 receptor antagonist, is in a phase 3 clinical trial, and other cough therapeutics are in development, including the neurokinin receptor antagonist orvepitant, a sodium channel NaV1.7 blocker, and others. The studies use both objective (24-h cough frequency) endpoints and patient-reported outcomes. By the end of the decade, several anti-cough drugs are expected to reach market maturity. documents.title: AAO-HNS clinical practice guideline polysomnography prior to tonsillectomy

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Over 750,000 adenotonsillectomies (AT) are performed annually in the United States, for which pediatric sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) is the indication in up to 77% of cases. – Pediatric SDB is a condition affecting up to 12% of children with presentations ranging from mild snoring to obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Polysomnography (PSG) is considered the gold standard for the diagnosis of SDB and assessment of SDB severity. Multiple organizations have published guidelines on the use of PSG prior to AT, including the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM), and American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery (AAO-HNS). The 2002 AAP and 2010 AASM guidelines both recommended PSG to confirm a diagnosis of OSA in any child being considered for AT. , In contrast, the 2011 AAO-HNS Clinical Practice Guideline: Polysomnography for Sleep-Disordered Breathing Prior to Tonsillectomy recommended pre-AT PSG in a more selective group of children considered at high risk for perioperative morbidity or where there is uncertainty regarding the diagnosis or severity of SDB due to discordance between reported symptoms and physical examination findings. Risk factors for perioperative morbidity included obesity, neuromuscular disorders, Down syndrome, sickle cell anemia, and craniofacial anomalies. Furthermore, severe OSA on PSG was recommended as an indication for overnight monitoring. The recent 2019 AAO-HNS Clinical Practice Guideline: Tonsillectomy in Children included the additional recommendation for pre-AT PSG in children aged less than 2 years. Despite various guideline recommendations, the majority of children who undergo AT for SDB do not have a preoperative PSG. , A recent study at our institution demonstrated that in children undergoing AT for SDB in the 12 months immediately following publication of the 2011 AAO-HNS guideline, age less than 3 years was the only independent predictor of obtaining pre-AT PSG. However important limitations of this study were assessment of a single time period immediately after 2011 AAO-HNS guideline publication and potential selection bias in including only patients who underwent AT. The purpose of the current study is therefore to assess the impact of the 2011 AAO-HNS guideline on practice patterns by comparing the predictors for obtaining preoperative PSG in all pediatric patients being considered for AT for SDB before and after publication of the guideline. METHODS This was a retrospective cohort study of all children who were referred to the multi-provider pediatric otolaryngology clinic at a single tertiary children’s hospital (Doernbecher Children’s Hospital at Oregon Health and Sciences University (OHSU)) for consideration for AT for SDB. The study was approved by the OHSU Institutional Review Board. Patients were identified by screening a billing database for International Classification of Diseases, 9th Revision (ICD-9) and 10th Revision (ICD-10) codes corresponding to snoring, OSA, and tonsillar hypertrophy (ICD-9 codes 786.09, 474.10; ICD-10 codes R06.83, J35.3, G47.30, G47.33, G43.39, G47.36, R06.81). Inclusion criteria were: (1) age less than 18 years at the time of encounter and (2) primary indications for AT of either SDB or OSA. Exclusion criteria were: (1) non-SDB primary indication for AT including tonsillitis or recurrent streptococcal pharyngitis and (2) presence of other known airway disorders such as laryngomalacia, subglottic stenosis, or tracheobronchomalacia. Patients were divided into two groups: patients seen from September 1, 2010 to September 30, 2011 (prior to publication of 2011 AAO-HNS guideline) and patients seen from October 1, 2015 to October 18, 2016 (after publication of 2011 AAO-HNS guideline). The electronic medical record (Epic Systems, Verona, Wisconsin, United States) was reviewed for demographic, insurance, comorbidity, Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire (PSQ), and PSG data. Demographic variables included age, which was grouped into age less than 3 and age greater than or equal to 3, and gender. Insurance types were grouped into Oregon Medicaid, Washington Medicaid or other, commercial, or none. Comorbidities assessed included neuromuscular disorder, craniofacial anomaly, Down syndrome, asthma, and congenital heart disease. Obesity was not assessed in this study due to a large proportion of patients with incomplete height and weight data in the electronic medical record. There were no patients meeting study criteria with mucopolysaccharidosis or sickle cell disease. Positive screen on PSQ was defined as a score greater than 0.33. The electronic medical record was reviewed for PSG tests ordered before and after each patient was seen in our pediatric otolaryngology clinic. Bivariate analysis using Student’s t-test for continuous variables and Pearson’s chi-square test for categorical variables was used to test for significant differences between patients seen from 2010–2011 and those seen from 2015–2016. Univariate logistic regression was performed on each variable to assess for significant associations with after-visit PSG orders. Variables with associations approaching significance (P < 0.2) were included in a multivariate logistic regression model to assess for independent significant associations with after-visit PSG orders. All analyses were performed with Stata 12.1 (College Station, Texas, United States). RESULTS A total of 1,852 patients were referred to our pediatric otolaryngology

clinic. Bivariate analysis using Student’s t-test for continuous variables and Pearson’s chi-square test for categorical variables was used to test for significant differences between patients seen from 2010–2011 and those seen from 2015–2016. Univariate logistic regression was performed on each variable to assess for significant associations with after-visit PSG orders. Variables with associations approaching significance (P < 0.2) were included in a multivariate logistic regression model to assess for independent significant associations with after-visit PSG orders. All analyses were performed with Stata 12.1 (College Station, Texas, United States). RESULTS A total of 1,852 patients were referred to our pediatric otolaryngology clinic for consideration of AT in 2010–2011 and 2015–2016, of which 1,669 patients met study criteria. Of these, 475 patients were seen for consideration of AT for SDB in 2010–2011 vs. 1,194 patients in 2015–2016. The overall mean age of the study population was 6.8 ± 3.8 years ( ). The mean age was slightly higher in the 2015–2016 group compared to the 2010–2011 group (7.1 ± 3.9 vs. 6.2 ± 3.3 years, P < 0.0001) ( ). The overall proportion of males in the study population was 55%. The majority of patients presented with Medicaid or commercial insurance, though the proportion of uninsured patients increased significantly between 2010–2011 and 2015–2016 (11% vs. 26%, P < 0.0001) ( ). The proportion of patients with craniofacial anomalies in the study population increased significantly from 3% in 2010–2011 to 6% in 2015–2016 (P < 0.002) ( ). The proportion of patients with all other included comorbidities (neuromuscular disorder, Down syndrome, asthma, congenital heart disease) remained stable between the two time periods. Asthma (12%) and neuromuscular disorders (9%) were the most common comorbidities in the study population overall. Approximately 16% of patients presented to our clinic with a history of previous PSG testing, which remained stable over time ( ). However, the overall proportion of patients in which an after-visit, pre-AT PSG was ordered increased from 22% in 2010–2011 to 30% in 2015–2016 (P < 0.001) ( ). The proportion of patients in which a PSG was ordered increased across most comorbidities including neuromuscular disorder (from 38% to 53%, P = 0.13), craniofacial anomaly (38% to 51%, P = 0.42), and congenital heart disease (50% to 53%, P = 0.80), however the only comorbidity for which this was statistically significant was asthma (17% to 39%, P = 0.004) ( ). Interestingly, the rate of testing among children with Down syndrome did not substantially change between the two time periods (56% to 57%, P = 0.94) ( ). In multivariable regression analysis, the only significant positive predictor of pre-AT PSG in 2010–2011 was presence of a neuromuscular disorder (OR 3.00, 95% CI [1.10, 8.06], P = 0.03) ( ). In contrast, in 2015–2016 presence of a neuromuscular disorder (OR 2.54, 95% CI [1.51, 4.29], P < 0.0001), craniofacial anomaly (OR 2.32, 95% CI [1.20, 4.50], P = 0.013), or Down syndrome (OR 3.45, 95% CI [1.54, 7.72], P = 0.003) were all significant positive predictors of pre-AT PSG ( ). Positive screen on PSQ was a consistently negative predictor of pre-AT PSG in both 2010–2011 (OR 0.34, 95% CI [0.18, 0.66], P = 0.001) and 2015–2016 (OR 0.54, 95% CI [0.38, 0.77], P = 0.001) ( ). The remaining covariates included in our model (age less than 3 years, gender, and insurance type) did not have significant associations with obtaining pre-AT PSG ( ). DISCUSSION Previous survey-based studies have demonstrated significant variability among otolaryngologists in adherence to AAO-HNS guidelines on pre-AT PSG. Friedman et al. compared data from surveys of American Society of Pediatric Otolaryngology (ASPO) members in 2004 and 2011 and noted overall increased utilization of PSG for SDB from 2004 to 2011, but inconsistent adherence to the specific recommendations of the 2011 AAO-HNS guideline. A more recent survey of ASPO members in 2016 found that only 21% of members had altered their utilization of PSG for SDB in response to the 2011 guideline. Unlike previous studies that have relied on survey data, the current study provides an objective assessment of predictors of ordering PSG and adherence to the 2011 AAO-HNS guideline at our institution. A prior study from our institution demonstrated an overall low rate of adherence to the 2011 AAO-HNS guideline in the 12 months immediately after its publication, with age less than 3 years being the only positive predictor for pre-AT PSG. Important limitations of this prior study were evaluation of a single time period immediately after guideline publication and inclusion of only patients who underwent AT. The current study assesses all patients seen in our clinic for evaluation of tonsillar hypertrophy or SDB, not only those who underwent AT, and directly compares two time points before and after guideline publication. With this larger and less selected sample, we found

overall low rate of adherence to the 2011 AAO-HNS guideline in the 12 months immediately after its publication, with age less than 3 years being the only positive predictor for pre-AT PSG. Important limitations of this prior study were evaluation of a single time period immediately after guideline publication and inclusion of only patients who underwent AT. The current study assesses all patients seen in our clinic for evaluation of tonsillar hypertrophy or SDB, not only those who underwent AT, and directly compares two time points before and after guideline publication. With this larger and less selected sample, we found significantly improved adherence to the guideline 4 years after publication of the 2011 AAO-HNS guideline compared to immediately prior to publication. Our results demonstrate a significant shift in utilization of PSG in patients presenting for consideration of AT for SDB. Prior to the guideline, the only positive predictor identified for pre-AT PSG was presence of neuromuscular disorder. After its publication, presence of neuromuscular disorder, craniofacial anomaly, or Down syndrome were all significantly associated with pre-AT PSG. Age less than 3 years was not an independent predictor of pre-AT PSG in the current study. Of note, age less than 3 years is not a recommended criterion for pre-AT PSG in the 2011 guideline but rather for hospital admission after AT. An important consideration is that this improvement in adherence may not be entirely driven by the 2011 guideline recommendations but by other factors such as increased access to PSG and a growing body of literature demonstrating associations of severe OSA and comorbidities such as neuromuscular disorders or obesity with increased risk of perioperative complications. − It is worth noting that while our data demonstrates that adherence to the guideline has modestly improved, overall adherence remains low as evidenced by 51–57% rates of ordering PSG in patients with high-risk comorbidities after guideline publication. It is possible that the relatively small sample sizes of patients with neuromuscular disorders or craniofacial anomalies limited the statistical power to detect a difference between the two time periods in simple bivariate analysis. A smaller sample size in the earlier time period may similarly have limited the power to detect significant associations in the multivariable analysis. Examination of the point estimates of association among the comorbidities suggests that while Down syndrome was not significantly associated with PSG testing in the earlier time period, the odds ratio point estimate was very similar to the odds ratio in the later time period, which is consistent with the very similar proportion of Down syndrome patients tested in the two time periods. Taken together, these results suggest that while there was a net increase in the proportion referred for PSG among patients with these comorbidities, the overall increase was modest, and it remains unclear whether this can be attributed to the guideline recommendations or to other unmeasured temporal trends. As with other institutions across the country, a likely significant contributor to low rates of PSG ordering is limited sleep lab capacity with long wait times of up to several months for PSG. , Other potential explanations for overall limited adherence to the guideline include controversy regarding the role of PSG in the diagnosis and management of SDB, , high cost of PSG testing, and use of alternative pre-AT diagnostic tools such as questionnaires or pulse oximetry. , Interestingly, a positive PSQ screen was a strongly negative predictor for obtaining pre-AT PSG during both time periods. Patient history and physical examination have been shown to poorly correlate with PSG results, however more recent screening questionnaires have shown significantly greater potential accuracy in diagnosing SDB. The PSQ questionnaire has been increasingly used in the research setting as a way to systematically screen for symptoms of SDB. Various studies have demonstrated rates of sensitivity for the PSQ ranging from 78% to 85% and specificity ranging from 72% to 87%. – This level of sensitivity and specificity is not generally considered adequate as a clinical substitute for the gold standard overnight PSG in diagnosing OSA. However, the PSG itself has been shown to be an imperfect gold standard, particularly with regard to assessing the effects of SDB or OSA on cognitive, behavioral, and quality of life outcomes. , , A recent study by Rosen et al. demonstrated that PSQ but not PSG data was predictive of improvements in executive functioning, behavior, sleepiness, and quality of life after AT. Potential explanations for our finding of decreased likelihood of obtaining a pre-AT PSG in patients with a positive PSQ include reliance on strong clinical suspicion of OSA in patients who are clearly symptomatic with a positive PSQ screen, and parental desire to avoid delaying treatment in the setting of potentially long wait times for PSG. It is important to recognize that the retrospective and single institutional nature of

Potential explanations for our finding of decreased likelihood of obtaining a pre-AT PSG in patients with a positive PSQ include reliance on strong clinical suspicion of OSA in patients who are clearly symptomatic with a positive PSQ screen, and parental desire to avoid delaying treatment in the setting of potentially long wait times for PSG. It is important to recognize that the retrospective and single institutional nature of the current study does potentially limit the generalizability of its findings. Additionally, the small number of patients with certain comorbidities including craniofacial anomaly and Down syndrome in the pre-guideline group may have been inadequate to demonstrate significance in aspects of the statistical analysis. Another limitation of the current study was the inability to perform a complete multivariate analysis of all recommendations from the 2011 AAO-HNS guideline due to incomplete patient height and weight data and low prevalence of sickle cell disease and mucopolysaccharidosis in our patient population. Additional guideline recommendations for pre-AT PSG in patients with discordant clinical examination findings and reported severity of SDB were also not evaluated in the current study. Therefore, future study with prospective, multi-institutional data would be valuable in understanding the true rate of adherence to AAO-HNS guidelines. CONCLUSIONS After publication of the 2011 AAO-HNS guideline, there was a significant but modest increase in pre-AT PSG utilization in children with SDB and high-risk comorbidities at our institution. Consistent with guideline recommendations, neuromuscular disorders, craniofacial anomalies, and Down syndrome were all associated with increased likelihood of obtaining a pre-AT PSG after guideline publication. However, overall guideline adherence remains low and may reflect limitations in PSG testing capacity.

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Sleep disturbances occur in nearly half of older adults. , These disturbances are associated with cognitive decline, depression, disability, institutionalization, and high healthcare costs, – calling for their accurate identification and treatment. Unfortunately, self-reported sleep may not accurately reflect habitual sleep, leading to missed treatment opportunities or overtreatment with high-risk medications. , , – Polysomnography (PSG), which includes electroencephalography (EEG), is the gold standard for evaluating sleep, but it is costly, burdensome, and may not reflect habitual sleep patterns. – Actigraphy (ACT) is the reference standard for objectively evaluating sleep over multiple nights, but it relies on activity counts to estimate sleep and wake time indirectly. As a result, ACT overestimates sleep time, underestimates time awake, and is less accurate in older adults with sleep disturbances or multiple chronic conditions. , , Thus, tools that feasibly and accurately characterize habitual sleep in older adults are needed to improve the targeting and monitoring of interventions to improve sleep health and prevent adverse outcomes. Recently, new wearable devices with EEG capability have been introduced. One such device is a multi-sensor EEG headband (HB). The HB was validated against PSG in small samples of healthy middle-aged adults (N=25 adults; average age 35 years) and older adults with Parkinson’s disease (N=10; average age 70 years), where it showed over 80% accuracy in both cases for sleep-staging compared to PSG. However, these studies excluded persons using hypnotic medications or with known insomnia or sleep apnea, resulting in diminished generalizability. , A recent study examined the performance of the HB vs. PSG in 62 older adults (average age 70 years), including 12 adults living with dementia, and found the HB to have acceptable performance for sleep-wake classification and more moderate performance for five-stage sleep classification. Average scores on validated sleep questionnaires were in the normal range in this study, suggesting most did not have disrupted sleep. The validity and usability of the HB in a more generalizable population of older adults with sleep disruption is needed, as this group has the highest prevalence of sleep disturbances and is also likely to experience disagreement between gold-standard and actigraphy measures of sleep. In the current study, we compared the agreement of HB-PSG and ACT-PSG in a sample of older adults with self-reported sleep disturbances. Participants wore the HB for up to 7 nights, ACT for 7 days and nights, and completed an in-home PSG. We hypothesized that sleep measures from the HB, measured via EEG rather than activity counts, would have higher agreement with PSG than ACT. We also assessed the feasibility of using the HB in this population. Due to its ergonomic design, we hypothesized that participants would have high rates of adherence to the 7-night protocol and report high rates of usability. METHODS Study Population and Protocol This is a cross-sectional study of community-living older adults in the greater New Haven area of Connecticut. Participants were ≥60 years and reported sleep disturbances, including insomnia symptoms (i.e., difficulties with sleep onset, sleep maintenance, or early morning awakenings) and/or daytime sleepiness (i.e., frequent dozing, needing to nap, or feeling like one could fall asleep easily during the day) at least once a week. Participants were recruited via flyers at Yale-New Haven Hospital-affiliated primary care clinics and local senior centers. We excluded participants with severe cognitive impairment (defined as ≥4 errors on the 6-item Callahan screener), and those who could not converse in English, refused or were unable to consent, lived in an assisted living or extended care facility, did not live within driving distance, or had an unplanned hospitalization in the past month. Importantly, we did not exclude otherwise eligible persons who were taking hypnotic medications or had a known diagnosis of sleep apnea, insomnia, or restless legs syndrome. All recruitment and data collection took place between January 2022 and December 2023. Of the 78 persons screened, 71 ultimately enrolled in the study (5 dropped before the baseline interview; 2 were not eligible [1 had an unplanned overnight hospitalization in the past month; 1 did not meet age requirements]). Among the 71 enrolled in the study, 8 did not complete the study protocol (6 dropped out of the study; 1 had no PSG data; 1 had no ACT data). Two additional participants were excluded due to HB data that could not be analyzed on the PSG night (1 had the HB off head for more than half the night; 1 had a HB recording that started in the middle of the PSG recording). Hence, the final analytical sample included 61 participants (85.9% of persons enrolled). The Yale University Human Investigation Committee approved the study protocol, and all participants provided written informed consent.
