IgG4-Associated Involvement of Salivary Glands IgG4-associated sialadenitis is an autoimmune disease characterized by a massive infiltration of IgG4-producing plasma cells into different organs including the major and minor salivary glands. It more often affects SMGs than PGs, more often bilateral than unilateral glands, and in some cases, all major salivary glands are involved. More than 30–40% of the patients are diagnosed as having an IgG4-related disease present with sialadenitis [ , , ]. The value of ultrasound was investigated in reports published in recent years with characteristic findings described [ , , , , , , ]. IgG4-associated sialadenitis may be considered as a “chameleon” concerning its variability of US findings. In one report, five patterns of ultrasound features were described: superficial hypoechoic, multiple hypoechoic foci, whole-gland heterogeneity, space occupying, and normal echo [ ]. Our experiences in IgG4-associated sialadenitis confirm this variability in US. The tissue texture of the parenchyma can appear hypoechoic only to a slight or diffuse and pronounced extent. It may also sometimes have a coarse aspect, a reticular or even a nodular tissue- or tumor-like pattern. Ducts can be dilated to a lesser or more pronounced extent, but megaducts are also observable ( A–E). As clinical symptoms are often unspecific, a distinct proportion of the patients present with a hard nodule in the submandibular space. In these cases, ultrasound shows changes in the submandibular gland characteristic for chronic fibrotic sialadenitis. The gland is hard on palpation and smaller. The parenchyma appears prominently hypoechoic, but in some cases can also be heterogeneous with hyperechoic reflexes. This constellation of findings can represent the final state of unspecific chronic sialadenitis caused by IgG4-related disease. A substantial part of similar changes observed in the SMG, previously termed as “Kuettner’s tumor” [ ], may in fact be chronic IgG4 disease-related sialadenitis. These pronounced hypoechoic changes may also involve only parts of the gland ( A,B), and then focal chronic sialadenitis must be differentiated. In the latter case, however, the regular gland anatomy and perfusion is unchanged (see above, ). Elastography showed that stiff elastographic changes of hypoechoic areas within the parenchyma, which indicate increased stiffness of the tissue, presumably caused by IgG4-positive lymphocytes, rapidly improved after systemic treatment with cortisone as a sign of recovery of the gland, indicating that monitoring after treatment seems possible [ ]. If US is used in IgG4-related sialadenitis, it is a very useful tool for suspecting this disease, but the final diagnosis can only be made based on clinical and serological findings and on gland biopsy [ , ]. Due to the variable appearance in US, the DD includes the whole spectrum of subacute or chronic sialadenitis with sialodochitis. Ning et al. used two different scoring systems in patients with SS and IgG4-related disease. They reported that scores were higher in IgG4-related sialadenitis compared to SS and that semiquantitative US scoring systems can not only evaluate and quantify the lesions of salivary glands in IgG4-related sialadenitis but also be helpful in the differential diagnosis of SS [ ]. 3.4.5. Sarcoidosis with Sialadenitis Out of the specific diseases with possible involvement of salivary glands, granulomatous diseases should also be mentioned. Sarcoidosis mostly involves bilateral glands and may involve all major salivary glands, but can be only be present unilaterally. Both PGs and/or SMGs can be affected [ , , ]. Salivary gland involvement, also including the presence of Heerfordt-syndrome, is rare. US experiences are rare, and particularly, findings in salivary glands in this disease were rarely reported [ , ]. Ultrasound shows enlargement of the gland parenchyma. Due to the invasion of granulocytes, diffuse or focal slight or pronounced hypoechoic changes are visible, and the parenchyma is heterogeneous with a more coarse than cloudy tissue texture. Vascularity is not notably affected ( A,B). A hallmark of sarcoidosis is lymphadenopathy. Peri- and intraglandular lymph nodes are mostly increased. The diagnosis can be suspected in connection with cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, further clinical signs and increased calcium and ACE levels in serology. DD should include intra- or periglandular lymphadenopathies and lymphoma of the salivary gland. With respect to possible focal changes in the gland parenchyma, the eosinophilic hyperplastic lymphogranuloma (aka Kimura’s disease) should

of granulocytes, diffuse or focal slight or pronounced hypoechoic changes are visible, and the parenchyma is heterogeneous with a more coarse than cloudy tissue texture. Vascularity is not notably affected ( A,B). A hallmark of sarcoidosis is lymphadenopathy. Peri- and intraglandular lymph nodes are mostly increased. The diagnosis can be suspected in connection with cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, further clinical signs and increased calcium and ACE levels in serology. DD should include intra- or periglandular lymphadenopathies and lymphoma of the salivary gland. With respect to possible focal changes in the gland parenchyma, the eosinophilic hyperplastic lymphogranuloma (aka Kimura’s disease) should also be considered, as the latter may also cause focal or diffuse hypoechoic, heterogeneous changes in the gland parenchyma. If subcutaneous nodules, lymphadenopathy, and increased IgE-levels are present, Kimura’s disease should be excluded [ , ]. In focal changes of sarcoidosis, focal chronic sialadenitis must also be distinguished. In contrast to the former, the tissue texture and perfusion is regular in the latter condition (see above, ). In summary, it must be highlighted that the mentioned diseases show some specific, but also less specific changes in US. US can be used to suspect a diagnosis but does not always allow establishing an exact DD. In particular, chronic sialodochitis may be difficult to distinguish from a (low grade) duct stenosis. Focal infiltration in IgG4-related disease and sarcoidosis is another critical point, and both must be differentiated from lymphoma. This has to be finally made by additional blood tests, histopathological examinations, and imaging extending beyond the head and neck region. The possibilities and the limits of US in the described diseases/conditions are summarized in . If the possibilities are considered, US can be regarded as an excellent method for primary screening, for making a suspicion diagnosis, for initiation of further management, and for monitoring in the follow-up of these conditions. 3.5. Ultrasound in Monitoring Gland Function at the Follow-up Examination in Inflammatory and Obstructive Salivary Gland Disease Post-therapeutic recovery of the gland after the treatment of inflammatory and/or obstructive diseases of the major salivary glands can be observed in 85–90% of cases [ , , ]. According to our experiences after the treatment of such diseases, recovery of the gland function can be observed and monitored by US. Hallmarks of a recovery of the gland function are a change in the tissue texture of the parenchyma from hypoechoic to slightly hyperechoic ( A,B). In addition to this, as mentioned earlier, the state of the secretory function of the gland can be roughly estimated after stimulation of the gland secretion [ , ]. If duct dilation can be observed directly after stimulation, it can be assumed that secretory function is present and not seriously compromised. Elastography may also be an interesting tool for monitoring the recovery of the gland parenchyma after the treatment of chronic obstructive sialadenitis [ , ]. Gland atrophy, caused by longstanding inflammatory or obstructive disease ( A), by irradiation of the head and neck region ( B) or by radio-iodine treatment due to carcinoma of the thyroid gland (see above), can be reliably diagnosed by US. Gland atrophy occurs mostly unilaterally, the gland volume is reduced, and the parenchyma has a mixed echogenicity due to fibrous (hyperechoic) and fatty (hypoechoic) degeneration ( A,B). Saliva secretion is not noted or cannot be provoked, and patients do not report relevant complaints. Elastography demonstrated an increase in shear wave velocity within SMGs after radiation of the head and neck region and may be used as an indicator for structural changes indicating gland atrophy [ ]. 4. Conclusions US is a valuable diagnostic tool in obstructive salivary gland diseases such as sialolithiasis and stenosis. The variable diseases associated with sialodochitis cannot always be distinguished with US. Primary inflammatory diseases like crjP, SS, IgG4-related disease or sarcoidosis show some specific features but can also share some sonographic signs. In these cases, the final diagnosis can be made only after the inclusion of an anamnesis, clinical symptoms, and serologic blood tests and by histopathologic investigation after gland biopsy ( ). Nevertheless, in the hands of the treating physician, US may not only be an excellent screening method, but also be used for adequately diagnosing a suspicion and improving further management.

Introduction Oral cancer is a common malignancy worldwide [ ], with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) being the most prevalent type, originating in the squamous cells of the oral mucosa. Salivary gland carcinomas (SGC), although less common, have gained significant attention due to their diverse subtypes and distinct tumor biology [ , ]. Surgical management for SCC typically involves ensuring a margin greater than 5 mm to reduce recurrence. While surgical management for SCC typically aims for clear margins greater than 5 mm to reduce recurrence [ ], the required margin for SGC is more nuanced and depends on histological subtype and grade. For instance, low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma may be adequately treated with closer margins, whereas adenoid cystic carcinoma, known for perineural invasion, often necessitates wider resection [ , ]. Postoperative radiotherapy is commonly used for SCC with high-risk factors such as close/positive margins or lymph node involvement [ ]. In SGC, its use is typically reserved for high-grade tumors, advanced T-stage, perineural invasion (particularly in adenoid cystic carcinoma), or positive surgical margins [ , ]. The five-year survival rate for SCC ranges from 40% to 63% [ ], while SGC has a more favorable survival rate of 86% to 92% [ , ]. These differences highlight the need for accurate diagnosis and tailored treatment strategies for both cancers. Current clinical guidelines recommend using fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) or ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy (CNB) [ ]. FNAC, while non-invasive, often has limited sensitivity (reported ranges from 77% to 86%) [ ] and a high rate of non-diagnostic or inconclusive results (up to 15–20%) [ ] in diagnosing salivary gland tumors [ ]. In contrast, despite its diagnostic superiority [ ], CNB is still not considered the reference standard due to its invasiveness, possible false negatives related to tumor heterogeneity [ ], and concerns, though low-level and controversial, regarding tumor seeding [ ]. Radiological imaging plays a crucial role in the diagnosis and staging of oral cancers. However, preoperative differentiation remains clinically challenging due to overlapping radiological features on conventional imaging modalities such as contrast-enhanced MRI. Both SCC and SGC can present as enhancing masses with infiltrative borders. In particular, infiltrative borders, a hallmark of SCC, can also be observed in low-grade SGCs such as adenoid cystic carcinoma [ ]. Ultrasound provides real-time tumor assessment [ ] but is operator-dependent and limited in evaluating deep tumors or areas like the floor of the mouth [ ]. Therefore, utilizing more advanced imaging techniques to effectively differentiate SCC from SGC is crucial for clinical management. Quantitative dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (qDCE-MRI) is an advanced imaging technique that offers a comprehensive assessment of tumor vascularity and perfusion by providing a range of pharmacokinetic parameters. These parameters are fundamental in characterizing the microvascular environment of tumors, which is crucial for understanding their biological behavior [ ]. Unlike conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which primarily provides morphological information, qDCE-MRI offers a functional assessment of tumor perfusion and microvascular permeability, which are critical in tumor differentiation. SCC is characterized by aggressive angiogenesis, often exhibiting higher K trans and K ep values due to increased vascular permeability [ , ]. In contrast, SGC, particularly adenoid cystic carcinoma, demonstrates lower perfusion rates with potentially distinct kinetic profiles [ , , ]. Furthermore, qDCE-MRI is less susceptible to variability introduced by differences in MRI scanner hardware, scan sequences, and contrast agent protocols, making it a more reliable tool for clinical and research applications [ , , ]. Previous research has demonstrated the high efficacy of qDCE-MRI in analyzing the aggressiveness of SGC [ ]. The technique has also been successfully applied to identify small salivary gland tumors as benign or malignant [ ], providing valuable preoperative information that can guide surgical planning and treatment strategies. Despite the established utility of qDCE-MRI in SGC, there is a relative scarcity of studies directly exploring its application in differentiating SCC from SGC. A few studies have employed DCE-MRI in head and neck cancers [ , , , ], but focused quantitative comparisons between oral SCC and minor SGC using pharmacokinetic parameters remain limited. Therefore, we conducted a prospective study developing a qDCE-MRI-based diagnostic model for SCC and minor SGC differentiation. By integrating functional parameters, we aimed to provide radiologists and surgeons with a non-invasive tool to guide preoperative planning, potentially reducing diagnostic delays and unnecessary invasive procedures. 2. Methods 2.1. Patients This prospective cohort study enrolled consecutive patients who were initially identified based on clinical suspicion (e.g., presence of a persistent oral ulcer, mass, or swelling) and/or radiologic suspicion on contrast-enhanced CT (e.g., a soft-tissue mass with irregular margins and heterogeneous enhancement in the oral cavity), between May 2023 and October 2024. Methods 2.1. Patients This prospective cohort study enrolled consecutive patients who were initially identified based on clinical suspicion (e.g., presence of a persistent oral ulcer, mass, or swelling) and/or radiologic suspicion on contrast-enhanced CT (e.g., a soft-tissue mass with irregular margins and heterogeneous enhancement in the oral cavity), between May 2023 and October 2024. The study protocol received ethical approval from the Institutional Review Board of Sun Yat-Sen Memorial Hospital, Sun Yat-Sen University (Guangzhou, China; Approval No. SYSKY-2023-432-02), with written informed consent obtained from all participants. Inclusion criteria required: (1) histopathological confirmation of SGC or SCC through postoperative specimen analysis, and (2) completion of preoperative qDCE-MRI within 7 days prior to surgical resection. Exclusion criteria included prior biopsy of the lesion, previous chemotherapy or radiotherapy in the head and neck region, lesions with a maximum diameter of less than 1 cm, significant motion artifacts on MRI, contraindications to gadolinium-based contrast agents or MRI (e.g., metal implants), and inability to provide informed consent. illustrates the flowchart for participant enrollment. Out of 70 participants recruited, 11 were excluded. Finally, 59 participants were included in the analysis. Clinical and pathological features were recorded, including patient sex, age, pathological type, differentiation grade, lymph node metastasis, tumor location, and tumor diameter (measured as the maximum diameter on axial T2-weighted MRI). 2.2. MR Imaging All subjects underwent preoperative qDCE-MRI examinations using a 3.0 Tesla Achieva scanner (Philips Medical Systems, Amsterdam, The Netherlands) equipped with a 16-channel neurovascular coil. The imaging protocol, conducted within 7 days prior to surgical resection, comprised standard multiplanar sequences, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), and dynamic contrast-enhanced acquisitions. Anatomical imaging included axial and sagittal T1-weighted imaging (TR/TE = 628/18 ms) as well as axial T2-weighted sequences (TR/TE = 2643/90 ms), supplemented by coronal fat-suppressed T2-weighted imaging (TR/TE = 3000/60 ms), all performed with a 90° flip angle, 220 × 220 mm 2 to 230 × 230 mm 2 field of view (FOV), 5.0 mm slice thickness, and 1.0 mm interslice gap. DWI was performed using a single-shot spin-echo echo-planar imaging (SE-EPI) sequence with the following parameters: TR/TE = 8000/78 ms, field of view = 250 × 250 mm 2 , matrix = 128 × 128, slice thickness = 5.0 mm with 0.5 mm gap, and b-values of 0 and 1000 s/mm 2 . Apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps were automatically generated and used for subsequent quantitative analysis. Dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging employed a 3D T1-weighted high-resolution isotropic volumetric excitation (THRIVE) sequence with TR/TE = 3.1/1.5 ms, 12° flip angle, 230 × 230 mm 2 FOV, and 8.0 mm slice thickness (4.0 mm gap). The dynamic series encompassed 110 phases with 3 s temporal resolution, preceded by T1 mapping using variable flip angles (2°, 4°, 7°, 9°, 12°). Intravenous administration of 0.1 mmol/kg Gd-DTPA-BMA (Omniscan, GE Healthcare, Carrigtohill, Ireland) was performed via antecubital vein using a Spectris dual-head power injector (Medrad, Pittsburgh, PA, USA) at 3 mL/s, followed by 20 mL saline flush, with the entire dynamic acquisition completed within 5.5 min. Post-contrast conventional T1-weighted imaging in axial, sagittal, and coronal planes replicated pre-contrast scan parameters. 2.3. Imaging Processing qDCE-MRI data processing was conducted using the Omni Kinetics quantitative analysis platform (GE Healthcare). To address motion artifacts, non-rigid registration with free-form deformation algorithms was applied for spatial alignment. Pharmacokinetic modeling was performed according to the extended Tofts two-compartment model [ ]. with individualized arterial input functions (AIFs) obtained from the ipsilateral carotid arteries using variable flip angle acquisition. Two board-certified head and neck radiologists (4 and 10 years of subspecialty experience) independently performed whole-lesion segmentation through slice-wise manual delineation of volumetric regions of interest (ROIs). They ensured they remained blinded to the histopathological outcomes when defining three-dimensional volumes of interest (3D VOIs). The ROIs excluded large feeding vessels and areas of necrosis. The qDCE-MRI parameters that were included in the analysis were volume transfer constant (K trans ), reverse reflux rate constant (K ep ), volume fraction of extravascular extracellular space (V e ), plasma volume fraction (V p ), time to peak (TTP), maximum concentration (MAXConc), maximal slope (MAXSlope), and area under the concentration-time curve (AUCt). 2.4. Statistical Analysis All analyses were performed using R software v3.6.0 (R Foundation, Austria). Continuous variables are expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Normality was assessed with the Shapiro–Wilk test. Interobserver agreement for ADC values and qDCE-MRI parameters was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), with consensus values from two radiologists used for subsequent analyses. Univariate logistic regression identified candidate discriminators, followed by multivariate analysis with stepwise variable selection established independent predictors and constructed the final model. Diagnostic performance was quantified by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, including the area under

and area under the concentration-time curve (AUCt). 2.4. Statistical Analysis All analyses were performed using R software v3.6.0 (R Foundation, Austria). Continuous variables are expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Normality was assessed with the Shapiro–Wilk test. Interobserver agreement for ADC values and qDCE-MRI parameters was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), with consensus values from two radiologists used for subsequent analyses. Univariate logistic regression identified candidate discriminators, followed by multivariate analysis with stepwise variable selection established independent predictors and constructed the final model. Diagnostic performance was quantified by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, including the area under the curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and accuracy. DeLong’s test compared AUC differences between clinical information and MRI parameter models. 3. Results 3.1. Study Population A total of 59 patients (36 males, 23 females; age range 29–75 years) were enrolled, comprising 19 with SGC (10 males, mean age 48 ± 11 years) and 40 with SCC (26 males, mean age 56 ± 13 years). SCC patients were significantly older than SGC patients ( p = 0.025) and exhibited higher lymph node metastasis ( p = 0.018, ). Tumor location differed significantly: SCC predominated in the tongue/buccal regions, whereas SGC occurred more frequently in the jaw ( p = 0.004). No intergroup differences were observed in sex, differentiation grade, and tumor diameter (all p > 0.05). ICC analysis demonstrated excellent interobserver agreement for both pharmacokinetic parameters and ADC values (ICC range 0.82–0.94). All pharmacokinetic parameters—including K trans , K ep , MAXConc, MAXSlope, TTP, V e , V p , and AUCt—demonstrated significant differences between SCC and SGC (all p < 0.05), while ADC values showed no intergroup difference ( p > 0.05). No intergroup differences were observed in sex, differentiation grade, and MRI-measured tumor diameter (all * p * > 0.05), suggesting that size alone is not a distinguishing factor. 3.2. Univariate and Multivariate Regression Analyses Univariate logistic regression identified both age ( p = 0.031) and tumor location ( p = 0.014) as significant discriminators between SCC and SGC ( , ). Among the qDCE-MRI parameters, K trans ( p = 0.002), K ep ( p < 0.001), AUCt ( p = 0.006), MAXConc ( p = 0.014), MAXSlope ( p = 0.005), TTP ( p = 0.003), and V e ( p = 0.023) also showed significant discriminatory ability ( , ). In multivariate analysis, tumor location remained the sole independent clinical predictor ( p = 0.014; ), while the qDCE-MRI parameters revealed MAXSlope ( p = 0.024) and K ep ( p = 0.001) as independent imaging biomarkers ( ). and present color-encoded overlay maps of pharmacokinetic parameters in representative SCC and SGC cases, respectively. In the SCC case ( ), the K ep value (1.205 min −1 ) is significantly higher than that in the SGC case (0.967 min −1 ; ). A similar difference is observed in the MAXSlope values (5.702 vs. 3.011). 3.3. Model Performance and Comparison Based on the aforementioned independent predictors, we constructed four distinct models: a clinical model (incorporating tumor location), a qDCE-MRI multiparametric model (integrating K ep and MAXSlope), along with two single-parameter models (K ep and MAXSlope, respectively). As shown in and , the clinical model demonstrated an AUC of 0.747 (95% CI: 0.622–0.873), with an accuracy of 78%, sensitivity of 88%, and specificity of 58%. The qDCE-MRI model achieved superior diagnostic performance, exhibiting an AUC of 0.945 (95% CI: 0.889–1.000), accuracy of 88%, sensitivity of 85%, and specificity of 95%. For the K ep model, the AUC was 0.891 (95% CI: 0.810–0.972), with an accuracy of 76%, sensitivity of 65%, and specificity of 100%. Similarly, the MAXSlope model yielded an AUC of 0.800 (95% CI: 0.688–0.912), accuracy of 71%, sensitivity of 63%, and specificity of 89%. The DeLong test revealed that the qDCE-MRI model demonstrated a significantly higher AUC than the clinical model (0.945 vs. 0.747; p = 0.012). Compared to the K ep model, it showed comparable AUC performance (0.945 vs. 0.891; p = 0.086), while significantly outperforming the MAXSlope model (0.945 vs. 0.800; p = 0.004). 4. Discussion This study suggests that qDCE-MRI holds promise in distinguishing between minor SGC and SCC, highlighting its potential as a valuable tool in oral oncology. Significant differences in pharmacokinetic parameters between minor SGC and SCC were identified, with K ep and MAXSlope emerging as independent predictors for distinguishing the two. Their integration further improves diagnostic performance. Minor SGC refers to malignant tumors originating from the numerous small salivary glands widely distributed within the oral submucosa (e.g., the palate and related subregions), while SCC arises from the squamous epithelium of the oral mucosa. However, preoperative differentiation remains clinically challenging [ ]. First, both tumors may present as submucosal masses with unclear morphological features

SGC and SCC, highlighting its potential as a valuable tool in oral oncology. Significant differences in pharmacokinetic parameters between minor SGC and SCC were identified, with K ep and MAXSlope emerging as independent predictors for distinguishing the two. Their integration further improves diagnostic performance. Minor SGC refers to malignant tumors originating from the numerous small salivary glands widely distributed within the oral submucosa (e.g., the palate and related subregions), while SCC arises from the squamous epithelium of the oral mucosa. However, preoperative differentiation remains clinically challenging [ ]. First, both tumors may present as submucosal masses with unclear morphological features on contrast-enhanced MRI, with the lesion borders potentially being ill-defined, especially when stromal infiltration or peritumoral inflammation is present [ ]. Second, enhancement patterns often overlap: SCC frequently shows heterogeneous enhancement due to necrosis and uneven vascular distribution, while minor salivary gland carcinomas may also display similar heterogeneous enhancement due to the mixture of solid and stromal components [ ]. Third, certain subtypes of minor SGC, particularly adenoid cystic carcinoma, may exhibit infiltrative growth and the potential for perineural or submucosal spread, leading to infiltrative margins on conventional imaging that mimic those of SCC [ ]. Finally, both tumors may show overlapping signal intensities on T1- and T2-weighted sequences, where SCC typically presents with low T1 signal, slightly elevated T2 signal, and variable enhancement, while minor SGCs show near-equal T1 signal, mildly elevated T2 signal, and significant enhancement. This overlap limits the diagnostic value of morphological evaluation alone [ ]. Collectively, these overlapping features highlight the necessity for quantitative functional imaging, such as qDCE-MRI. In the present study, advanced acquisition strategies reported in the previous literature were adopted in the design of the qDCE-MRI protocol to enhance the reliability and reproducibility of pharmacokinetic parameter quantification [ , , , ]. Specifically, during baseline T1 mapping, a multiple flip-angle acquisition scheme using five variable flip angles was applied, which effectively corrects the nonlinear relationship between MRI signal intensity and contrast agent concentration, thereby providing more accurate and robust T1 mapping and pharmacokinetic parameter estimation within a relatively short acquisition time [ , , ]. The temporal resolution of 3 s used in this study represents an optimal balance between spatial resolution and signal quality, facilitating improved image clarity while accurately capturing the hemodynamic behavior of the contrast agent [ ]. In addition, compared with population-based AIFs, the use of individually derived AIFs in this study more accurately reflects patient-specific arterial input characteristics, further improving the accuracy of quantitative analysis [ ]. The significant age difference observed between SCC and SGC patients aligns with previous reports [ ], indicating that SCC typically appears at an older age, whereas SGC tends to occur in slightly younger populations. SCC patients were also more likely to have lymph node involvement, which is primarily due to SCC’s higher local invasiveness. SCC mainly occurs in the oral cavity, where its anatomical location makes it more prone to early spread through the lymphatic system. In contrast, SGC originates in the salivary glands, initially having less exposure to the lymphatic system, resulting in a relatively lower incidence of lymph node metastasis [ , ]. Additionally, tumor location also showed discriminatory value between minor SGC and SCC, likely reflecting differences in tissue of origin. Specifically, minor SGC arises from salivary gland tissue, which is more abundant in regions such as the hard palate and posterior tongue, whereas SCC originates from the oral mucosal epithelium, which is widely distributed throughout the oral cavity (e.g., the tongue, floor of the mouth, buccal mucosa, hard and soft palate, gingiva, and lips) [ ]. In our study, qDCE-MRI parameters, including K trans , K ep , AUCt, MAXConc, MAXSlope, TTP, V e , and V p , demonstrated significant discriminative power in differentiating SCC from SGC. Firstly, the significant difference in AUCt indicates that the cumulative contrast agent concentration in SCC patients is significantly higher than in SGC patients, possibly due to the higher angiogenesis and blood flow in SCC tumors. The differences in K ep and K trans suggest that SCC tumors have higher contrast agent transfer rates and vascular permeability than SGC, reflecting the higher angiogenesis and permeability characteristics of SCC tumors [ ]. The significant differences in MAXConc and MAXSlope further support the conclusion of higher angiogenic activity in SCC tumors. MAXConc reflects the peak contrast agent concentration within the tumor, while MAXSlope reflects the rate at which the contrast agent concentration reaches its peak, both of which are significantly higher in SCC patients than in SGC patients [ ]. The TTP results show that SGC patients have a longer TTP, indicating that the contrast agent takes longer to reach its peak concentration within SGC tumors, consistent with the lower angiogenesis and slower blood flow in SGC [ ]. The differences

MAXConc reflects the peak contrast agent concentration within the tumor, while MAXSlope reflects the rate at which the contrast agent concentration reaches its peak, both of which are significantly higher in SCC patients than in SGC patients [ ]. The TTP results show that SGC patients have a longer TTP, indicating that the contrast agent takes longer to reach its peak concentration within SGC tumors, consistent with the lower angiogenesis and slower blood flow in SGC [ ]. The differences in V e and V p also reveal that SCC tumors have more complex and extensive vascular structures and volumes, possibly due to their higher invasiveness and angiogenic capabilities [ ]. Interestingly, while all analyzed qDCE-MRI parameters showed significant differences, ADC values did not. This insensitivity may be attributed to overlapping tissue microstructures: both SCC and SGC can contain areas of high cellularity, necrosis, or stromal components (e.g., mucin or collagen) that influence water diffusion in complex ways, leading to similar mean ADC values [ ]. Furthermore, the region-of-interest analysis might average out microscopic histological differences that perfusion parameters like K ep and MAXSlope are more sensitive to. It is important to note that minor SGC subtypes (e.g., adenoid cystic carcinoma vs. mucoepidermoid carcinoma) are heterogeneous, and their perfusion characteristics may vary, a factor not analyzed in the current study due to sample size constraints [ ]. In our study, multivariate analysis revealed that tumor location was the only independent predictor for distinguishing SCC from SGC, indicating that it contains a wealth of discriminative information that may overlap with other clinical features, such as age and lymph node involvement, potentially masking the effects of other variables in multivariable adjustments. Additionally, qDCE-MRI parameters, MAXSlope and K ep , emerged as independent discriminators. Although other qDCE-MRI parameters were also significant in univariate analysis, MAXSlope and K ep provided sufficient information in multivariate analysis, rendering the contributions of other parameters insignificant. These findings suggest that MAXSlope and K ep capture key hemodynamic characteristics related to tumor type and remain statistically independent in multivariable analysis. Histopathologic angiogenesis markers most commonly include microvessel density (MVD) quantified by endothelial immunohistochemistry (e.g., CD31/CD34) and VEGF-related signaling. These markers directly measure angiogenic activity and remain important tissue-based indicators in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma research [ , ]. In contrast, MAXSlope and K ep provide whole-tumor functional assessments of contrast agent inflow kinetics and reflux/permeability-related behavior, which are biologically influenced by microvessel density, vessel maturity, and endothelial permeability [ , ]. The Delong test results showed a significant difference between the qDCE-MRI and clinical models (AUC: 0.945 vs. 0.747; p = 0.012), confirming the superior discriminative ability of the qDCE-MRI parameters. This indicates that qDCE-MRI provides a more refined and detailed tumor characterization that traditional clinical predictors might not capture. While clinical predictors like location offer anatomical clues, qDCE-MRI parameters like K ep and MAXSlope directly quantify physiological processes (angiogenesis, vascular permeability) that are central to tumor biology and may not be inferable from anatomy alone [ ]. The combination of MAXSlope and K ep (qDCE-MRI model) provided a higher (though not statistically significant, p = 0.086) AUC compared to K ep alone (0.945 vs. 0.891) and a significantly higher AUC than MAXSlope alone ( p = 0.004), suggesting complementary information from these two hemodynamic parameters. The high accuracy and specificity of the qDCE-MRI model highlight its potential in improving personalized diagnostic and treatment strategies for cancer patients. For example, more accurate differentiation between SCC and minor SGC could influence decisions regarding surgical margin planning, the extent of neck dissection, and the consideration of adjuvant radiotherapy [ , , , ]. Previous studies have explored the application of qDCE-MRI parameters in head and neck tumors, but most have focused on tumor characterization, staging, or treatment monitoring, rather than specifically distinguishing oral SCC from minor SGC [ , , ]. For instance, Chikui et al. studied a cohort of 85 oral SCC patients and found that DCE-MRI pharmacokinetic parameters such as K trans and v e were correlated with clinical N stage, suggesting that perfusion characteristics are linked to tumor invasiveness [ ]. However, the study did not evaluate its diagnostic value for differentiating SCC from other tumor types. Similarly, Guo et al. confirmed that qDCE-MRI parameters, including K trans and K ep , could serve as biomarkers to predict the pathological stage of tongue SCC [ ]. While this study reinforced the value of perfusion imaging for assessing tumor biology, it focused only on SCC staging and did not compare it with other malignancies. Hisatomi et al. reported that conventional DCE-MRI, using contrast index curves such as T max and washout rate (WR), could differentiate benign from

to tumor invasiveness [ ]. However, the study did not evaluate its diagnostic value for differentiating SCC from other tumor types. Similarly, Guo et al. confirmed that qDCE-MRI parameters, including K trans and K ep , could serve as biomarkers to predict the pathological stage of tongue SCC [ ]. While this study reinforced the value of perfusion imaging for assessing tumor biology, it focused only on SCC staging and did not compare it with other malignancies. Hisatomi et al. reported that conventional DCE-MRI, using contrast index curves such as T max and washout rate (WR), could differentiate benign from malignant major salivary gland tumors [ ]. Unlike prior studies that primarily examined perfusion metrics within a single tumor type, our findings suggest that qDCE-MRI may help differentiate minor SGC from oral SCC in a mixed clinical cohort. This observation adds supportive evidence for the potential subtype-specific utility of qDCE-MRI in the preoperative evaluation of these two oral malignancies. Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. Firstly, the relatively modest sample size and single-center design may limit the generalizability of our findings, and external validation in independent, multicenter cohorts is required. Secondly, although significant differences in qDCE-MRI parameters were observed between SCC and minor SGC, subgroup analyses within minor SGC were not performed. Given the biological heterogeneity among minor SGC subtypes (e.g., adenoid cystic carcinoma and mucoepidermoid carcinoma), perfusion characteristics may vary across histologies, which warrants further investigation in larger datasets. Thirdly, variations in MRI acquisition protocols, scanner hardware, and post-processing approaches may influence quantitative parameter measurements. Therefore, future studies should emphasize protocol standardization, inter-scanner reproducibility testing, and assessment of interobserver variability to facilitate broader clinical applicability. Fourthly, whole-lesion segmentation was performed manually, which is time-consuming and may introduce operator dependence despite the use of experienced readers and blinding. Future work should evaluate semi-automated or fully automated segmentation methods to improve efficiency and reproducibility. Fifthly, the high diagnostic performance (AUC 0.945) of our model was derived from the same cohort used for feature selection and model building, without internal cross-validation or an independent external validation set. This can lead to optimistic performance estimates. External validation in a separate patient population is essential to confirm the model’s generalizability and clinical utility. Finally, this study focused on diagnostic performance and did not evaluate the impact of qDCE-MRI–based differentiation on clinical decision-making or patient outcomes. Prospective decision-impact and outcome-based studies are needed to determine the true clinical utility of incorporating qDCE-MRI into multidisciplinary management. 5. Conclusions In conclusion, our study suggests that a qDCE-MRI diagnostic model incorporating MAXSlope and K ep shows promising diagnostic accuracy for differentiating between SCC and minor SGC in this initial cohort. However, further validation in independent, multicenter populations is required to confirm generalizability. With standardized acquisition/analysis protocols and assessment of interobserver reproducibility, qDCE-MRI may serve as a useful adjunct to routine imaging. The potential clinical impact on treatment planning remains to be established, and future prospective studies should evaluate decision impact and patient outcomes when incorporating the model into multidisciplinary management.

chunks.content: Introduction Mandibular third molar (MTM) are frequently extracted due to caries, pericoronitis or orthodontic problems [ ], especially in adolescent patients [ ]. The difficulty of surgical resection depends on the thickness of the surrounding bone, the depth of the impaction, in addition to the close relationship with the second molar and the inferior alveolar nerve (IAN) [ ]. Medically induced injury to the IAN as a result of MTM extractions can lead to sensory deficits ranging from partial loss of sensitivity to complete neurosensory loss [ ], which have been reported in the literature to occur at an incidence of approximately 4% [ ]. This can lead to a reduced quality of life, often accompanied by psychological and social problems [ ]. The largest branches of the IAN are located within the inferior alveolar canal (IAC), therefore, accurate preoperative visualization of the IAN is of clinical significance in reducing the risk of nerve injury in various alveolar surgical interventions such as removal of MTM [ ], which relies on radiological assessment, a common option is panoramic radiography (PAN) [ ]. In some cases where anatomical structures are superimposed, PAN provides very limited information, and 3D imaging modalities are important in most cases [ ]. Cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) has been increasingly used in dentistry since the late 1990s. As a commonly used technique, CBCT can be used to evaluate the three-dimensional structure of the MTM-IAN relationship [ ]. However, the sharpness of CBCT is positively correlated with the applied dose of radiation [ , ]. Cumulative exposure to ionizing radiation can cause damage to radiation-sensitive organs such as the thyroid gland [ ] and may lead to harmful cellular mutations that increase the risk of cancer [ ], such as an increased incidence of meningiomas [ ]. This limits its use especially in radiation-sensitive populations (e.g., young people or pregnant women) [ ]. Some findings suggest that dental radiological applications may account for 26%-32% of all diagnostic radiology-based applications worldwide [ ]. Therefore, it is crucial to find a radiation-free and accurate clinical diagnostic method to more accurately assess tissue diseases in the oral cavity [ ]. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a powerful diagnostic imaging tool that has received a lot of attention in recent years in the field of dentistry because it allows imaging of teeth and periodontal structures in the absence of ionizing radiation [ , ], enabling three-dimensional measurements of the mandible [ ]. Although dentin itself has a low signal on MRI, the position of the teeth can be visualized based on the contrast between the teeth and cancellous bone [ ]. Moreover, conventional x-ray based radiographic modalities such as PAN, CBCT or CT, can show the bony borders of the IAC, whereas the nerve itself cannot be shown. In contrast, some previous studies have shown that MRI can clearly demonstrate the IAN [ , , ], assess the localization of the IAN, and be used for diagnostic or preoperative evaluation of the relationship between the IAN and the root [ ]. The soft tissue differentiation of MRI is superior to diagnostic imaging of mandibular morphology when compared to CBCT, so that potential anomalies or lesions within the surrounding soft tissues can be readily identified prior to surgical intervention. In contrast to CBCT, the clinical application of MRI is not limited by the ALARA (as low as reasonably achievable) principle [ ]. Therefore, patients can use MRI for diagnostic imaging without regard to ionizing radiation, both preoperatively and postoperatively, respectively. However, MRI is still not a routine clinical option compared with CBCT due to scanning time and resolution. Previous studies have made great efforts to reduce the scan time and increase the resolution. Goto TK achieved a resolution of 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7 mm using the 3D fast spoiled gradient echo (QUICK3D) sequence on a 1.5T MRI scanner in 6.5 min. The article mentions that excessive scanning time can lead to motion artefacts [ ]. Chau A reduced the scan time to 4 min and achieved a resolution of 0.8 × 0.8 × 1 mm using the QUICK3D sequence on a 3T MRI scanner [ ]. Two studies by Tymofiyeva O used the 3D modulated flip angle technique in refocused imaging with extended echo train (MX3D) sequence on 1.5T MRI scanners, using a radiofrequency coil, allowed for increased resolution. This resulted in a resolution of 0.78 × 0.78 × 1 mm to 0.8 × 0.8 × 1 mm in a scan duration of 4 to 5 min [ , ]. The article mentions that the magnitude of susceptibility artifacts is related to the type of imaging sequence used, MX3D sequences with a short echo time have been suggested to decrease the severity of the susceptibility artifact [ ]. Deepho C obtained a

the 3D modulated flip angle technique in refocused imaging with extended echo train (MX3D) sequence on 1.5T MRI scanners, using a radiofrequency coil, allowed for increased resolution. This resulted in a resolution of 0.78 × 0.78 × 1 mm to 0.8 × 0.8 × 1 mm in a scan duration of 4 to 5 min [ , ]. The article mentions that the magnitude of susceptibility artifacts is related to the type of imaging sequence used, MX3D sequences with a short echo time have been suggested to decrease the severity of the susceptibility artifact [ ]. Deepho C obtained a resolution of 0.78 × 0.78 × 0.78 mm using the QUICK3D sequence on a 3T MRI scanner using a contrast agent in 3 min 35 s. In this study, some images were affected by the patient’s movement, resulting in motion artifacts [ ]. However, it has been shown in the literature that, in certain populations such as patients with chronic kidney disease and abnormal creatinine values, contrast agents for MRI should be used with caution due to the risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis [ ]. Maximizing image quality without extending scan time, or shortening scan time without compromising image quality, can enhance the clinical feasibility of MRI. Recently, 5T MRI has been introduced into the research and clinical settings [ ], showing better image imaging than 3T MRI in some in vivo studies of other structures [ – ], but studies and reports in the oral cavity are lacking. The accuracy of localizing the IAN prior to surgical intervention depends on the achievable resolution, while nerve identification depends on the contrast of the image. Previous studies have shown that the use of higher field strength MRI can improve spatial resolution and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) to show dental structures with high imaging quality [ ]. Because of the need to observe the direction of the IAC in relation to the MTM from a three-dimensional direction, most of the previous studies have been performed using 3D sequences. QUICK3D and MX3D sequences have been used in previous studies with good imaging results [ , – ]. In this study, we investigated for the first time the effect of 5T magnetic resonance 3D imaging on the identification of MTM and IAN and compared it with 3T MRI and CBCT. Four sequences, T1 QUICK3D, T1 QUICK3D FS, T1 MX3D and T2 MX3D FS were used for quantitative and qualitative comparisons. Materials and methods Study participants This study recruited 16 volunteers (10 females, 6 males, mean age 25.69 ± 2.23 years) who attended the Department of Stomatology in hospital during 2024.3-2025.5 and wanted to undergo mandibular third molar extraction, with a total of 24 MTMs (The clinical trial registration number is “ChiCTR2300074886”. Trial Registration date is 2023.08.18). The volunteers were in good general health, with all the teeth in their mouths (except for the third molar) being permanent teeth with complete apical development, healthy periodontal tissues, probing depth (PD) ≤ 3 mm, Bleeding on Probing (BOP) < 10%, no redness, swelling and pus of the gingiva, normal periodontal spaces, and no bone resorption and root bifurcation lesions. There were no metal fillings, metal restorations or implants in the mouth, no orthodontic braces, and no metal implants in the body. The procedure, exclusion criteria and possible risks of the examination were explained to the volunteers and written informed consent was obtained from each volunteer at least 24 h prior to the examination. The study protocol was approved by the Ethical Review Committee (No. XHEC-C-2023-135-1). No volunteers refused to participate in the study or were excluded due to contraindications. All examinations at 5T, 3T and CBCT were performed successfully and were well tolerated by the subjects without any injury. Image acquisition CBCT Images were acquired using a CBCT (OP 3D VISION, Dental imaging technologies corporation, America), a CBCT unit with a resolution of 0.25 mm, an effective field of view (FOV) of 16 × 10 cm 2 , and an average effective dose of 35 µSv. MRI For each volunteer, MRI examinations were performed using a 5T whole-body ultra-high field scanner (uMR Jupiter, United Imaging Healthcare, Shanghai, China) with a 48-channel head-neck coil, and a 3T scanner (uMR 770, United Imaging Healthcare, Shanghai, China) with a 24-channel head-neck coil. The MRI protocol included four sequences, T1 QUICK3D, T1 QUICK3D FS, T1 MX3D and T2 MX3D FS. Further details of the protocol parameters are listed in Table . Image analysis Qualitative image analysis All qualitative analyses were performed blindly and independently by an experienced dentist and a radiologist. Overall image quality was assessed based on the contour of the MTM, IAN. Image contrast and edge sharpness were evaluated based on the integrity and continuity of the MTM, IAN and cancellous bone. The scoring was performed on a 5-point Likert

770, United Imaging Healthcare, Shanghai, China) with a 24-channel head-neck coil. The MRI protocol included four sequences, T1 QUICK3D, T1 QUICK3D FS, T1 MX3D and T2 MX3D FS. Further details of the protocol parameters are listed in Table . Image analysis Qualitative image analysis All qualitative analyses were performed blindly and independently by an experienced dentist and a radiologist. Overall image quality was assessed based on the contour of the MTM, IAN. Image contrast and edge sharpness were evaluated based on the integrity and continuity of the MTM, IAN and cancellous bone. The scoring was performed on a 5-point Likert scale (5 = very clear outline, distinct from surrounding tissue, 4 = clear outline, visible border with surrounding tissue, 3 = indistinct outline, border with surrounding tissue can be recognized, 2 = very indistinct outline, border with surrounding tissue cannot be recognized, 1 = outline not visible). Artifacts (mainly motion artifacts) were also scored (5 = no artefacts, 4 = slight artefacts, 3 = moderate artefacts but sufficient for clinical use, 2 = substantial artefacts, 1 = severe artefacts that prevent diagnosis). Quantitative image analysis A dentist and a radiologist worked together to place region of interest (ROI) on the following structures: dentin, cancellous bone, IAN. The results of the dentin represented the teeth. To minimize spatial variation, the ROI were of the same size on the same structure. Regarding the calculation of the SNR, dentin was performed in the sagittal section, the results were averaged for 37, 38, 47 and 48 (missing teeth were not counted in the values). Cancellous bone was taken in the sagittal section at the corresponding positions of 37, 38, 47 and 48 apices, and the results were averaged. For IAN, the average of the results of the segments 37, 38, 47 and 48 was taken in the sagittal section. All images were placed in the same position to avoid the error of including confusing structures. SNR was calculated according to the following equation: where SI ( tissue ) represents the mean signal intensity of the measured tissue and SD ( air ) is the standard deviation of noise intensity in the background area. It is worth noting that the SNR calculation using the above method relies on two key assumptions: (1) The background noise is spatially uniform; (2) The background noise follows a Rayleigh distribution. However, performing direct and accurate SNR measurements in dental imaging of volunteers is extremely challenging. Therefore, we conducted phantom experiments, and employed the difference method to quantify the system’s relative inherent SNR performance (SNR diff ) [ ]. SNR diff is calculated by determining the ratio of the mean value of the sum image to the standard deviation of the difference image for signal intensities (SI(t 1 ), SI(t 2 )) of two phantom scans within a specific ROI, then dividing by √2. We provided theoretical prediction and methodological validation for comparing SNR of human teeth through the phantom experiments. Regarding the calculation of the contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), the display effect of MTM was based on the contrast between dentin and the surrounding cancellous bone, and the display effect of IAN was based on the contrast between IAN and the surrounding cancellous bone. CNR was calculated according to the following equation: where SI ( surrounding tissue ) represents the mean signal intensity of the surrounding contrasting tissue used as reference. Statistical analyses The Cohen’s Kappa was used to quantify the inter-observer agreement and intra-observer concordance of the qualitative scores. And the intra-class coefficients (ICCs) were calculated to quantify the inter-observer agreement and intra-observer concordance of the SNR and CNR measurements. The agreements were interpreted as excellent for Kappa/ICCs = 0.8-1.0, substantial for Kappa/ICCs = 0.6–0.8, moderate for Kappa/ICCs = 0.4–0.6, fair for Kappa/ICCs = 0.2–0.4, and poor for Kappa/ICCs < 0.2. The non-parametric tests including Wilcoxon signed-rank test and Friedman test were carried out to compare the qualitative assessments of 3T, 5T and CBCT. The Shapiro-Wilk test was used to test the normality of SNR and CNR measurements. And the paired T-test was applied to assess the differences in SNR and CNR between 3T and 5T. The pairwise Games-Howell post-hoc test was performed to compare the qualitative ratings, SNR and CNR between different sequences at 5T. A p value of less than 0.05 indicates significant differences. All the statistical analyses were performed using Python (version 3.8). Results The consistency assessments showed good inter- and intra-observer agreements, with Kappa values ranging from 0.590 to 1.000 ( p < 0.001) for qualitative analyses and ICC values ranging from 0.645 to 0.991 ( p < 0.05) for quantitative analyses, as detailed in the Supplementary Material. The averages of the scores and measurements from both evaluators across the two assessments were used for subsequent analyses. Comparison of 5T MRI and 3T MRI Both

and CNR between different sequences at 5T. A p value of less than 0.05 indicates significant differences. All the statistical analyses were performed using Python (version 3.8). Results The consistency assessments showed good inter- and intra-observer agreements, with Kappa values ranging from 0.590 to 1.000 ( p < 0.001) for qualitative analyses and ICC values ranging from 0.645 to 0.991 ( p < 0.05) for quantitative analyses, as detailed in the Supplementary Material. The averages of the scores and measurements from both evaluators across the two assessments were used for subsequent analyses. Comparison of 5T MRI and 3T MRI Both qualitative and quantitative analyses revealed consistent advantages of 5T MRI over 3T MRI across all evaluated sequences (Tables and ). Qualitatively, 5T MRI exhibited superior overall image quality, contrast, edge sharpness and fewer artifacts (all p < 0.05). Quantitatively, SNR and CNR for all analyzed structures were significantly higher at 5T than at 3T across all four sequences (all p < 0.001). Phantom experiments further substantiated these findings. The SNR diff values for the 5T MRI across the four sequences—T1 QUICK3D, T1 QUICK3D FS, T1 MX3D and T2 MX3D FS—were 164.00, 191.91, 238.76, 205.31, respectively. In comparison, the corresponding values for the 3T MRI were 81.15, 60.63, 113.19, and 104.10. Thus, the intrinsic SNR gain coefficients of the 5T system relative to the 3T system were 2.02, 3.17, 2.11, 1.97, respectively. The apparent SNR improvements observed in vivo aligned with these intrinsic SNR gains. Furthermore, 5T MRI achieved significantly shorter scan times across all four sequences, with reductions ranging from 35.27% to 63.07% (parameters shown in Table ). Comparison of 3T MRI and CBCT According to the data in Table , CBCT demonstrated significantly better performance than 3T MRI across all four sequences in terms of overall image quality, contrast, artifact control, and edge sharpness (all p < 0.05). This indicates a substantial performance gap between 3T MRI and CBCT for 3D imaging of impacted teeth. Comparison of 5T MRI and CBCT As shown in Table , the comparison between 5T MRI and CBCT yielded more nuanced results. In terms of overall image quality, the T1 MX3D sequence performed equivalently to CBCT (4.56 ± 0.46 vs. 4.56 ± 0.46, p = 1.0). Regarding contrast, all four 5T MRI sequences achieved results comparable to CBCT ( p > 0.05), with the T1 MX3D sequence even scoring significantly higher than CBCT (4.56 ± 0.46 vs. 4.13 ± 0.45, p = 0.019). However, CBCT remained superior in controlling artifacts ( p < 0.001). For edge sharpness, both the T1 MX3D and T1 QUICK3D FS sequences were not statistically different from CBCT (4.61 ± 0.44 / 4.39 ± 0.46 vs. 4.59 ± 0.44, p = 1.0 and p = 0.085, respectively). In summary, the T1 MX3D sequence on 5T had comparable results to CBCT in MTM and IAN imaging, with overall image quality and edge sharpness comparable to CBCT scores, contrast superior to CBCT, but artefact score was inferior to those of CBCT. Inter-sequence comparison for 5T MRI Further analysis was conducted to compare the four sequences performed on the 5T MRI. Refer to Table for specific data. Qualitatively, the T1 MX3D sequence received the highest scores across all metrics (overall image quality, contrast, edge sharpness and artifacts), though it did not differ significantly from the T1 QUICK3D FS sequence, identifying these two as the top-performing sequences in subjective assessment. Quantitative analysis provided complementary insights. The CNR between dentin and cancellous bone, indicative of MTM visibility, was highest for T1 MX3D (72.68 ± 1.35), followed by T1 QUICK3D (58.52 ± 2.00), T2 MX3D FS (23.65 ± 1.35), and T1 QUICK3D FS (22.06 ± 0.87) ( p < 0.05), confirming the superior contrast of T1 MX3D for MTM imaging. For IAN visibility, characterized by the CNR between IAN and cancellous bone, the order was T1 QUICK3D FS (74.82 ± 3.23) > T2 MX3D FS (53.81 ± 2.55) > T1 MX3D (45.62 ± 1.79) > T1 QUICK3D (14.83 ± 0.92) ( p < 0.001), establishing T1 QUICK3D FS as the most suitable sequence for IAN visualization. Based on the inter-sequence comparisons, a streamlined clinical imaging protocol is suggested. For comprehensive evaluation of both MTM and IAN using 5T MRI, employing only the T1 MX3D and T1 QUICK3D FS sequences is sufficient to ensure high imaging quality for both structures while minimizing total scan time. Discussion This pilot study aimed to evaluate the performance of 5T MRI for 3D imaging of impacted MTM and IAN, comparing it against both 3T MRI and CBCT (Fig. ). Additionally, we sought to identify the most effective imaging sequences for these structures on 5T MRI. Although CBCT allows the acquisition of 3D high-resolution images [ ], the contrast between nerves and their surrounding tissue (cancellous bone) is inherently weak. This is

using 5T MRI, employing only the T1 MX3D and T1 QUICK3D FS sequences is sufficient to ensure high imaging quality for both structures while minimizing total scan time. Discussion This pilot study aimed to evaluate the performance of 5T MRI for 3D imaging of impacted MTM and IAN, comparing it against both 3T MRI and CBCT (Fig. ). Additionally, we sought to identify the most effective imaging sequences for these structures on 5T MRI. Although CBCT allows the acquisition of 3D high-resolution images [ ], the contrast between nerves and their surrounding tissue (cancellous bone) is inherently weak. This is a direct result of the sensitivity of CT to varying radiation absorption rates. The CBCT signal depends on the attenuation of the tissue to the incident x-ray beam. The imaging representation of the IAN is radiolucent and is only indirectly demonstrated by outlining the cortical borders of the IAC on CBCT scans [ ]. The appearance of the IAC is determined by the density of trabeculae in the mandible, and when the trabeculae of the mandible are sparse the x-rays do not visibly show the IAC [ ]. Moreover, CT has limitations in the visibility of the IAC. In previous reports, the percentage of visible IAC ranged from 42% to 92% [ – ]. In contrast, MRI provides better soft tissue differentiation. Eggers [ ] evaluated the ability of different MRI sequences to depict the IAN at a field strength of 1.5T. The use of MRI in visualizing MTM and IAN has been attempted in a number of previous studies, demonstrating the accuracy of MRI compared to CT images [ , – ]. Goto reported that QUICK3D images on 1.5T MRI can clearly show the structure of the mandible [ ]. Kreutner used T1 QUICK3D and T1 MX3D sequences on 1.5T MRI for comparison and showed that both sequences resulted in good high-resolution images and could be used for precise positioning of the IAN. The image quality of both sequences was very good and the high resolution allowed visualization of small anatomical details. The course of the IAN can be followed from the mental foramen to the mandibular foramen without interruption [ ]. Tymofiyeva used the MX3D sequence on 1.5T MRI to show that MRI can be used for 3D localization of impacted teeth in children and adults [ ]. Another of their studies showed that MRI is a well-tolerated imaging modality to diagnose dental anomalies in children and is particularly suitable for repeat examinations in children [ ]. Chau used T1 QUICK3D FS sequences on 3T MRI and CBCT for comparison, and the results of their study showed that MRI can perform structural identification of IAN well, with a significantly lower variance of the evaluator than the CBCT images, and can be used to identify IAN that are not detected in CBCT images [ ]. Wanner used the MX3D sequence on 3T MRI to show that the soft tissue image provided by MRI can be combined with the high resolution display of the alveolar bone provided by CBCT to optimize imaging results [ ]. However, so far, this part of the study is still relatively small and mainly focused on 1.5T MRI and 3T MRI, and the results cannot be directly applied to 5T MRI. Deepho used the QUICK3D sequence on 3T MRI which was shown to accurately depict the IAN. When CT does not depict the IAN well, they can suggest MRI [ ] which uses an enhancement protocol with Gd injection. Our pilot study demonstrated that T1 MX3D sequences of 5T MRI achieves imaging capability comparable to CBCT for visualizing oral structures such as the MTM and IAN, without the need for contrast agents or exposing patients to ionizing radiation (Fig. ). Moreover, compared to 3T MRI, the 5T system provides shorter imaging times, higher SNR and CNR, as well as superior overall image quality, underscoring its high clinical value. A critical aspect of our study was the intra-system comparison of sequences on the 5T scanner. We found that for the visibility comparison of MTM (Fig. ), two sequences, T1 MX3D and T1 QUICK3D were optimal. This may be due to the better visualization of hard tissues in the T1 sequence, in which the bone cancellous shows as a higher signal, contrasting well with the lower signal of dentin. In contrast, the visibility of the IAN (Fig. ) was better with the T1 QUICK3D FS and T2 MX3D FS sequences. In these fat-suppressed sequences, the bone cancellous signal is lower, which forms a good contrast with the higher signal of the IAN. The bifid mandibular canal (BiMC) is even clearly visible on 5T MRI, which is superior to CBCT (Fig. ). Therefore, for a comprehensive evaluation of both MTM and IAN, we recommend a protocol utilizing the

in the T1 sequence, in which the bone cancellous shows as a higher signal, contrasting well with the lower signal of dentin. In contrast, the visibility of the IAN (Fig. ) was better with the T1 QUICK3D FS and T2 MX3D FS sequences. In these fat-suppressed sequences, the bone cancellous signal is lower, which forms a good contrast with the higher signal of the IAN. The bifid mandibular canal (BiMC) is even clearly visible on 5T MRI, which is superior to CBCT (Fig. ). Therefore, for a comprehensive evaluation of both MTM and IAN, we recommend a protocol utilizing the T1 MX3D and T1 QUICK3D FS sequences to ensure high-quality visualization of both structures while maintaining a clinically acceptable total scan time. However, there are limitations to this study. First, it is difficult to ensure that 3T MRI and 5T MRI use the exact the identical software platform and phased array coils, which makes it challenging to compare image quality and SNR across devices. Nevertheless, the apparent SNR ratio between 5T and 3T was qualitatively consistent with the inherent gain observed in our phantom experiments. This consistency indicated that the observed SNR improvement in images primarily stemmed from the higher inherent SNR capability of 5T. Therefore, the inherent SNR advantage provided by 5T (as demonstrated by phantom experiments) translated directly into perceptible improvements in image quality during in vivo dental imaging. Second, the relatively small study population does not preclude selection bias. This is primarily because our study imaged two MRIs (5T and 3T) and CBCT simultaneously, and four sequences were selected for each MRI, with long overall scanning time for a single volunteer, limiting our ability to expand the sample size. Subsequent studies will prioritize patients with confirmed IAN proximity, bifid canals, or pericoronal pathology to validate the diagnostic value of 5T MRI in challenging scenarios. Third, although 5T MRI has significantly reduced scanning time compared to 3T MRI, it still has a longer scanning time compared to CBCT imaging. Future research could focus on the development and use of oral-specific coils [ ], as well as the construction of a specialized MRI dental imaging system [ ] to reduce the cost of imaging and further improve the scanning resolution of 5T MRI in the oral cavity, while shortening the scanning time and reducing the artefacts. Conclusions In conclusion, 5T MRI poses as a powerful and reliable complement to current imaging techniques for third molar extraction. It offers high clinical utility by enabling non-invasive assessment without exposure to ionizing radiation, which helps to minimize radiation hazards in dental clinics. chunks.content: Introduction Laryngeal cancer is a common type of head and neck cancer, responsible for 1.1% of all cancer cases and 0.6% of cancer-related deaths. Laryngeal cancer is aggressive, has a poor prognosis, and is invasive, with a five-year overall survival rate of 61.6%. Approximately 98% of laryngeal cancers are squamous cell carcinomas . Early diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment are of critical importance for survival in LC . Despite the treatment approaches and therapeutics developed in the last decade, a 23% increase in laryngeal cancer cases has been observed , . Therefore, designing new therapeutic strategies in laryngeal cancer is of great importance. Phytochemicals obtained from plants have significant potential in the development of preventive and/or therapeutic agents for chronic, complex, infectious, inflammatory and metabolic diseases . Phytochemical studies constitute an important part of pharmacology and are very important for the discovery of new pharmacophores . Artocarpus lakoocha Roxb. ( Monkeyjack , A. lakoocha , A. lacucha Buch.-Ham , AL ), referred as “lakuchi” in India, “lokhat” in Thailand and “tampang” in Malaysia, is well known for its wood and edible fruits due to its excellent nutraceutical properties . Along with lectins, flavonols, glycosides, the main active ingredient of AL is oxyresveratrol, a polyphenolic stilbene found predominantly in the heartwood of the plant. AL is characterized by high oxyresveratrol (2,3′,4,5′-tetrahydroxystilbene) content, low molecular weight, non-toxicity and good lipo-solubility, and can easily cross the blood brain barrier – . Many bioactive properties of AL such as antihelmintic, anticancer, antidiabetic, antityrosinase, antitubercular, antifungal, antiplatelet, antiarthritic, antibacterial, antiviral, antioxidant, cytotoxicity, anti-inflammatory, and melanogenesis inhibitory have been reported – . Considering the current literature review, the various bioactive properties of AL can complement current therapeutic strategies to combat laryngeal cancer and reduce the disadvantages of current approaches , , . Therefore, the aim of our study was to evaluate the total phenolic amount, antioxidant capacity, cytotoxic potential, antiproliferative, proapoptotic and antimigratory effects of AL on human laryngeal cancer (Hep-2, SCC-90) and Detroit-551 fibroblast cell lines. Materials and methods The total phenolic compound (TPC) amount of <italic toggle="yes">Artocarpus lakoocha</italic> Roxb A commercial ethanol extract of AL heartwood (ARTONOX ® ) was used in this study. The extract (Product Code: 0102; Batch No.: S200119) was supplied by Sabinsa Corporation/Sami Labs Limited, Bangalore, India. It was prepared from wood with an extraction ratio of 200:1 using ethanol as the extraction solvent and standardized to contain 95.1% oxyresveratrol (w/w, HPLC). The amount of TPC in the AL ethanol extract was determined by the gallic acid equivalent (GAE) species per dry weight by “Folin-Ciocalteu” method. The 100 µL of extract was mixed with deionized water (100 µL) and 200 µL of 10% (v/v) Folin-Ciocalteu reagent, followed by the addition of 100 µL of 7.5% (w/v) Na 2 CO 3 solution was added. After 30 min incubation at 40 °C, the absorbance of the samples was measured by spectrophotometer at 760 nm wavelength. A calibration curve was prepared using gallic acid (GA) standards (0–200 µg/mL) to quantify the TPC. The results were expressed as mg of GAE per gram of dry extract and all measurements were performed in triplicate . The antioxidant capacity of <italic toggle="yes">Artocarpus lakoocha</italic> Roxb The antioxidant activity of AL extract was evaluated by the DPPH radical scavenging assay. The extract of AL at different concentrations (7.8–1000 µg/mL) was mixed with 100 µM DPPH solution prepared in methanol and incubated for 30 min at room temperature. The absorbance was measured at 517 nm. Absorbance was also measured for a solvent blank containing DPPH solution without extract. BHT, GA and ascorbic acid were used as positive controls. The extract concentration required to reduce 50% of DPPH free radicals (IC₅₀) was determined by nonlinear regression analysis. The percentage of DPPH radical scavenging activity (% inhibition) was calculated using the following equation: 1 where Abscontrol​ is the absorbance of the DPPH solution without extract and Abssample​ is the absorbance of the reaction mixture containing the extract. All measurements were performed in triplicate. Cell culture and conditions HEp-2, SCC-90 cancer cell lines (at the 20th-25th passages), along with the Detroit 551 normal human fibroblast cell line (at the 10th-15th passages) were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). The characteristics of the cell lines were summarized in Table . HEp-2 cells were maintained in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM, Sigma-Aldrich, Germany), whereas SCC-90 and Detroit 551 cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium (Sigma-Aldrich, Germany) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Hyclone, GE Healthcare, USA), 1% Penicillin (100 U/mL)-Streptomycin (100 µg/mL) (Hyclone, GE Healthcare, USA) and 1% mL L-Glutamin (Hyclone, GE Healthcare, USA). Discussion This study revealed that AL increased the expression of pro-apoptotic CASP-3 and BAX genes at mRNA and protein levels, decreased the expression of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 and reduced the survival, proliferation, and migratory behavior of cancer cells in squamous cell laryngeal cancer. Therefore, this study provides initial in-vitro evidence regarding the potential anticancer effects of AL in laryngeal cancer. However, the effective compounds and underlying mechanisms remain to be fully clarified. Analyzing the phytochemical compositions of AL and identifying the molecule(s) responsible for anticancer activity may contribute to the observed in-vitro antimigratory effects. These results suggest that AL , the main source of oxyresveratrol, a natural compound with high phenolic content, antioxidant capacity, and anticancer activity, represents a promising candidate for further investigation for laryngeal cancer, providing a basis for the development of improved treatment strategies. Natural products and plant extracts have been applied in traditional medicine for centuries in the treatment and prevention of diseases and are considered important for the discovery of new therapeutic agents . Phytochemicals obtained from plants are known to play important bioactive roles in antimutagenic, anticarcinogenic, anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic, antioxidant and scavenging free radicals , . AL is a species belonging to the Artocarpus genus of the Moraceae family, which is rich in phenolic compounds including oxyresveratrol, chalcones, triterpenoids, stilbenoids, arylbenzofurons, fatty acids and Jacalin, a lectin . It has been reported that some phenolics in Artocarpus species exhibit anticancer functions against reactive oxygen species (ROS) , . One of the most widely used methods for analyzing the total phenolic content in plant extracts is the Folin-Ciocalteu method. The basic principle of the method is the spectrophotometric determination of the color change caused by the reduction of phenolic compounds in the extract by the reagent . Therefore, the amount of TFC in the commercial extract of AL heartwood obtained with ethanol by maceration was analyzed by the “Folin-Ciocalteu” method. In this study, the total phenol content of the AL ethanol extract was calculated as 541.3 ± 14.1 mg GAE/g. Charirak and Ratananikom (2022) reported that the TPC amount of AL ethanol extract was 423.53 ± 11.48 mg GAE/g . In another study, the TPC amount of AL ethanol extract was shown as 423.53 ± 11.48 mg GAE/g . In a study, it was shown that ethanol solvent can extract oxyresveratrol, an important phenolic compound, from AL heartwood with the highest efficiency by maceration . The amount of TPC in this study is consistent with the range in the literature and may be related to the fact that ethanol, which has a wide polarity range for the extraction of polar or semi-polar compounds, allows the dissolution of bioactive compounds. Cytotoxicity testing is a cell culture-based in vitro toxicity test used to evaluate the health safety of drugs, cosmetics, and food additives. However, this test is one of the primary tests used to evaluate the antitumor activity and drug candidate compounds against rapidly proliferating cancer cells with loss of cell-cycle control . Recently, it has been reported that various bioactive compounds obtained from plants may be potential drug candidates for combating cancer . Artocarpin, an isoprenyl flavonoid from Artocarpus lakoocha , significantly induced apoptosis and decreased viability in non-small cell lung cancer cell lines (A549, H460) via ROS-mediated MAPK and Akt signaling . Lakoochin B , a stilbene derivative found in AL, has been reported to have cytotoxic effects against breast cancer (IC 50 value 3.1 µM/mL) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma cell lines (IC 50 value 6.1 µM/mL) , . In a different study, the IC 50 value of artocarpin, one of the active components of AL , was determined to be approximately 3–8 µM/mL in lung cancer cell lines and it was reported to have strong anticancer activity . AL agglutinin induced the proliferation of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) (maximum effect 1 ng/mL). However, it showed a strong antiproliferative effect on leukemic cells Jurkat and U937 lines with IC 50 value of 13.15 ng/mL and 25.14 ng/mL, respectively . Likhitwitayawuid et al. also reported that 24-phenolic compounds including oxyresveratrol obtained from AL exhibited no toxicity to PBMC, human T lymphoblasts cell (CEM) and monkey kidney cell (Vero) up to 100 µM concentration . Rahman et al. (2017) also showed that oxyresveratrol treatment significantly reduced both human SH-SY5Y and rat B103 neuroblastoma cell viability in a dose-dependent manner . However, oxyresveratrol exhibited very low cytotoxicity to rat fibroblasts (Rat-2), human embryonic kidney cells (HEK293), mouse fibroblasts (NIH-3T3) and PBMCs. Metastasis is an important process of cancer cell migration from the primary focus to different locations and is the main cause of cancer-related deaths . Therefore, increased cell movement and migration capacity is a critical step for successful metastasis and deepening carcinogenesis . The A. lakoocha plant contains diverse bioactive compounds, including artocarpin, oxyresveratrol, and various flavonoids, which have demonstrated significant pharmacological effects such as antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and anticancer activities in preclinical models . Ethnopharmacological studies have shown that polyphenolic components and antioxidants are needed to neutralize free radicals formed during wound healing in a healthy cell . Sintuyanon et al. reported in 2017 that VEGF expression was high in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cells compared to healthy normal fibroblasts, but oxyresveratrol treatment inhibited cell viability and significantly suppressed angiogenesis via VEGF. (2018) observed that oxyresveratrol (25, 50, 100 µM) treatment suppressed proliferation and migration in in vitro hepatic carcinoma line SMMC-7721 and QGY-7701 cells dose-dependently at 24 h using MTT and transwell migration tests .
